                ["Bias $b$", "Shifts the decision boundary away from the origin, so the boundary need not pass through $(0,0)$"],
                ["Net input $z$", "Geometrically: the (signed) distance of a point from the decision hyperplane"],
                ["Activation $f(z)$", "Converts the continuous net input into a discrete class decision (0 or 1)"],
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u1-l2-s2",
          title: "Geometric interpretation — linear separability",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "The equation $\\sum w_ix_i + b = 0$ defines a **straight line** (2 inputs), a **plane** (3 inputs), or a **hyperplane** ($n$ inputs) that separates the input space into two half-spaces.",
                "A perceptron can classify a dataset correctly **only if the two classes are linearly separable** — i.e. some hyperplane can separate them completely.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "widget",
              widgetId: "u1-perceptron-lab",
              title: "Perceptron playground",
              description: "Drag the weights and bias to move the decision line. Try the AND, OR and XOR presets — watch how XOR can never be separated by one straight line.",
            },

        {
          id: "u1-l2-s3",
          title: "The perceptron learning algorithm",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value: "Weights are learned iteratively so that the perceptron's output matches the desired target for every training example.",
            },
            {
              type: "numbered",
              items: [
                "**Initialise** — set weights $w_i$ and bias $b$ to 0 (or small random values); choose a learning rate $\\eta$, $0 < \\eta \\le 1$.",
                "**For every training pair $(x, t)$** — (a) compute the net input $z = \\sum w_ix_i + b$; (b) compute the predicted output $y = f(z)$; (c) compute the error $e = t - y$; (d) update every weight $w_i \\leftarrow w_i + \\eta \\cdot e \\cdot x_i$; (e) update the bias $b \\leftarrow b + \\eta \\cdot e$.",
                "**Repeat** — one pass over all examples is one **epoch**. Repeat over multiple epochs until an entire epoch produces **zero errors** (convergence), or a maximum number of epochs is reached.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "w_i(\\text{new}) = w_i(\\text{old}) + \\eta\\,(t-y)\\,x_i \\qquad b(\\text{new}) = b(\\text{old}) + \\eta\\,(t-y)",
              caption: "The perceptron learning rule",
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "info",
              title: "Why does this update rule work?",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "bullets",
                  items: [
                    "If the prediction is already correct ($e = 0$): no change is made — there is nothing to fix.",
                    "If $t = 1$ but $y = 0$ ($e = +1$): weights increase along $x_i$, raising $z$ next time so it is more likely to cross the threshold and fire.",
                    "If $t = 0$ but $y = 1$ ($e = -1$): weights decrease, lowering $z$ next time so it stays below threshold.",
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "key",
              title: "Perceptron Convergence Theorem",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "If the two classes are linearly separable, this algorithm is **guaranteed** to find a separating hyperplane in a finite number of steps.",
                },
              ],
            },
          ],

      minutes: 16,
      sections: [
        {
          id: "u1-l5-s1",
          title: "Why is backpropagation needed?",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "A single perceptron can only learn a **linear boundary**. Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) stack hidden layers to model **non-linear** relationships.",
                "But the simple perceptron rule does not say how to update weights feeding **hidden neurons** — there is no direct target for a hidden neuron's output.",
                "Backpropagation solves this: it propagates the output error **backward through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule**, to compute $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for every weight — including hidden-layer weights.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u1-l5-s2",
          title: "The chain rule of differentiation",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\text{If } y = f(u) \\text{ and } u = g(x), \\quad \\text{then } \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy}{du}\\times\\frac{du}{dx}",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Chain rule warm-up: y = (2x+1)² at x = 3",
              steps: [
                { label: "Substitute u = 2x+1", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "u = 2(3)+1 = 7, \\quad y = u^2 = 49" }] },
                { label: "Local derivatives", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{du} = 2u = 14, \\qquad \\frac{du}{dx} = 2" }] },
                { label: "Multiply", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{dx} = 14 \\times 2 = 28 \\;\\checkmark \\;(\\text{matches } 4(2x+1) = 28)" }] },
                {
                  label: "Significance",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "text",
                      value:
                        "In a network, the Loss depends on a weight through a chain of nested functions (weight → net input → activation → … → Loss). Backpropagation is simply this chain rule applied repeatedly, one layer at a time.",
                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u1-l5-s3",
          title: "Forward pass and backward pass",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "compare",
              pairs: [
                {
                  label: "Forward pass",
                  left: [
                    "Inputs flow **left-to-right** through the network to produce a prediction",
                    "Every intermediate activation is **stored** for later use",
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Backward pass",
                  left: [
                    "Starting from the loss, gradients flow **right-to-left** using the chain rule",
                    "Computes $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for **every** weight",
                    "Update: every weight is then adjusted by gradient descent",
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u1-l5-s4",
          title: "Complete worked example — 2-2-1 sigmoid network",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "widget",
              widgetId: "u1-backprop-lab",
              title: "Backpropagation lab — walk the exact numbers",
              description: "Step through the forward pass, both backward passes and the weight update of the notes' 2-2-1 network. Change the inputs and watch every gradient recompute live.",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Forward pass → backward pass → update (full calculation)",
              given: [
                "Network: 2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons (sigmoid) → 1 output neuron (sigmoid)",
                "Inputs $x_1 = 0.5$, $x_2 = 0.3$ · Target = 1.0 · Learning rate $\\eta = 0.5$",
                "Weights $w_1..w_6$ = 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, 0.5, 0.6 · Biases $b_{h1} = 0.25$, $b_{h2} = 0.20$, $b_o = 0.4$",
                "Loss $L = \\frac{1}{2}(\\text{target} - \\text{output})^2$ · Sigmoid: $\\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$, $\\sigma'(z) = \\sigma(z)(1-\\sigma(z))$",
              ],
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Forward pass",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_1^{in} = 0.5(0.2)+0.3(0.4)+0.25 = 0.4700 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_1^{out} = \\sigma(0.47) = 0.6154" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_2^{in} = 0.5(0.3)+0.3(0.1)+0.20 = 0.3800 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_2^{out} = \\sigma(0.38) = 0.5939" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "o_{in} = 0.6154(0.5)+0.5939(0.6)+0.4 = 1.0640 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; o_{out} = \\sigma(1.064) = 0.7435" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "L = \\tfrac{1}{2}(1 - 0.7435)^2 = \\tfrac{1}{2}(0.2565)^2 = 0.0329" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Backward pass: output layer",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial o_{out}} = -(1 - 0.7435) = -0.2565" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial o_{out}}{\\partial o_{in}} = 0.7435(1-0.7435) = 0.1907 \\;(\\text{sigmoid derivative})" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\delta_o = -0.2565 \\times 0.1907 = -0.0489" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial w_5} = \\delta_o \\times h_1^{out} = -0.0301, \\qquad \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial w_6} = \\delta_o \\times h_2^{out} = -0.0291" },
                    {
                      type: "text",
                      value:
                        "$\\delta_o$ summarises “how much the loss would change per unit change in the output neuron's net input”. It is computed once and reused for every weight feeding that neuron.",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Backward pass: hidden layer",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial h_1^{out}} = \\delta_o \\times w_5 = -0.0245" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\delta_{h1} = -0.0245 \\times 0.6154(1-0.6154) = -0.0245 \\times 0.2367 = -0.0058" },

                    {

                    },

                "**Translation invariance** — because the filter scans the whole image, the network can recognise an object even after it shifts position within the frame.",

      subtitle: "Controlling output size with zero borders and step lengths — and why stacked small filters beat one big one.",

          blocks: [

          title: "The training loop — overview",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "Training a CNN means repeatedly adjusting every filter weight and bias so that the network's predictions get closer to the true labels. This happens in a **four-step loop, repeated for every mini-batch, for many epochs**:",
            },
            { type: "widget", widgetId: "u2-train-loop", title: "The training loop, step by step", description: "Walk the four stages — forward pass, loss, backward pass, weight update — on the single neuron of Example 5.1 and watch the loss fall as the weights move." },
            {
              type: "numbered",
              items: [
                "**Forward Pass** — push a batch of images through every conv, pooling, and FC layer to get predictions.",
                "**Compute Loss** — compare the predictions with the true labels using a loss function $L$.",
                "**Backward Pass (Backpropagation)** — use the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in the network.",
                "**Update Weights (Gradient Descent)** — nudge every weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss.",

        {
          id: "u2-l5-s2",
          title: "Loss functions",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "**Cross-Entropy Loss** — the standard choice for classification. For $C$ classes with true one-hot label $y$ and predicted probabilities $\\hat{y}$ (from softmax):",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "L = -\\sum_{c=1}^{C} y_c \\log(\\hat{y}_c)",
              caption: "Cross-entropy loss for classification",

              type: "text",
              value:

              caption: "Mean squared error (per-sample form used in the worked example)",

        {
          id: "u2-l5-s3",
          title: "Backpropagation — the chain rule",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "Backpropagation computes $\\partial L/\\partial w$ (how much the loss changes if a weight $w$ changes) for **every weight** in the network, working backwards from the output.",
                "Each layer only needs two things: the gradient arriving from the layer in front of it (the **upstream gradient**), and its own **local derivative**. Multiplying these together (the chain rule) gives the gradient to pass further back.",
                "This is why deep networks are trainable at all — a complicated end-to-end derivative is broken into a **product of simple, local derivatives**, one layer at a time.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u2-l5-s4",
          title: "Worked example — full forward + backward pass for one neuron",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Example 5.1 — Full forward + backward pass for one neuron",
              given: [
                "A single neuron with sigmoid activation",
                "Input $x = 2$, weight $w = 0.5$, bias $b = 0.1$, target $y = 1$, learning rate $\\eta = 0.1$",
                "Sigmoid activation: $a = \\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$",
              ],
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "STEP 1 — Forward pass: compute z",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "z = wx + b = (0.5)(2) + 0.1 = 1.1" }],
                },
                {
                  label: "STEP 2 — Forward pass: apply the activation",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "a = \\sigma(1.1) = \\frac{1}{1 + e^{-1.1}} = \\frac{1}{1 + 0.3329} \\approx 0.7503" }],
                },
                {
                  label: "STEP 3 — Compute the loss (MSE)",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "L = \\frac{1}{2}(y - a)^2 = 0.5 \\times (1 - 0.7503)^2 = 0.5 \\times (0.2497)^2 \\approx 0.0312" }],
                },
                {
                  label: "STEP 4 — Backward pass: apply the chain rule",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "text", value: "We need $\\partial L/\\partial w$. The chain rule breaks it into three easy local derivatives:" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial w} = \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial a} \\times \\frac{\\partial a}{\\partial z} \\times \\frac{\\partial z}{\\partial w}" },
                    {
                      type: "bullets",
                      items: [
                        "$\\partial L/\\partial a = -(y - a) = -(1 - 0.7503) = -0.2497$ (derivative of the MSE loss)",
                        "$\\partial a/\\partial z = a(1 - a) = 0.7503 \\times 0.2497 \\approx 0.1874$ (the well-known derivative of the sigmoid function)",
                        "$\\partial z/\\partial w = x = 2$ (since $z = wx + b$)",

                },
                {
                  label: "The bias, similarly",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "text", value: "A similar calculation gives $\\partial L/\\partial b = -0.0468$ (since $\\partial z/\\partial b = 1$), so:" },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "b_{\\text{new}} = 0.1 - (0.1)(-0.0468) = 0.1047" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Significance",
                  blocks: [

                      value:
                        "The weight moved from 0.5 to 0.5094 — a small step in the direction that would have made $a$ closer to the target $y = 1$. Repeating this **thousands of times, on thousands of examples, is literally what 'training' a network means**.",
                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },

                "**Internal covariate shift**: as training progresses, the parameters of every earlier layer keep changing, so the distribution of inputs reaching each later layer keeps shifting too.             },

            },

                  ],

          id: "u2-l7-s2",

          blocks: [

            {

            },
            {

    {
      id: "u2-l8",
      title: "Dropout",
      subtitle: "Randomly switching neurons off to prevent co-adaptation — and the inverted scaling trick.",
      minutes: 10,
      sections: [
        {
          id: "u2-l8-s1",
          title: "The overfitting problem",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "Large networks with many parameters can end up **memorising the training data** instead of learning patterns that generalise — especially when training data is limited. This is called **overfitting**.",
                "**Dropout** is a simple and remarkably effective way to fight overfitting.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u2-l8-s2",
          title: "How dropout works",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "During training, each neuron in the layer(s) where dropout is applied is **temporarily switched off** (its output forced to 0) with **probability p**, independently, on every forward pass.",
                "A **different random subset is dropped each time**. This stops neurons from **co-adapting** (relying too heavily on one specific other neuron always being present), forcing each neuron to learn features that are useful in many different random combinations.",
                "Dropout can be viewed as implicitly training a **huge number of different 'thinned' sub-networks simultaneously**, all sharing the same weights, and then approximately **averaging them at test time**.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u2-l8-s3",
          title: "Inverted dropout — the scaling trick",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "If we simply zero out a fraction $p$ of the neurons during training, the total signal reaching the next layer **shrinks**. But at test time we want to use the full network (no dropping) — which would suddenly produce a **larger** total signal than the next layer ever saw during training. This mismatch would hurt accuracy.",
                "**Inverted dropout fixes this**: during training, the surviving activations are **scaled up by $1/(1-p)$** (i.e. divided by the keep-probability) immediately after masking. This keeps the expected total signal the same as it will be at test time — so **at test time, nothing needs to change at all**; the full network is simply used as-is.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u2-l8-s4",
          title: "Worked example",
          blocks: [
            { type: "widget", widgetId: "u2-dropout-lab", title: "Dropout simulator", description: "Set the dropout rate, roll a random mask and watch the surviving activations get scaled by 1/(1−p) exactly as in Example 8.1 — then compare with test-time behaviour." },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Example 8.1 — Applying inverted dropout",
              given: [
                "5 neuron activations $[0.5, 0.8, 0.3, 0.9, 0.6]$",
                "Dropout rate $p = 0.4$ (so keep-probability $= 1 - p = 0.6$)",
                "Suppose the random mask happens to drop neurons 2 and 5",
              ],
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Apply the binary mask [1, 0, 1, 1, 0] (multiply element-wise)",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "[0.5 \\times 1,\\; 0.8 \\times 0,\\; 0.3 \\times 1,\\; 0.9 \\times 1,\\; 0.6 \\times 0] = [0.5,\\; 0,\\; 0.3,\\; 0.9,\\; 0]" }],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Scale the surviving values by 1/(1−p) = 1/0.6 ≈ 1.667",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "[0.5 \\times 1.667,\\; 0,\\; 0.3 \\times 1.667,\\; 0.9 \\times 1.667,\\; 0] = [0.833,\\; 0,\\; 0.500,\\; 1.500,\\; 0]" }],
                },
                {
                  label: "Significance",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "text",
                      value:
                        "At test time, all 5 neurons are used with **no dropping and no scaling at all** — the scaling was already 'baked in' during training.                     },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u2-l8-s5",
          title: "Where and how to use dropout",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "Most commonly applied to **fully connected layers**, which hold the majority of a CNN's parameters and are most prone to overfitting.",
                "Used more sparingly (or skipped) in **convolution layers**, since weight sharing already gives conv layers far fewer parameters.",
                "Typical rates: **p ≈ 0.5 for FC layers**; **p ≈ 0.1–0.25 for conv layers**, if used at all.",

              blocks: [

      id: "u3-l3",
      title: "Training RNNs — BPTT & the Vanishing Gradient",
      subtitle: "Unroll and backpropagate through time: the complete BPTT worked example, and why gradients vanish or explode as λᵀ.",
      minutes: 15,
      sections: [
        {
          id: "u3-l3-s1",
          title: "Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT)",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**Idea:** unroll the RNN for all $T$ time steps, which turns it into one large feedforward computational graph — then apply **ordinary backpropagation** to that graph.",
                "Because the same weight matrix (say $W_{hh}$) is reused at every time step, its **total gradient is the sum** of the gradient contributed at every time step:",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial W_{hh}} = \\sum_{t=1}^{T} \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial a_t} \\otimes h_{t-1}",
              caption: "Total W\u2095\u2095 gradient = sum over all time steps (⊗ = outer product)",
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "Each backward step from $h_t$ to $h_{t-1}$ multiplies the incoming gradient by $W_{hh}^{T}$ and by the local tanh derivative — this **repeated multiplication** is the root cause of the vanishing/exploding gradient problem. In the unrolled picture, the loss gradient flows backward through every copy of the network, moving from $h_3$ back to $h_2$, $h_1$ and $h_0$.",
            },
            { type: "widget", widgetId: "u3-bptt-lab", title: "BPTT gradient-flow lab", description: "Watch the loss gradient flow backward from the output through every copy of the unrolled network — one matrix multiply and one tanh squeeze per step." },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u3-l3-s2",

                "Squared-error loss applied at the final time step only (a many-to-one setup):",
                "$L = \\frac{1}{2}\\|y_3 - target_3\\|^2 = \\frac{1}{2}\\|[-0.1790, 0.0788] - [1.0000, 0.0000]\\|^2 = 0.6981$",

          id: "u3-l3-s3",
          title: "The vanishing and exploding gradient problem",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "Look again at Steps 5–6 above: every step back multiplies the gradient by $W_{hh}^{T}$ and by a tanh-derivative factor that is **always ≤ 1**.",
                "Over $T$ time steps this becomes roughly a product of $T$ such factors — informally, **gradient $\\propto \\lambda^{T}$**, where $\\lambda$ reflects the typical size of $W_{hh}^{T} \\times \\tanh'$.",
                "If $\\lambda < 1$: the product **shrinks exponentially** with $T$ — the **vanishing gradient** problem. Early time steps receive a near-zero learning signal, so the network effectively cannot learn long-range dependencies.",
                "If $\\lambda > 1$: the product **grows exponentially** — the **exploding gradient** problem. Weight updates become huge and training diverges (loss becomes NaN / oscillates wildly).",

              caption:

            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u3-l3-s4",
          title: "Standard mitigations",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**Gradient clipping** — rescale the gradient if its norm exceeds a threshold; a simple, effective fix for exploding gradients.",
                "**Careful weight initialisation** (e.g. orthogonal initialisation of $W_{hh}$) — keeps $\\lambda$ close to 1 for longer.",
                "**Truncated BPTT** — limit how many steps gradients are propagated back through, trading long-range learning for stability/speed.",
                "**Gated architectures — LSTM and GRU** — redesign the recurrence itself so that gradients can flow across many steps largely unimpeded. This is the main solution used in practice, and is the subject of the next two lessons.",
              ],
            },

              type: "callout",
              variant: "exam",

              blocks: [

                  value:
                    "Match the mitigation to the disease: **gradient clipping** targets *exploding* gradients (it caps update size but does nothing for vanishing); **gated architectures (LSTM/GRU)** target *vanishing* gradients (they build an additive path the gradient can travel).                 },
              ],

            {

                "**Three gates** (small neural networks with sigmoid outputs in $(0, 1)$) learn **when to write to, erase from, and read from** this memory.",

        },

            {

            },

      id: "u3-l5",
      title: "Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)",
      subtitle: "Two gates, no separate cell state — the complete GRU worked example and the three-architecture comparison.",
      minutes: 14,
      sections: [
        {

          blocks: [
            {

                "GRU merges the forget and input gates into a **single update gate**, and removes the separate cell state entirely — **the hidden state itself carries long-term memory**.",
                "Fewer gates means **fewer parameters** and typically **faster training**, while remaining competitive with LSTM on many tasks.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u3-l5-s2",
          title: "Architecture — two gates, one state",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**Update gate $z_t$** — decides how much of the old hidden state to keep versus how much of the new candidate to mix in. It plays the combined role of LSTM's forget and input gates.",
                "**Reset gate $r_t$** — decides how much of the past hidden state to use when forming the new candidate content.",
                "**Candidate hidden state $\\tilde{h}_t$** — a proposed new hidden-state value, computed using the reset (partially forgotten) past state.",
                "**No separate cell state** — $h_t$ itself is the blend of old and new content.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "In the GRU diagram, the final blend node interpolates between the old hidden state and the new candidate, controlled entirely by the update gate $z_t$.",
            },
            { type: "widget", widgetId: "u3-gru-lab", title: "GRU cell lab", description: "Toggle the update and reset gates and watch the final blend interpolate between the old hidden state and the new candidate." },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u3-l5-s3",
          title: "Equations and their significance",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "z_t = [\\,h_{t-1};\\; x_t\\,]",
              caption: "Concatenate the previous hidden state and the current input (same as LSTM)",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "z_t = \\sigma(W_z z_t + b_z)",
              caption: "Update gate — keep vs replace",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "r_t = \\sigma(W_r z_t + b_r)",
              caption: "Reset gate — how much past feeds the candidate",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\tilde{h}_t = \\tanh\\big(W_h\\,[\\,r_t \\odot h_{t-1};\\; x_t\\,] + b_h\\big)",
              caption: "Candidate hidden state — built from the reset past + current input",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "h_t = (1 - z_t) \\odot h_{t-1} + z_t \\odot \\tilde{h}_t",
              caption: "Final blend — a convex combination of old state and new candidate",
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "info",
              title: "Notation caution",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "The source notes use the symbol $z_t$ for both the concatenated input and the update gate — context keeps them apart. Where they must be distinguished (as in Worked Example 4), the concatenated input is written $z_t(\\text{input})$.",
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "heading",
              value: "Significance of each equation",
            },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**Update gate** — close to 0 keeps the old state almost unchanged; close to 1 replaces it almost entirely with the new candidate.",
                "**Reset gate** — close to 0 makes the candidate ignore the past and depend mostly on the current input (useful when starting a new, unrelated chunk of a sequence, e.g. a new sentence).",
                "**Final blend** — a **convex combination** (weights sum to 1) of old state and new candidate. Like the LSTM cell-state update, this blend is dominated by simple arithmetic rather than repeated matrix multiplication, which is what protects the gradient.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },

          id: "u3-l5-s4",

              rows: [
                [
                  "Undercomplete",
                  "Bottleneck dim < input dim",
                  "Forces compression; simplest, most common form",
                  "Dimensionality reduction, feature learning",
                ],
                [
                  "Overcomplete",
                  "Bottleneck dim ≥ input dim",
                  "Needs an extra constraint (below) or it just learns identity",
                  "Used only combined with sparsity / noise / contractive penalty",
                ],
                [
                  "Sparse",
                  "Penalise number of “active” hidden units",
                  "Adds sparsity penalty (e.g. KL-divergence) on hidden activations",
                  "Learn interpretable, disentangled features",
                ],
                [
                  "Denoising (DAE)",
                  "Reconstruct clean $x$ from corrupted $\\tilde{x}$",
                  "Input is corrupted (noise / masking) before encoding; target is original $x$",
                  "Robust features, noise removal",
                ],
                [
                  "Contractive (CAE)",
                  "Penalise sensitivity to input",
                  "Adds $\\|\\partial h / \\partial x\\|^2$ penalty (Jacobian norm) to loss",
                  "Robust, locally-invariant representations",
                ],
              ],
              caption: "The five autoencoder flavours — a favourite exam table.",
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "warning",
              title: "The overcomplete trap",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "If the bottleneck is as wide as (or wider than) the input and no extra constraint is added, the network can trivially learn the identity mapping — and learns nothing useful. Overcomplete autoencoders are only meaningful together with a sparsity, denoising or contractive penalty.",
                },
              ],
            },
            { type: "heading", value: "Sparse autoencoder — the sparsity penalty" },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "Let $\\rho$ be the desired (small) target sparsity, e.g. 0.05, and $\\hat{\\rho}_j$ the average activation of hidden unit $j$ over the training batch. The sparsity penalty for unit $j$ is the KL-divergence between two Bernoulli distributions:",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "KL(\\rho \\,\\|\\, \\hat{\\rho}_j) = \\rho \\log\\frac{\\rho}{\\hat{\\rho}_j} + (1-\\rho)\\log\\frac{1-\\rho}{1-\\hat{\\rho}_j}",
              caption: "Sparsity penalty — exactly 0 only when ρ̂ⱼ matches the target ρ",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Worked Example 2.2 — Sparsity Penalty Computation",
              given: [
                "Target sparsity $\\rho = 0.05$",
                "Observed average activation $\\hat{\\rho} = 0.20$",
                "Find the KL penalty (natural log).",
              ],
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — First term (penalises unit being “on” too often relative to target)",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "0.05 \\times \\ln(0.05/0.20) = 0.05 \\times \\ln(0.25) = 0.05 \\times (-1.3863) = -0.0693",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Second term (penalises the “off” probability mismatch)",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "0.95 \\times \\ln(0.95/0.80) = 0.95 \\times \\ln(1.1875) = 0.95 \\times 0.1718 = 0.1632",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Sum",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "KL(0.05 \\,\\|\\, 0.20) = -0.0693 + 0.1632 = 0.0939 \\text{ nats}" },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "info",
              title: "Interpretation",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "Since $\\hat{\\rho}$ (0.20) is far above the target $\\rho$ (0.05), the penalty is clearly positive; it would be exactly 0 if $\\hat{\\rho} = \\rho$, and gradient descent pushes $\\hat{\\rho}$ back toward $\\rho$, i.e. towards a sparser (mostly-off) hidden layer.",
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "quiz",
              items: [
                {
                  id: "u4-check-1",
                  question: "What is the primary purpose of the bottleneck (latent) layer in an autoencoder?",
                  options: [
                    "To increase the model's raw capacity",
                    "To force the network to learn a compressed, useful representation of the input",
                    "To add regularisation noise to the gradients",
                    "To speed up training regardless of representation quality",
                  ],
                  correct: 1,
                  explanation:
                    "The bottleneck is narrower than the input, so the network cannot simply copy — it must retain only the most important information needed to reconstruct x, which is exactly what makes the learned code z useful.",
                },
                {
                  id: "u4-check-2",
                  question: "In an undercomplete autoencoder, the dimensionality of the hidden (latent) layer is:",
                  options: [
                    "Greater than the input dimension",

                    "Always exactly 1, regardless of input size",
                  ],
                  correct: 2,
                  explanation:
                    "“Undercomplete” means the code is lower-dimensional than the input — this is exactly what forces compression.",
                },

          blocks: [

                "**Pre-training** deep networks layer-by-layer before supervised fine-tuning.",

    {
      id: "u4-l3",
      title: "Variational Autoencoders (VAE)",
      subtitle: "Make the latent space a Gaussian — the reparameterization trick and the ELBO, derived step by step.",
      minutes: 18,
      sections: [
        {
          id: "u4-l3-s1",
          title: "Motivation: why not just use a plain autoencoder?",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "A plain autoencoder's latent space has **no structure** — codes for real inputs may be scattered in isolated clusters with large empty gaps between them.",
                "If we pick a random point $z$ in that space and decode it, the result is usually **garbage** — so plain autoencoders are poor generative models.",
                "A VAE fixes this by treating the code as **random, not deterministic**: it forces the distribution of $z$ (for all the data) to look like a simple, known prior, typically $N(0, I)$.",
                "Because the whole latent space is now “filled in” and shaped like a Gaussian, **any $z$ sampled from $N(0, I)$ decodes into something realistic** — the VAE can generate new data.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "compare",
              pairs: [
                {
                  label: "Plain autoencoder",
                  left: [
                    "Deterministic code — one point $z = f(x)$ per input",
                    "Latent space full of gaps — decoding a gap point gives garbage",
                    "Optimises reconstruction only",
                    "Compresses and denoises well; generates poorly",
                  ],
                  right: [],
                },
                {
                  label: "Variational autoencoder",
                  left: [
                    "Random code — a distribution $q_\\phi(z|x)$ per input",
                    "KL term shapes the whole space toward $N(0, I)$ — no gaps",
                    "Optimises the ELBO — reconstruction + KL regulariser",
                    "Compresses **and** generates new samples",
                  ],
                  right: [],
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l3-s2",
          title: "Probabilistic formulation",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "Assume the data is generated as: sample a latent $z \\sim p(z) = N(0, I)$, then sample $x \\sim p_\\theta(x|z)$ — the **decoder**.",
                "We want the true posterior $p(z|x)$, but it is **intractable**, so we approximate it with an encoder network $q_\\phi(z|x)$ — this is why the method is called **“variational”** (variational = approximate inference).",
                "$q_\\phi(z|x)$ is chosen to be Gaussian: $q_\\phi(z|x) = N\\left(\\mu(x), \\sigma^2(x)\\right)$, with $\\mu(x)$ and $\\sigma(x)$ output by the encoder network.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "**Architecture (Fig. 3.1):** the encoder no longer outputs a point but a **distribution** — a mean $\\mu$ and standard deviation $\\sigma$ for every latent dimension. A sample $z$ is drawn from that distribution via the **reparameterization trick**, and the decoder reconstructs $x$ from it.",
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l3-s3",
          title: "The reparameterization trick",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "**Problem:** we need to backpropagate through the sampling step $z \\sim N(\\mu, \\sigma^2)$, but sampling is a random, **non-differentiable** operation.",
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "**Trick:** rewrite the random sample as a deterministic function of $\\mu$, $\\sigma$ and an independent noise source $\\varepsilon$:",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "z = \\mu + \\sigma \\odot \\varepsilon, \\qquad \\varepsilon \\sim N(0, I)",
              caption: "The reparameterization trick — randomness moved outside the network",
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "key",
              title: "Why this works",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "Now the randomness ($\\varepsilon$) is external to the network, and $z$ is a **differentiable function of $\\mu$ and $\\sigma$** — gradients can flow from the reconstruction loss, through $z$, back into the encoder's $\\mu$ and $\\sigma$ outputs, and hence into all encoder weights.",
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l3-s4",
          title: "Deriving the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "We cannot maximise $\\log p(x)$ directly (it needs the intractable integral over $z$), so we derive a tractable lower bound on it, step by step:",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "The 4-step ELBO derivation",
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Introduce the latent variable by marginalisation",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\log p(x) = \\log \\int p(x, z)\\, dz" }],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Multiply and divide by q_φ(z|x) (valid since q_φ(z|x) > 0)",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\log p(x) = \\log \\mathbb{E}_{q}\\!\\left[\\frac{p(x, z)}{q_\\phi(z|x)}\\right]",
                    },
                    { type: "text", value: "This turns the integral into an expectation under $q$." },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Apply Jensen's Inequality (log is concave, so log E[X] ≥ E[log X])",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\log p(x) \\ge \\mathbb{E}_{q}\\!\\left[\\log p(x, z) - \\log q_\\phi(z|x)\\right] \\equiv \\text{ELBO}",
                    },
                    {
                      type: "text",
                      value:
                        "**Significance:** this step is what makes the objective tractable — we now have a lower bound we **CAN** compute and maximise, instead of the exact $\\log p(x)$ which we cannot.",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 4 — Factor p(x,z) = p(x|z)·p(z) and split the expectation into two interpretable terms",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\text{ELBO} = \\mathbb{E}_{q}\\!\\left[\\log p_\\theta(x|z)\\right] - KL\\!\\left(q_\\phi(z|x) \\,\\|\\, p(z)\\right)",
                    },
                    {
                      type: "bullets",
                      items: [
                        "**Reconstruction term** $E_q[\\log p_\\theta(x|z)]$: how well the decoder reconstructs $x$ from a sampled $z$ — pulls $z$ toward encoding useful information.",
                        "**Regularisation term** $KL(q_\\phi(z|x) \\| p(z))$: keeps the encoder's distribution close to the prior $N(0,I)$ — keeps the latent space smooth and generative.",
                      ],
                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "**Final VAE training objective (minimised).** Since we minimise a loss rather than maximise the ELBO, we flip the sign:",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "L_{VAE} = -\\mathbb{E}_{q}\\!\\left[\\log p_\\theta(x|z)\\right] + KL\\!\\left(q_\\phi(z|x) \\,\\|\\, p(z)\\right)",
              caption: "≡ Reconstruction Loss + KL Divergence Loss",
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "For a Gaussian encoder $q_\\phi(z|x) = N(\\mu, \\sigma^2)$ and prior $N(0,1)$, the KL term has a convenient closed form (per latent dimension):",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "KL\\!\\left(N(\\mu, \\sigma^2) \\,\\|\\, N(0,1)\\right) = \\frac{1}{2}\\left(\\mu^2 + \\sigma^2 - \\ln \\sigma^2 - 1\\right)",
              caption: "Closed-form KL for a Gaussian encoder against the standard normal prior",
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "tip",
              title: "What maximising the ELBO really does",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "The gap between the ELBO and $\\log p(x)$ is exactly $KL(q_\\phi(z|x) \\,\\|\\, p(z|x))$ — so maximising the ELBO also implicitly makes $q_\\phi$ a better approximation of the true posterior.",
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "tip",
              title: "The weighted form — β-VAE",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "In practice the total loss is written $L = \\text{Reconstruction} + \\beta \\cdot KL$. With $\\beta = 1$ this is the standard VAE; a $\\beta > 1$ (as in the **β-VAE**) weights the KL term more, trading reconstruction sharpness for a more disentangled, more regularised latent space.",
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Worked Example 3.1 — Reparameterization and KL Divergence",
              given: [
                "The encoder, for a given $x$, outputs $\\mu = 0.3$, $\\sigma = 0.5$.",
                "A noise sample $\\varepsilon = 1.0$ is drawn from $N(0,1)$.",
                "Find (a) the sampled latent $z$, and (b) the KL-divergence loss term.",
              ],
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Reparameterization trick (this IS the sampling step, made differentiable)",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "z = \\mu + \\sigma \\cdot \\varepsilon = 0.3 + (0.5)(1.0) = 0.8" }],
                },

                  label: "Step 2 — Compute σ² and ln(σ²) needed for the KL formula",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\sigma^2 = 0.25, \\qquad \\ln(0.25) = -1.3863" }],

                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Substitute into the closed-form KL expression",
                  blocks: [

              type: "callout",

    {
      id: "u4-l4",
      title: "Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN)",
      subtitle: "A forger and a detective: the minimax game, the optimal discriminator, and why training is hard.",
      minutes: 18,
      sections: [
        {
          id: "u4-l4-s1",
          title: "Concept: a two-player game",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "A GAN trains **two networks that compete** against each other:",
                "**Generator $G$:** takes random noise $z \\sim p(z)$ and tries to produce fake samples $G(z)$ that look real.",
                "**Discriminator $D$:** takes a sample (real or fake) and outputs the probability that it is real.",
                "$G$ is trained to **fool** $D$; $D$ is trained to **catch** $G$. Neither ever sees labelled data — the “supervision” comes entirely from this competition, so training is **unsupervised at the data level**.",
                "Unlike the VAE, a GAN has **no explicit reconstruction loss and no explicit density $p(x)$** — it learns to sample from $p(x)$ **implicitly**.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "**Architecture (Fig. 4.1):** the generator produces fakes from noise; the discriminator scores real vs. fake; gradients flow back to train both networks.",
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l4-s2",
          title: "The minimax objective",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\min_G \\max_D V(D,G) = \\mathbb{E}_{x \\sim p_{data}}\\left[\\log D(x)\\right] + \\mathbb{E}_{z \\sim p_z}\\left[\\log\\left(1 - D(G(z))\\right)\\right]",
              caption: "The GAN value function — a two-player zero-sum game",
            },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**$D$ wants to maximise $V$:** push $D(x) \\to 1$ for real $x$, and $D(G(z)) \\to 0$ for fakes.",
                "**$G$ wants to minimise $V$:** push $D(G(z)) \\to 1$, i.e. make the discriminator think fakes are real.",
                "**Training alternates:** a few steps of gradient ascent on $D$ (with $G$ fixed), then a step of gradient descent on $G$ (with $D$ fixed).",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "widget",
              widgetId: "u4-gan-lab",
              title: "GAN training arena",
              description:
                "Step through the minimax game — the discriminator learns to separate real from fake while the generator fights back. Watch the losses, D(G(z)) and the road to the D* = 1/2 equilibrium.",
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l4-s3",
          title: "The optimal discriminator — derivation and worked example",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "For a fixed generator $G$ (hence a fixed generator distribution $p_g$), find the $D$ that maximises $V$:",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Deriving the Optimal Discriminator D*(x)",
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Rewrite the second expectation as an integral over x using x = G(z)",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "V(D,G) = \\int_x \\left[ p_{data}(x) \\log D(x) + p_g(x) \\log(1 - D(x)) \\right] dx",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label:
                    "Step 2 — For each fixed x this is a scalar function of y = D(x) alone: f(y) = a·log y + b·log(1−y), with a = p_data(x), b = p_g(x). Maximise using df/dy = 0",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\frac{a}{y} - \\frac{b}{1-y} = 0 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; a(1-y) = by \\;\\Rightarrow\\; y = \\frac{a}{a+b}",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Substitute back a, b",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "D^*(x) = \\frac{p_{data}(x)}{p_{data}(x) + p_g(x)}",
                      caption: "The optimal discriminator for a fixed generator",
                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "key",
              title: "Significance — the Nash equilibrium",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "At the Nash equilibrium the generator matches the data exactly, $p_g = p_{data}$, so $D^*(x) = 1/2$ everywhere — the best possible discriminator can do no better than a **coin flip**. This is the theoretical training target for a GAN.",
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Worked Example 4.1 — Discriminator and Generator Loss",
              given: [
                "For one real sample, $D(x) = 0.7$.",
                "For one fake sample, $D(G(z)) = 0.4$.",
                "Compute the discriminator loss and the (non-saturating) generator loss.",
              ],
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Discriminator loss (negative of what D maximises — D wants this LOW)",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "L_D = -\\left[\\log D(x) + \\log(1 - D(G(z)))\\right] = -\\left[\\ln(0.7) + \\ln(0.6)\\right]",
                    },
                    { type: "formula", tex: "= -\\left[(-0.3567) + (-0.5108)\\right] = 0.8675" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Generator loss, non-saturating form (used in practice — G wants this LOW)",
                  blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "L_G = -\\log D(G(z)) = -\\ln(0.4) = 0.9163" }],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "info",
              title: "Interpretation",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "$D(G(z)) = 0.4$ means $D$ is already leaning toward “fake” but is not fully certain — both losses are moderate, meaning both networks still have learning signal to improve.",
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l4-s4",
          title: "Training challenges",
          blocks: [
            { type: "heading", value: "(a) Vanishing gradients — why the non-saturating loss is used" },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "The original minimax loss for $G$ is $\\log(1 - D(G(z)))$, minimised by $G$.",
                "Early in training, $G$ is poor, so $D$ confidently rejects fakes: $D(G(z))$ is small (say 0.2). Compare the gradient magnitude of the two loss formulations with respect to $s = D(G(z))$ at $s = 0.2$:",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\text{Original:} \\quad \\frac{d}{ds}\\left[\\log(1-s)\\right] = -\\frac{1}{1-s} = -\\frac{1}{0.8} = -1.25",
              caption: "Gradient of the original generator loss at s = 0.2",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\text{Non-saturating:} \\quad \\frac{d}{ds}\\left[-\\log s\\right] = -\\frac{1}{s} = -\\frac{1}{0.2} = -5.00",
              caption: "Gradient of the non-saturating generator loss at s = 0.2",
            },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "The non-saturating gradient (5.00) is **4× larger in magnitude exactly when G is performing badly** — it gives a much stronger learning signal precisely when $G$ needs it most.",
                "This is why in practice $G$ is trained to **maximise $\\log D(G(z))$** (equivalently, minimise $-\\log D(G(z))$) instead of minimising $\\log(1 - D(G(z)))$.",
              ],
            },
            { type: "heading", value: "(b) Mode collapse" },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "warning",
              title: "Mode collapse — symptom and remedies",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "$G$ discovers a few outputs that reliably fool $D$, and collapses to producing only those — **losing the diversity of $p_{data}$.               items: [

              ],
            },

      sections: [
        {
          id: "u4-l5-s1",
          title: "Entropy — a recap",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "Entropy measures the **uncertainty / unpredictability** of a random variable $X$ with distribution $p$. Discrete case:",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "H(p) = -\\sum_{x} p(x) \\log p(x)",
              caption: "Entropy of a discrete distribution",
            },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**High entropy** = very unpredictable (close to uniform); **low entropy** = predictable (probability mass concentrated on few outcomes).",
                "The base of the log sets the unit: **base-2 → bits, base-e → nats**.",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "widget",
              widgetId: "u4-entropy-lab",

            },

        },
        {
          id: "u4-l5-s2",
          title: "The Maximum Entropy Principle",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "Stated by **E.T. Jaynes (1957)**: given only partial information about a distribution (some constraints, e.g. its mean), choose the distribution that has **maximum entropy while satisfying those constraints**.",
                "**Why?** The max-entropy distribution is the “most honest” / least biased choice — it assumes **nothing beyond what is actually known**. Any other distribution satisfying the same constraints implicitly encodes extra, unjustified assumptions.",
                "This turns distribution selection into a **constrained optimisation problem**, solved using **Lagrange multipliers**.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l5-s3",
          title: "Derivation 1 — no constraints ⇒ uniform distribution",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "For a discrete variable with $n$ outcomes, maximise $H(p)$ subject only to normalisation $\\sum_i p_i = 1$.",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Derivation 1 — No Constraints ⇒ Uniform Distribution",
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Form the Lagrangian",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\mathcal{L} = -\\sum_i p_i \\ln p_i + \\lambda\\left(\\sum_i p_i - 1\\right)" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Differentiate w.r.t. each p_i and set to 0",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial p_i} = -\\ln p_i - 1 + \\lambda = 0 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; \\ln p_i = \\lambda - 1",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Since the right side has no i in it, every p_i must be the SAME constant c",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "p_i = e^{\\lambda-1} = c \\qquad (\\text{same for all } i)" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 4 — Apply normalisation to solve for c",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "n \\cdot c = 1 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; c = \\frac{1}{n} \\;\\Rightarrow\\; p_i = \\frac{1}{n} \\text{ for every } i",
                      caption: "— the UNIFORM distribution",
                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "key",
              title: "Significance",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "With no information at all except that probabilities sum to 1, spreading probability equally is the least-biased choice — this confirms intuition.",
                },
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l5-s4",
          title: "Derivation 2 — mean & variance known ⇒ Gaussian distribution",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "For a continuous variable, maximise $H[p] = -\\int p(x) \\ln p(x)\\, dx$ subject to **three constraints**: normalisation, a fixed mean $\\mu$, and a fixed variance $\\sigma^2$.",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Derivation 2 — Mean & Variance Known ⇒ Gaussian Distribution",
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Lagrangian with one multiplier per constraint",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\mathcal{L} = -\\int p \\ln p\\, dx + \\lambda_0\\left(\\int p\\, dx - 1\\right) + \\lambda_1\\left(\\int x p\\, dx - \\mu\\right) + \\lambda_2\\left(\\int (x-\\mu)^2 p\\, dx - \\sigma^2\\right)",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 2 — Take the functional derivative w.r.t. p(x) and set to 0",
                  blocks: [

                },

                  blocks: [

                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "p(x) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi\\sigma^2}} \\exp\\left(-\\frac{(x-\\mu)^2}{2\\sigma^2}\\right)",

                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],

                },

      id: "u4-l6",
      title: "Restricted Boltzmann Machines & Deep Belief Networks",
      subtitle: "Energy-based bipartite machines trained by Contrastive Divergence — then stacked greedily into DBNs.",
      minutes: 22,
      sections: [
        {
          id: "u4-l6-s1",
          title: "RBM structure",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "An RBM is an **energy-based, undirected, probabilistic model** with two layers (Fig. 6.1 — fully bipartite-connected, no intra-layer edges):",
            },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**Visible layer $v$** — the observed data (e.g. pixel values).",
                "**Hidden layer $h$** — latent feature detectors.",
                "**“Restricted”** means connections exist **only between the two layers (bipartite)** — no visible-visible or hidden-hidden connections. This restriction is exactly what will make inference tractable.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l6-s2",
          title: "Energy function and joint probability",
          blocks: [
            { type: "text", value: "Every configuration $(v,h)$ is assigned an energy:" },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "E(v,h) = -\\sum_i a_i v_i - \\sum_j b_j h_j - \\sum_{i,j} v_i h_j W_{ij}",
              caption: "RBM energy — biases plus a bilinear interaction term",
            },
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "where $a, b$ are visible / hidden biases and $W$ is the weight matrix. The probability of a configuration follows the **Boltzmann (Gibbs) distribution** — exactly the maximum-entropy form derived in Lesson 5:",
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "P(v,h) = \\frac{\\exp(-E(v,h))}{Z}, \\qquad Z = \\sum_{v,h} \\exp(-E(v,h))",
              caption: "Boltzmann distribution with partition function Z",
            },
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "**Significance:** lower energy ⇒ higher probability. Training adjusts $W, a, b$ so that configurations resembling the training data get low energy (high probability) and everything else gets high energy.",
                "$Z$ (the partition function) sums over **ALL possible $(v,h)$** — exponentially many — so it is **intractable** to compute directly. This motivates Contrastive Divergence, which sidesteps ever needing $Z$.",
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
        {
          id: "u4-l6-s3",
          title: "Deriving the conditional probabilities",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "Because there are no intra-layer connections, we can show the hidden units are **conditionally independent given $v$**.",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Deriving P(h_j = 1 | v) and P(v_i = 1 | h)",
              steps: [
                {
                  label: "Step 1 — Regroup the energy so every term involving h_j is collected together",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "E(v,h) = -a^\\top v - \\sum_j h_j\\left(b_j + \\sum_i v_i W_{ij}\\right)",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label:
                    "Step 2 — Substitute into P(v,h) ∝ exp(−E(v,h)); since the exponent is now a SUM over j, the exponential FACTORISES into a product over j",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "P(v,h) \\propto \\exp(a^\\top v) \\times \\prod_j \\exp\\left(h_j\\left(b_j + \\sum_i v_i W_{ij}\\right)\\right)",
                    },
                    {
                      type: "text",
                      value:
                        "This product-over-$j$ form means, given $v$, every $h_j$ is independent of every other $h_k$ — a direct consequence of the “restricted” (bipartite) structure.",
                    },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label:
                    "Step 3 — Each factor is an unnormalised Bernoulli variable in h_j ∈ {0,1}; normalising it over h_j = 0 and 1 gives the logistic sigmoid",
                  blocks: [

                      tex: "P(h_j = 1 \\mid v) = \\sigma\\left(b_j + \\sum_i v_i W_{ij}\\right)",
                      caption: "Hidden unit activation — bottom-up",
                    },
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "P(v_i = 1 \\mid h) = \\sigma\\left(a_i + \\sum_j h_j W_{ij}\\right)",
                      caption: "Visible unit activation — by the symmetric argument",
                    },
                  ],
                },
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "callout",
              variant: "key",
              title: "Significance",
              blocks: [

                },

        {
          id: "u4-l6-s4",
          title: "Training RBMs — Contrastive Divergence (CD-k)",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "text",
              value:
                "The exact gradient of the log-likelihood has a clean form but an intractable piece:",
            },

              type: "formula",

              caption: "Data correlations minus model correlations",
            },

              type: "bullets",

                "**Negative phase $\\langle v_i h_j \\rangle_{model}$: hard** — needs samples from the model's own equilibrium distribution, which exactly needs $Z$ — intractable.",
                "**Contrastive Divergence (Hinton, 2002):** approximate the negative phase using only **$k$ steps of block Gibbs sampling, starting the chain from the training example itself** (instead of running to equilibrium). **CD-1 ($k=1$) is used in practice and works remarkably well.**",
              ],
            },
            { type: "heading", value: "The CD-1 algorithm" },
            {
              type: "numbered",
              items: [
                "Start with a training vector $v^0$.",
                "Compute $P(h^0|v^0)$ using the sigmoid formula; sample / obtain $h^0$ (**positive phase**).",
                "Compute $P(v^1|h^0)$; this “reconstruction” $v^1$ is the model's guess at regenerating $v^0$.",
                "Compute $P(h^1|v^1)$ (**negative phase**).",
                "Update weights and biases:",
              ],
            },
            {
              type: "formula",
              tex: "\\Delta W_{ij} = \\eta\\left(v_i^0 h_j^0 - v_i^1 h_j^1\\right), \\qquad \\Delta a_i = \\eta\\left(v_i^0 - v_i^1\\right), \\qquad \\Delta b_j = \\eta\\left(h_j^0 - h_j^1\\right)",
              caption: "CD-1 update rules — positive-phase statistics minus negative-phase statistics",
            },
            {
              type: "example",
              title: "Worked Example 6.2 — One Step of CD-1 (single visible / single hidden unit, for clarity)",

                  label: "Step 1 — Positive phase: probability hidden unit turns on, given the data",

                  label: "Step 2 — Reconstruction: probability visible unit turns back on, given h⁰ (the model “imagining” the data back)",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "v^1 = P(v=1 \\mid h^0) = \\sigma(0.6225 \\times 0.5) = \\sigma(0.3113) = 0.5773" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 3 — Negative phase: probability hidden unit turns on, given the reconstruction",
                  blocks: [
                    { type: "formula", tex: "h^1 = P(h=1 \\mid v^1) = \\sigma(0.5773 \\times 0.5) = \\sigma(0.2887) = 0.5717" },
                  ],
                },
                {
                  label: "Step 4 — CD-1 weight update (positive-phase correlation minus negative-phase correlation)",
                  blocks: [
                    {
                      type: "formula",
                      tex: "\\Delta W = \\eta(v^0 h^0 - v^1 h^1) = 0.1 \\times (1 \\times 0.6225 - 0.5773 \\times 0.5717) = 0.1 \\times (0.6225 - 0.3300) = 0.02925",

                    { type: "formula", tex: "W_{new} = 0.5 + 0.02925 = 0.52925" },

                },

            },

              variant: "info",
              title: "Interpretation",
              blocks: [
                {
                  type: "text",
                  value:
                    "The positive-phase correlation (0.6225) exceeds the negative / reconstruction-phase correlation (0.3300), so $W$ is increased — the model strengthens this v–h connection to make the real data configuration more probable (lower energy) relative to what it currently “fantasises” / reconstructs.",
                },
              ],

                },

            },

          title: "Deep Belief Networks (DBN): stacking RBMs",
          blocks: [
            {
              type: "bullets",
              items: [
                "A DBN **stacks several RBMs**: $v \\to h^1 \\to h^2 \\to h^3 \\dots$",
                "Only the **top two layers remain an undirected RBM**; all lower connections become **directed, pointing downward** (a “sigmoid belief network”).",
                "This mixed directed / undirected structure is what distinguishes a DBN from a **Deep Boltzmann Machine** (Lesson 7, which is fully undirected).",
              ],
            },
            { type: "heading", value: "Greedy layer-wise pretraining" },
            {
              type: "numbered",
              items: [
                "Train $RBM_1$ on the raw data $v$ using CD, learning $h^1$.",
                "**Freeze $RBM_1$.** Treat $P(h^1|v)$ (or samples from it) as “data” and train $RBM_2$ on top of it, learning $h^2$.",
                "Repeat, adding one RBM / layer at a time — each new layer is trained on the activations of the previous, already-fixed layer.",
                "Optionally **fine-tune** the whole stack afterward (e.g. wake-sleep algorithm, or backpropagation if a classifier layer is attached on top).",
                "Because each layer is trained one at a time on a shallow (1-layer) problem, this **avoids the vanishing-gradient difficulty** of training a deep directed network from scratch — historically the technique that first made training deep networks practical.",
              ],

import * as React from "react"

const MOBILE_BREAKPOINT = 768

export function useIsMobile() {
  const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = React.useState<boolean | undefined>(undefined)

  React.useEffect(() => {
    const mql = window.matchMedia(`(max-width: ${MOBILE_BREAKPOINT - 1}px)`)
    const onChange = () => {
      setIsMobile(window.innerWidth < MOBILE_BREAKPOINT)
    }
    mql.addEventListener("change", onChange)
    setIsMobile(window.innerWidth < MOBILE_BREAKPOINT)
    return () => mql.removeEventListener("change", onChange)
  }, [])

  return !!isMobile
}

"use client"

// Inspired by react-hot-toast library
import * as React from "react"

import type {
  ToastActionElement,
  ToastProps,
} from "@/components/ui/toast"

const TOAST_LIMIT = 1
const TOAST_REMOVE_DELAY = 1000000

type ToasterToast = ToastProps & {
  id: string
  title?: React.ReactNode
  description?: React.ReactNode
  action?: ToastActionElement
}

const actionTypes = {
  ADD_TOAST: "ADD_TOAST",
  UPDATE_TOAST: "UPDATE_TOAST",
  DISMISS_TOAST: "DISMISS_TOAST",
  REMOVE_TOAST: "REMOVE_TOAST",
} as const

let count = 0

function genId() {
  count = (count + 1) % Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
  return count.toString()
}

type ActionType = typeof actionTypes

type Action =
  | {
    type: ActionType["ADD_TOAST"]
    toast: ToasterToast
  }
  | {
    type: ActionType["UPDATE_TOAST"]
    toast: Partial<ToasterToast>
  }
  | {
    type: ActionType["DISMISS_TOAST"]
    toastId?: ToasterToast["id"]
  }
  | {
    type: ActionType["REMOVE_TOAST"]
    toastId?: ToasterToast["id"]
  }

interface State {
  toasts: ToasterToast[]
}

const toastTimeouts = new Map<string, ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>>()

const addToRemoveQueue = (toastId: string) => {
  if (toastTimeouts.has(toastId)) {
    return
  }

  const timeout = setTimeout(() => {
    toastTimeouts.delete(toastId)
    dispatch({
      type: "REMOVE_TOAST",
      toastId: toastId,
    })
  }, TOAST_REMOVE_DELAY)

  toastTimeouts.set(toastId, timeout)
}

export const reducer = (state: State, action: Action): State => {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "ADD_TOAST":
      return {
        ...state,
        toasts: [action.toast, ...state.toasts].slice(0, TOAST_LIMIT),
      }

    case "UPDATE_TOAST":
      return {
        ...state,
        toasts: state.toasts.map((t) =>
          t.id === action.toast.id ? { ...t, ...action.toast } : t
        ),
      }

    case "DISMISS_TOAST": {
      const { toastId } = action

      // ! Side effects ! - This could be extracted into a dismissToast() action,
      // but I'll keep it here for simplicity
      if (toastId) {
        addToRemoveQueue(toastId)
      } else {
        state.toasts.forEach((toast) => {
          addToRemoveQueue(toast.id)
        })
      }

      return {
        ...state,
        toasts: state.toasts.map((t) =>
          t.id === toastId || toastId === undefined
            ? {
              ...t,
              open: false,
            }
            : t
        ),
      }
    }
    case "REMOVE_TOAST":
      if (action.toastId === undefined) {
        return {
          ...state,
          toasts: [],
        }
      }
      return {
        ...state,
        toasts: state.toasts.filter((t) => t.id !== action.toastId),
      }
  }
}

const listeners: Array<(state: State) => void> = []

let memoryState: State = { toasts: [] }

function dispatch(action: Action) {
  memoryState = reducer(memoryState, action)
  listeners.forEach((listener) => {
    listener(memoryState)
  })
}

type Toast = Omit<ToasterToast, "id">

function toast({ ...props }: Toast) {
  const id = genId()

  const update = (props: ToasterToast) =>
    dispatch({
      type: "UPDATE_TOAST",
      toast: { ...props, id },
    })
  const dismiss = () => dispatch({ type: "DISMISS_TOAST", toastId: id })

  dispatch({
    type: "ADD_TOAST",
    toast: {
      ...props,
      id,
      open: true,
      onOpenChange: (open) => {
        if (!open) dismiss()
      },
    },
  })

  return {
    id: id,
    dismiss,
    update,
  }
}

function useToast() {
  const [state, setState] = React.useState<State>(memoryState)

  React.useEffect(() => {
    listeners.push(setState)
    return () => {
      const index = listeners.indexOf(setState)
      if (index > -1) {
        listeners.splice(index, 1)
      }
    }
  }, [state])

  return {
    ...state,
    toast,
    dismiss: (toastId?: string) => dispatch({ type: "DISMISS_TOAST", toastId }),
  }
}

export { useToast, toast }

/**
 * Content model for the interactive Deep Learning course.
 * Text fields support inline math wrapped in $...$ (rendered via KaTeX).
 */

export type Block =
  | { type: "text"; value: string }
  | { type: "bullets"; items: string[] }
  | { type: "numbered"; items: string[] }
  | { type: "heading"; value: string }
  | { type: "formula"; tex: string; caption?: string }
  | {
      type: "callout";
      variant: "info" | "tip" | "warning" | "key" | "exam";
      title: string;
      blocks: Block[];
    }
  | { type: "table"; headers: string[]; rows: string[][]; caption?: string }
  | {
      type: "example";
      title: string;
      given?: string[];
      steps: { label: string; blocks: Block[] }[];
    }
  | { type: "widget"; widgetId: string; title?: string; description?: string }
  | { type: "quiz"; items: QuizItem[] }
  | { type: "compare"; pairs: { label: string; left: string[]; right?: string[] }[] };

export interface QuizItem {
  id: string;
  question: string;
  options: string[];
  correct: number;
  explanation: string;
}

export interface Section {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  blocks: Block[];
}

export interface Lesson {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  subtitle?: string;
  minutes: number;
  sections: Section[];
}

export interface Unit {
  id: string;
  number: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4;
  code: string;
  title: string;
  subtitle: string;
  description: string;
  sourceFile: string;
  topics: string[];
  lessons: Lesson[];
  quiz: QuizItem[];
}
