    87→    87→1. Introduction to Deep Learning
    88→    88→
    89→    89→1.1 What is Deep Learning?
    90→    90→Deep Learning (DL) is the branch of Machine Learning that uses multi-layered (“deep”) artificial neural
    91→    91→networks to learn directly from data.
    92→    92→  ● Deep Learning is a subset of Machine Learning (ML), which itself is a subset of Artificial
    93→    93→    Intelligence (AI).
    94→    94→  ● It uses artificial neural networks with many hidden layers to automatically learn hierarchical
    95→    95→    representations of raw data.
    96→    96→  ● Unlike classical ML, DL removes the need for manual / hand-crafted feature engineering – the
    97→    97→    network learns useful features by itself.
    98→    98→      – Example (image recognition): early layers detect edges → middle layers detect shapes/textures
    99→    99→         → deeper layers detect object parts → final layers recognise the whole object.
   100→   100→
   101→   101→

   112→   112→1.2 Why Deep Learning Now? – The Three Enablers
   113→   113→  ● Big Data: massive labelled and unlabelled datasets are now available (e.g. ImageNet, web-scale
   114→   114→    text) to train large models.
   115→   115→  ● Compute Power: GPUs / TPUs allow the huge number of matrix multiplications in deep networks
   116→   116→    to be parallelised efficiently.
   117→   117→  ● Algorithmic Advances: better activation functions (ReLU), optimisers (Adam, RMSProp), and
   118→   118→    regularisation techniques (Dropout, Batch Normalisation) made very deep networks trainable.

   129→   129→1.4 Biological Inspiration – From Neuron to Perceptron
   130→   130→Artificial neurons are loosely inspired by biological neurons in the brain:
   131→   131→  ● Dendrites receive electrical/chemical signals from other neurons — analogous to inputs x₁, x₂, …,
   132→   132→    xₙ.
   133→   133→  ● The Soma (cell body) accumulates the incoming signals — analogous to the weighted summation
   134→   134→    Σ.
   135→   135→  ● If the accumulated signal crosses a threshold, the neuron “fires” through its Axon — analogous to
   136→   136→    an activation function producing an output.
   137→   137→  ● The strength of a connection (synapse) is analogous to a weight wᵢ — learning = adjusting these
   138→   138→    weights.

   149→   149→
   150→   150→2. The Perceptron
   151→   151→
   152→   152→2.1 Definition and Historical Note
   153→   153→  ● Proposed by Frank Rosenblatt (1958), building on the earlier McCulloch–Pitts neuron model (1943).
   154→   154→  ● A perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron: it performs binary classification by drawing a straight-
   155→   155→    line (linear) decision boundary between two classes.
   156→   156→  ● It is the fundamental building block from which larger neural networks (Multi-Layer Perceptrons)
   157→   157→    are constructed.
   158→   158→
   159→   159→2.2 Mathematical Model
   160→   160→A perceptron performs two operations in sequence — a weighted summation, followed by a non-linear
   161→   161→activation:
   162→   162→
   163→   163→                          Net input:   z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ + b = ∑ wᵢxᵢ + b
   164→   164→                   Output:    y = f(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0 ,                 0 if z < 0              (unit-step activation)
   165→   165→
   166→   166→
   167→   167→
   168→   168→
   169→   169→Figure: Block diagram of a perceptron – inputs are weighted, summed with a bias, and passed through an activation
   170→   170→                                                    function.
   171→   171→
   172→   172→Significance of each component
   173→   173→  ● Inputs (x₁…xₙ): the numeric feature values describing the pattern to be classified.
   174→   174→  ● Weights (w₁…wₙ): learnable parameters that decide how strongly each input influences the
   175→   175→    output; learned from data.
   176→   176→  ● Bias (b): shifts the decision boundary away from the origin, so the boundary need not pass
   177→   177→    through (0,0,…).
   178→   178→  ● Net input (z): a linear combination of inputs – geometrically, it measures the (signed) distance of
   179→   179→    a point from the decision hyperplane.
   180→   180→  ● Activation f(z): converts the continuous net input into a discrete class decision (0 or 1).
   181→   181→                                       Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 5 of 36
   182→   182→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                       Manipal University Jaipur
   183→   183→
   184→   184→2.3 Geometric Interpretation – Linear Separability
   185→   185→  ● The equation ∑wᵢxᵢ + b = 0 defines a straight line (2 inputs), a plane (3 inputs), or a hyperplane (n
   186→   186→    inputs) that separates the input space into two half-spaces.
   187→   187→  ● A perceptron can classify a dataset correctly only if the two classes are linearly separable – i.e. some
   188→   188→    hyperplane can separate them completely.
   189→   189→
   190→   190→2.4 Perceptron Learning Algorithm
   191→   191→Weights are learned iteratively so that the perceptron's output matches the desired target for every
   192→   192→training example.
   193→   193→Step 1 — Initialise
   194→   194→  ● Set weights wᵢ and bias b to 0 (or small random values); choose a learning rate η, where 0 < η ≤ 1.
   195→   195→Step 2 — For every training pair (x, t), where t is the target output
   196→   196→  ● (a) Compute the net input: z = ∑ wᵢxᵢ + b
   197→   197→  ● (b) Compute the predicted output: y = f(z)
   198→   198→  ● (c) Compute the error: e = t − y
   199→   199→  ● (d) Update every weight: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η·e·xᵢ
   200→   200→  ● (e) Update the bias: b ← b + η·e
   201→   201→Step 3 — Repeat
   202→   202→  ● Repeat Step 2 for every example in the training set — this is one epoch.
   203→   203→  ● Repeat over multiple epochs until an entire epoch produces zero errors (convergence), or a
   204→   204→    maximum number of epochs is reached.
   205→   205→
   206→   206→    wᵢ(new) = wᵢ(old) + η (t − y) xᵢ            b(new) = b(old) + η (t − y)
   207→   207→
   208→   208→
   209→   209→  Why does this update rule work?
   210→   210→  If prediction is already correct (e = 0): no change is made — there is nothing to fix.
   211→   211→  If target = 1 but output = 0 (e = +1): weights are increased along xⁱ, raising z next time so it is more
   212→   212→  likely to cross the threshold and fire (output 1).
   213→   213→  If target = 0 but output = 1 (e = −1): weights are decreased, lowering z next time so it is more likely
   214→   214→  to stay below threshold (output 0).
   215→   215→  Perceptron Convergence Theorem: if the two classes are linearly separable, this algorithm is
   216→   216→  guaranteed to find a separating hyperplane in a finite number of steps.
   217→   217→
   218→   218→
   219→   219→
   220→   220→

   328→   328→2.6 Limitation of the Perceptron — The XOR Problem
   329→   329→A single-layer perceptron can only separate linearly separable classes. The XOR function is the classic
   330→   330→counter-example:
   331→   331→              x₁                   x₂                              Target = XOR                                         Class
   332→   332→ 0                        0                           0                                                  Class 0
   333→   333→ 0                        1                           1                                                  Class 1
   334→   334→ 1                        0                           1                                                  Class 1
   335→   335→ 1                        1                           0                                                  Class 0
   336→   336→
   337→   337→
   338→   338→  ● Class 0 points {(0,0),(1,1)} and Class 1 points {(0,1),(1,0)} lie on opposite diagonals of the unit
   339→   339→    square — no single straight line can separate them.
   340→   340→
   341→   341→  ● Formally: no w₁, w₂, b exist that satisfy all four inequalities implied by the XOR truth table
   342→   342→    simultaneously (this can be shown leads to a contradiction, e.g. adding the inequalities for (0,0) and
   343→   343→    (1,1) contradicts those for (0,1) and (1,0)).
   344→   344→
   345→   345→  ● This limitation, highlighted by Minsky & Papert (1969), was resolved by stacking multiple
   346→   346→    perceptron layers — the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) — trained using the Backpropagation
   347→   347→    algorithm (Section 5).
   348→   348→  ● XOR is not linearly separable, so a single-layer perceptron fails. It is solved by a 2-2-1 Multi-Layer
   349→   349→    Perceptron (2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons → 1 output neuron) using a hard step (threshold) activation:
   350→   350→
   351→   351→(The output effectively computes h1 AND (NOT h2 ).)
   352→   352→
   353→   353→
   354→   354→
   355→   355→
   356→   356→                                    Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 10 of 36

   360→   360→3. Learning and Recognition
   361→   361→“Learning” in a neural network means automatically adjusting weights from data. “Recognition” is the
   362→   362→use of the trained network to identify / classify new, unseen patterns. Based on the nature of the training
   363→   363→data, learning is broadly divided into supervised and unsupervised learning.
   364→   364→
   365→   365→3.1 Supervised Learning
   366→   366→  ● Training data consists of input–output pairs (X, Y), where Y is the known, correct “label” or “target”
   367→   367→    for each input X.
   368→   368→  ● The algorithm learns a mapping f: X → Y that minimises the difference between predicted and
   369→   369→    actual outputs.
   370→   370→  ● Two main task types:
   371→   371→      – Classification: output is a discrete category (e.g. spam / not spam, digit 0–9).
   372→   372→      – Regression: output is a continuous numeric value (e.g. house price, temperature).
   373→   373→  ● Examples: email spam detection, disease diagnosis from labelled scans, house-price prediction, the
   374→   374→    AND-gate perceptron of Section 2.
   375→   375→
   376→   376→3.2 Unsupervised Learning
   377→   377→  ● Training data consists of only inputs X, with no associated target labels.
   378→   378→  ● The algorithm discovers hidden structure, patterns, or groupings in the data by itself.
   379→   379→  ● Common tasks: clustering (grouping similar points), dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection.
   380→   380→  ● Examples: customer segmentation for marketing, grouping news articles by topic, anomaly
   381→   381→    detection in network traffic.
   382→   382→
   383→   383→
   384→   384→
   385→   385→
   386→   386→    Figure: Supervised learning uses labelled data to learn a direct input→output mapping; unsupervised learning
   387→   387→                                         discovers structure without labels.
   388→   388→
   389→   389→
   390→   390→

   392→   392→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                     Manipal University Jaipur
   393→   393→
   394→   394→3.3 Supervised vs Unsupervised — Comparison
   395→   395→              Aspect                  Supervised Learning                                     Unsupervised Learning
   396→   396→ Training data               Labelled (X, Y)                                        Unlabelled (X only)
   397→   397→ Goal                        Learn mapping X → Y                                    Discover hidden structure
   398→   398→ Feedback                    Direct error signal (loss)                             No explicit error signal
   399→   399→ Typical tasks               Classification, Regression                             Clustering, Dimensionality reduction
   400→   400→ Example algorithm           Perceptron, Logistic Regression, CNN                   K-Means, PCA, Autoencoders
   401→   401→ Data cost                   Expensive (needs human labelling)                      Cheaper (labels not required)
   402→   402→

   405→   405→3.4 Worked Numerical Example — K-Means Clustering (1 iteration)
   406→   406→K-Means is a classic unsupervised algorithm that groups data into k clusters by iteratively updating
   407→   407→cluster centroids. Consider 4 points and k = 2:
   408→   408→  ● Points: A(1,1), B(2,1), C(4,3), D(5,4)
   409→   409→  ● Initial centroids (chosen as first/last point): C₁ = (1,1), C₂ = (5,4)
   410→   410→Step 1 — Assign each point to its nearest centroid (Euclidean distance)
   411→   411→  ● A(1,1): dist to C₁ = 0.00, dist to C₂ = √[(1−5)²+(1−4)²] = √25 = 5.00 → closer to C₁ → Cluster 1
   412→   412→  ● B(2,1): dist to C₁ = √[(2−1)²+(1−1)²] = 1.00, dist to C₂ = √[(2−5)²+(1−4)²] = 4.24 → Cluster 1
   413→   413→  ● C(4,3): dist to C₁ = √[(4−1)²+(3−1)²] = 3.61, dist to C₂ = √[(4−5)²+(3−4)²] = 1.41 → Cluster 2
   414→   414→  ● D(5,4): dist to C₁ = √[(5−1)²+(4−1)²] = 5.00, dist to C₂ = 0.00 → Cluster 2
   415→   415→Step 2 — Recompute centroids as the mean of assigned points
   416→   416→  ● Cluster 1 = {A(1,1), B(2,1)} → new C₁ = ((1+2)/2, (1+1)/2) = (1.50, 1.00)
   417→   417→  ● Cluster 2 = {C(4,3), D(5,4)} → new C₂ = ((4+5)/2, (3+4)/2) = (4.50, 3.50)
   418→   418→  ● Significance: each iteration pulls the centroid toward the centre of mass of its assigned points; the
   419→   419→    process repeats until centroids stop moving (convergence) — all without ever using a target label.
   420→   420→

    87→1. Introduction to Deep Learning
    88→
    89→1.1 What is Deep Learning?
    90→Deep Learning (DL) is the branch of Machine Learning that uses multi-layered (“deep”) artificial neural
    91→networks to learn directly from data.
    92→  ● Deep Learning is a subset of Machine Learning (ML), which itself is a subset of Artificial
    93→    Intelligence (AI).
    94→  ● It uses artificial neural networks with many hidden layers to automatically learn hierarchical
    95→    representations of raw data.
    96→  ● Unlike classical ML, DL removes the need for manual / hand-crafted feature engineering – the
    97→    network learns useful features by itself.
    98→      – Example (image recognition): early layers detect edges → middle layers detect shapes/textures
    99→         → deeper layers detect object parts → final layers recognise the whole object.
   100→
   101→
   102→
   103→
   104→           Figure: Deep Learning is a subset of Machine Learning, which is a subset of Artificial Intelligence.
   105→
   106→
   107→
   108→
   109→                                         Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 3 of 36
   110→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                            Manipal University Jaipur
   111→
   112→1.2 Why Deep Learning Now? – The Three Enablers
   113→  ● Big Data: massive labelled and unlabelled datasets are now available (e.g. ImageNet, web-scale
   114→    text) to train large models.
   115→  ● Compute Power: GPUs / TPUs allow the huge number of matrix multiplications in deep networks
   116→    to be parallelised efficiently.
   117→  ● Algorithmic Advances: better activation functions (ReLU), optimisers (Adam, RMSProp), and
   118→    regularisation techniques (Dropout, Batch Normalisation) made very deep networks trainable.
   119→
   120→1.3 Applications of Deep Learning
   121→                   Domain                                                     Example Applications
   122→ Computer Vision                               Image classification, object detection, face recognition
   123→ Natural Language Processing                   Machine translation, chatbots, sentiment analysis
   124→ Speech Processing                             Speech-to-text, voice assistants
   125→ Healthcare                                    Disease diagnosis from scans, drug discovery
   126→ Autonomous Systems                            Self-driving cars, robotic control
   127→
   128→
   129→1.4 Biological Inspiration – From Neuron to Perceptron
   130→Artificial neurons are loosely inspired by biological neurons in the brain:
   131→  ● Dendrites receive electrical/chemical signals from other neurons — analogous to inputs x₁, x₂, …,
   132→    xₙ.
   133→  ● The Soma (cell body) accumulates the incoming signals — analogous to the weighted summation
   134→    Σ.
   135→  ● If the accumulated signal crosses a threshold, the neuron “fires” through its Axon — analogous to
   136→    an activation function producing an output.
   137→  ● The strength of a connection (synapse) is analogous to a weight wᵢ — learning = adjusting these
   138→    weights.
   139→
   140→
   141→
   142→
   143→                Figure: Biological neuron (left) and its simplified artificial analogue, the perceptron (right).

   147→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                        Manipal University Jaipur
   148→
   149→
   150→2. The Perceptron
   151→
   152→2.1 Definition and Historical Note
   153→  ● Proposed by Frank Rosenblatt (1958), building on the earlier McCulloch–Pitts neuron model (1943).
   154→  ● A perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron: it performs binary classification by drawing a straight-
   155→    line (linear) decision boundary between two classes.
   156→  ● It is the fundamental building block from which larger neural networks (Multi-Layer Perceptrons)
   157→    are constructed.
   158→
   159→2.2 Mathematical Model
   160→A perceptron performs two operations in sequence — a weighted summation, followed by a non-linear
   161→activation:
   162→
   163→                          Net input:   z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ + b = ∑ wᵢxᵢ + b
   164→                   Output:    y = f(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0 ,                 0 if z < 0              (unit-step activation)
   165→
   166→
   167→
   168→
   169→Figure: Block diagram of a perceptron – inputs are weighted, summed with a bias, and passed through an activation
   170→                                                    function.
   171→
   172→Significance of each component
   173→  ● Inputs (x₁…xₙ): the numeric feature values describing the pattern to be classified.
   174→  ● Weights (w₁…wₙ): learnable parameters that decide how strongly each input influences the
   175→    output; learned from data.
   176→  ● Bias (b): shifts the decision boundary away from the origin, so the boundary need not pass
   177→    through (0,0,…).
   178→  ● Net input (z): a linear combination of inputs – geometrically, it measures the (signed) distance of
   179→    a point from the decision hyperplane.
   180→  ● Activation f(z): converts the continuous net input into a discrete class decision (0 or 1).
   181→                                       Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 5 of 36
   182→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                       Manipal University Jaipur
   183→
   184→2.3 Geometric Interpretation – Linear Separability
   185→  ● The equation ∑wᵢxᵢ + b = 0 defines a straight line (2 inputs), a plane (3 inputs), or a hyperplane (n
   186→    inputs) that separates the input space into two half-spaces.
   187→  ● A perceptron can classify a dataset correctly only if the two classes are linearly separable – i.e. some
   188→    hyperplane can separate them completely.
   189→
   190→2.4 Perceptron Learning Algorithm
   191→Weights are learned iteratively so that the perceptron's output matches the desired target for every
   192→training example.
   193→Step 1 — Initialise
   194→  ● Set weights wᵢ and bias b to 0 (or small random values); choose a learning rate η, where 0 < η ≤ 1.
   195→Step 2 — For every training pair (x, t), where t is the target output
   196→  ● (a) Compute the net input: z = ∑ wᵢxᵢ + b
   197→  ● (b) Compute the predicted output: y = f(z)
   198→  ● (c) Compute the error: e = t − y
   199→  ● (d) Update every weight: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η·e·xᵢ
   200→  ● (e) Update the bias: b ← b + η·e
   201→Step 3 — Repeat
   202→  ● Repeat Step 2 for every example in the training set — this is one epoch.
   203→  ● Repeat over multiple epochs until an entire epoch produces zero errors (convergence), or a
   204→    maximum number of epochs is reached.
   205→
   206→    wᵢ(new) = wᵢ(old) + η (t − y) xᵢ            b(new) = b(old) + η (t − y)
   207→
   208→
   209→  Why does this update rule work?
   210→  If prediction is already correct (e = 0): no change is made — there is nothing to fix.
   211→  If target = 1 but output = 0 (e = +1): weights are increased along xⁱ, raising z next time so it is more
   212→  likely to cross the threshold and fire (output 1).
   213→  If target = 0 but output = 1 (e = −1): weights are decreased, lowering z next time so it is more likely
   214→  to stay below threshold (output 0).
   215→  Perceptron Convergence Theorem: if the two classes are linearly separable, this algorithm is
   216→  guaranteed to find a separating hyperplane in a finite number of steps.
   217→
   218→
   219→
   220→
   221→                                       Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 6 of 36
   222→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                    Manipal University Jaipur
   223→
   224→2.5 Worked Numerical Example — Learning the AND Function
   225→We train a single perceptron to reproduce the 2-input AND logic gate.
   226→                 x₁                        x₂                                          Target t = x₁ AND x₂
   227→ 0                           0                                     0
   228→ 0                           1                                     0
   229→ 1                           0                                     0
   230→ 1                           1                                     1
   231→
   232→
   233→Initial settings: w₁ = 0, w₂ = 0, b = 0, learning rate η = 1, activation: unit step with threshold z ≥ 0 →
   234→1.
   235→
   236→Detailed walk-through of Epoch 1
   237→Sample 1: x = (0,0), target t = 0
   238→ ● z = (0)(0) + (0)(0) + 0 = 0 → since z ≥ 0, y = 1
   239→ ● error e = t − y = 0 − 1 = −1 (wrong prediction → update needed)
   240→ ● w₁ ← 0 + 1(−1)(0) = 0, w₂ ← 0 + 1(−1)(0) = 0, b ← 0 + 1(−1) = −1
   241→     – Significance: both inputs are 0, so only the bias absorbs the correction — weights cannot
   242→        change when their input is 0.
   243→Sample 2: x = (0,1), target t = 0
   244→ ● z = (0)(0) + (0)(1) + (−1) = −1 → since z < 0, y = 0
   245→ ● error e = 0 − 0 = 0 → prediction already correct, no update
   246→     – Significance: zero error means the current weights already work for this sample — the rule
   247→        leaves them untouched.
   248→Sample 3: x = (1,0), target t = 0
   249→ ● z = (0)(1) + (0)(0) + (−1) = −1 → y = 0, error e = 0 → no update
   250→Sample 4: x = (1,1), target t = 1
   251→ ● z = (0)(1) + (0)(1) + (−1) = −1 → since z < 0, y = 0
   252→ ● error e = 1 − 0 = 1 (wrong prediction → update needed)
   253→ ● w₁ ← 0 + 1(1)(1) = 1, w₂ ← 0 + 1(1)(1) = 1, b ← −1 + 1(1) = 0
   254→     – Significance: the only positive example was misclassified as 0, so weights increase along both
   255→        active inputs, pushing z upward for this pattern next time.

   327→
   328→2.6 Limitation of the Perceptron — The XOR Problem
   329→A single-layer perceptron can only separate linearly separable classes. The XOR function is the classic
   330→counter-example:
   331→              x₁                   x₂                              Target = XOR                                         Class
   332→ 0                        0                           0                                                  Class 0
   333→ 0                        1                           1                                                  Class 1
   334→ 1                        0                           1                                                  Class 1
   335→ 1                        1                           0                                                  Class 0
   336→
   337→
   338→  ● Class 0 points {(0,0),(1,1)} and Class 1 points {(0,1),(1,0)} lie on opposite diagonals of the unit
   339→    square — no single straight line can separate them.
   340→
   341→  ● Formally: no w₁, w₂, b exist that satisfy all four inequalities implied by the XOR truth table
   342→    simultaneously (this can be shown leads to a contradiction, e.g. adding the inequalities for (0,0) and
   343→    (1,1) contradicts those for (0,1) and (1,0)).
   344→
   345→  ● This limitation, highlighted by Minsky & Papert (1969), was resolved by stacking multiple
   346→    perceptron layers — the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) — trained using the Backpropagation
   347→    algorithm (Section 5).
   348→  ● XOR is not linearly separable, so a single-layer perceptron fails. It is solved by a 2-2-1 Multi-Layer
   349→    Perceptron (2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons → 1 output neuron) using a hard step (threshold) activation:
   350→
   351→(The output effectively computes h1 AND (NOT h2 ).)
   352→
   353→
   354→
   355→
   356→                                    Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 10 of 36
   357→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                       Manipal University Jaipur
   358→
   359→
   360→3. Learning and Recognition
   361→“Learning” in a neural network means automatically adjusting weights from data. “Recognition” is the
   362→use of the trained network to identify / classify new, unseen patterns. Based on the nature of the training
   363→data, learning is broadly divided into supervised and unsupervised learning.
   364→
   365→3.1 Supervised Learning
   366→  ● Training data consists of input–output pairs (X, Y), where Y is the known, correct “label” or “target”
   367→    for each input X.
   368→  ● The algorithm learns a mapping f: X → Y that minimises the difference between predicted and
   369→    actual outputs.
   370→  ● Two main task types:
   371→      – Classification: output is a discrete category (e.g. spam / not spam, digit 0–9).
   372→      – Regression: output is a continuous numeric value (e.g. house price, temperature).
   373→  ● Examples: email spam detection, disease diagnosis from labelled scans, house-price prediction, the
   374→    AND-gate perceptron of Section 2.
   375→
   376→3.2 Unsupervised Learning
   377→  ● Training data consists of only inputs X, with no associated target labels.
   378→  ● The algorithm discovers hidden structure, patterns, or groupings in the data by itself.
   379→  ● Common tasks: clustering (grouping similar points), dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection.
   380→  ● Examples: customer segmentation for marketing, grouping news articles by topic, anomaly
   381→    detection in network traffic.
   382→
   383→
   384→
   385→
   386→    Figure: Supervised learning uses labelled data to learn a direct input→output mapping; unsupervised learning
   387→                                         discovers structure without labels.
   388→
   389→
   390→
   391→                                      Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 11 of 36
   392→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                     Manipal University Jaipur
   393→
   394→3.3 Supervised vs Unsupervised — Comparison
   395→              Aspect                  Supervised Learning                                     Unsupervised Learning
   396→ Training data               Labelled (X, Y)                                        Unlabelled (X only)
   397→ Goal                        Learn mapping X → Y                                    Discover hidden structure
   398→ Feedback                    Direct error signal (loss)                             No explicit error signal
   399→ Typical tasks               Classification, Regression                             Clustering, Dimensionality reduction
   400→ Example algorithm           Perceptron, Logistic Regression, CNN                   K-Means, PCA, Autoencoders
   401→ Data cost                   Expensive (needs human labelling)                      Cheaper (labels not required)
   402→
   403→
   404→
   405→3.4 Worked Numerical Example — K-Means Clustering (1 iteration)
   406→K-Means is a classic unsupervised algorithm that groups data into k clusters by iteratively updating
   407→cluster centroids. Consider 4 points and k = 2:
   408→  ● Points: A(1,1), B(2,1), C(4,3), D(5,4)
   409→  ● Initial centroids (chosen as first/last point): C₁ = (1,1), C₂ = (5,4)
   410→Step 1 — Assign each point to its nearest centroid (Euclidean distance)
   411→  ● A(1,1): dist to C₁ = 0.00, dist to C₂ = √[(1−5)²+(1−4)²] = √25 = 5.00 → closer to C₁ → Cluster 1
   412→  ● B(2,1): dist to C₁ = √[(2−1)²+(1−1)²] = 1.00, dist to C₂ = √[(2−5)²+(1−4)²] = 4.24 → Cluster 1
   413→  ● C(4,3): dist to C₁ = √[(4−1)²+(3−1)²] = 3.61, dist to C₂ = √[(4−5)²+(3−4)²] = 1.41 → Cluster 2
   414→  ● D(5,4): dist to C₁ = √[(5−1)²+(4−1)²] = 5.00, dist to C₂ = 0.00 → Cluster 2
   415→Step 2 — Recompute centroids as the mean of assigned points
   416→  ● Cluster 1 = {A(1,1), B(2,1)} → new C₁ = ((1+2)/2, (1+1)/2) = (1.50, 1.00)
   417→  ● Cluster 2 = {C(4,3), D(5,4)} → new C₂ = ((4+5)/2, (3+4)/2) = (4.50, 3.50)
   418→  ● Significance: each iteration pulls the centroid toward the centre of mass of its assigned points; the
   419→    process repeats until centroids stop moving (convergence) — all without ever using a target label.
   420→
   421→
   422→
   423→
   424→                                    Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 12 of 36
   425→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                        Manipal University Jaipur
   426→
   427→
   428→4. Loss Functions
   429→
   430→4.1 What Is a Loss Function?
   431→  ● A loss function L(Y, Ŷ) quantifies how far the model's prediction Ŷ is from the actual target Y —
   432→    a single number that training tries to minimise.
   433→  ● It is the objective that backpropagation differentiates and that gradient descent minimises (Sections
   434→    5 and 6).
   435→  ● Choice of loss function depends on the task: regression uses distance-based losses; classification
   436→    uses probability-based losses.
   437→
   438→
   439→
   440→
   441→ Figure: The loss function sits at the centre of the training loop: it compares prediction with ground truth and drives
   442→                                                   every weight update.
   443→
   444→
   445→
   446→
   447→                                       Unit 1: Introduction to Deep Learning | Page 13 of 36
   448→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                         Manipal University Jaipur
   449→
   450→4.2 Regression Loss — Mean Squared Error (MSE)
   451→For n samples with actual values yᵢ and predictions ŷᵢ:
   452→
   453→                                               MSE = (1/n) ∑ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²
   454→
   455→  ● Squaring is used instead of the raw error because: (i) it removes the sign so positive and negative
   456→    errors do not cancel, and (ii) it penalises large errors much more heavily than small ones (a useful,
   457→    differentiable property for gradient-based learning).
   458→
   459→Numerical Example — MSE / MAE
   460→Predicted vs actual house prices (in ₹ lakh):
   461→           Actual (y)                 Predicted (ŷ)                          Error (y−ŷ)                           Squared error
   462→ 50                              48                                 2                                       4
   463→ 60                              65                                 −5                                      25
   464→ 70                              68                                 2                                       4
   465→
   466→
   467→  ● MSE = (1/3)(4 + 25 + 4) = (1/3)(33) = 11.00
   468→  ● For comparison, Mean Absolute Error MAE = (1/3)(|2|+|−5|+|2|) = (1/3)(9) = 3.00
   469→  ● Significance: MSE (11.0) is pulled upward by the single larger error of −5, illustrating how
   470→    squaring emphasises big mistakes more than MAE does.
   471→
   472→4.3 Classification Loss — Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE)
   473→For a binary label y ∈ {0,1} and predicted probability p = P(y=1):
   474→
   475→                                      BCE = −[ y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p) ]
   476→
   477→  ● This comes from Maximum Likelihood: for y=1 we want p close to 1 (loss = −log p, small when
   478→    p→1); for y=0 we want p close to 0 (loss = −log(1−p), small when p→0).
   479→
   480→Numerical Example — Binary Cross-Entropy
   481→      y (actual)           p (predicted prob.)                     Loss formula used                                        Loss value
   482→ 1                        0.90                       −log(0.90)                                                   0.1054
   483→ 0                        0.20                       −log(1−0.20) = −log(0.80)                                    0.2231
   484→ 1                        0.60                       −log(0.60)                                                   0.5108
   485→
   486→
   487→  ● Average BCE over the 3 samples = (0.1054+0.2231+0.5108)/3 = 0.2798
   488→  ● Significance: sample 3 (y=1, p=0.60) contributes the largest loss because the model was correct
   489→    but not confident — BCE rewards confident, correct predictions and punishes confident, wrong

   191→                "**Initialise** — set weights $w_i$ and bias $b$ to 0 (or small random values); choose a learning rate $\\eta$, $0 < \\eta \\le 1$.",
   192→                "**For every training pair $(x, t)$** — (a) compute the net input $z = \\sum w_ix_i + b$; (b) compute the predicted output $y = f(z)$; (c) compute the error $e = t - y$; (d) update every weight $w_i \\leftarrow w_i + \\eta \\cdot e \\cdot x_i$; (e) update the bias $b \\leftarrow b + \\eta \\cdot e$.",
   193→                "**Repeat** — one pass over all examples is one **epoch**. Repeat over multiple epochs until an entire epoch produces **zero errors** (convergence), or a maximum number of epochs is reached.",
   194→              ],
   195→            },
   196→            {
   197→              type: "formula",
   198→              tex: "w_i(\\text{new}) = w_i(\\text{old}) + \\eta\\,(t-y)\\,x_i \\qquad b(\\text{new}) = b(\\text{old}) + \\eta\\,(t-y)",
   199→              caption: "The perceptron learning rule",
   200→            },
   201→            {
   202→              type: "callout",
   203→              variant: "info",
   204→              title: "Why does this update rule work?",
   205→              blocks: [
   206→                {
   207→                  type: "bullets",
   208→                  items: [
   209→                    "If the prediction is already correct ($e = 0$): no change is made — there is nothing to fix.",
   210→                    "If $t = 1$ but $y = 0$ ($e = +1$): weights increase along $x_i$, raising $z$ next time so it is more likely to cross the threshold and fire.",
   211→                    "If $t = 0$ but $y = 1$ ($e = -1$): weights decrease, lowering $z$ next time so it stays below threshold.",
   212→                  ],
   213→                },
   214→              ],
   215→            },

   223→                  value:

   767→            {
   768→              type: "bullets",
   769→              items: [
   770→                "A single perceptron can only learn a **linear boundary**. Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) stack hidden layers to model **non-linear** relationships.",
   771→                "But the simple perceptron rule does not say how to update weights feeding **hidden neurons** — there is no direct target for a hidden neuron's output.",
   772→                "Backpropagation solves this: it propagates the output error **backward through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule**, to compute $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for every weight — including hidden-layer weights.",
   773→              ],
   774→            },
   775→          ],
   776→        },
   777→        {
   778→          id: "u1-l5-s2",

   781→            {
   782→              type: "formula",
   783→              tex: "\\text{If } y = f(u) \\text{ and } u = g(x), \\quad \\text{then } \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy}{du}\\times\\frac{du}{dx}",
   784→            },
   785→            {
   786→              type: "example",

   790→                { label: "Local derivatives", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{du} = 2u = 14, \\qquad \\frac{du}{dx} = 2" }] },
   791→                { label: "Multiply", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{dx} = 14 \\times 2 = 28 \\;\\checkmark \\;(\\text{matches } 4(2x+1) = 28)" }] },
   792→                {
   793→                  label: "Significance",
   794→                  blocks: [
   795→                    {
   796→                      type: "text",
   797→                      value:
   798→                        "In a network, the Loss depends on a weight through a chain of nested functions (weight → net input → activation → … → Loss). Backpropagation is simply this chain rule applied repeatedly, one layer at a time.",
   799→                    },

   856→                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_2^{in} = 0.5(0.3)+0.3(0.1)+0.20 = 0.3800 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_2^{out} = \\sigma(0.38) = 0.5939" },

  1010→                "$\\eta$ (learning rate) controls the step size. **Too small** → very slow convergence. **Too large** → the loss can oscillate or diverge.",

   349→                "This limitation, highlighted by **Minsky & Papert (1969)**, was resolved by stacking multiple perceptron layers — the **Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)** — trained with **Backpropagation**.",
   350→                "XOR is solved by a **2-2-1 MLP** (2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons → 1 output neuron) with hard step activations — the output effectively computes $h_1 \\text{ AND } (\\text{NOT } h_2)$.",
   351→              ],
   352→            },

   758→      id: "u1-l5",
   759→      title: "Backpropagation",
   760→      subtitle: "The chain rule, applied layer by layer — with the complete 2-2-1 network worked example.",
   761→      minutes: 16,
   762→      sections: [
   763→        {
   764→          id: "u1-l5-s1",
   765→          title: "Why is backpropagation needed?",
   766→          blocks: [
   767→            {
   768→              type: "bullets",
   769→              items: [
   770→                "A single perceptron can only learn a **linear boundary**. Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) stack hidden layers to model **non-linear** relationships.",
   771→                "But the simple perceptron rule does not say how to update weights feeding **hidden neurons** — there is no direct target for a hidden neuron's output.",
   772→                "Backpropagation solves this: it propagates the output error **backward through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule**, to compute $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for every weight — including hidden-layer weights.",
   773→              ],
   774→            },
   775→          ],
   776→        },
   777→        {
   778→          id: "u1-l5-s2",
   779→          title: "The chain rule of differentiation",
   780→          blocks: [
   781→            {
   782→              type: "formula",
   783→              tex: "\\text{If } y = f(u) \\text{ and } u = g(x), \\quad \\text{then } \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy}{du}\\times\\frac{du}{dx}",
   784→            },
   785→            {
   786→              type: "example",
   787→              title: "Chain rule warm-up: y = (2x+1)² at x = 3",
   788→              steps: [
   789→                { label: "Substitute u = 2x+1", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "u = 2(3)+1 = 7, \\quad y = u^2 = 49" }] },
   790→                { label: "Local derivatives", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{du} = 2u = 14, \\qquad \\frac{du}{dx} = 2" }] },
   791→                { label: "Multiply", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{dx} = 14 \\times 2 = 28 \\;\\checkmark \\;(\\text{matches } 4(2x+1) = 28)" }] },
   792→                {
   793→                  label: "Significance",
   794→                  blocks: [
   795→                    {
   796→                      type: "text",
   797→                      value:
   798→                        "In a network, the Loss depends on a weight through a chain of nested functions (weight → net input → activation → … → Loss). Backpropagation is simply this chain rule applied repeatedly, one layer at a time.",
   799→                    },
   800→                  ],
   801→                },
   802→              ],
   803→            },
   804→          ],
   805→        },
   806→        {
   807→          id: "u1-l5-s3",
   808→          title: "Forward pass and backward pass",
   809→          blocks: [
   810→            {
   811→              type: "compare",
   812→              pairs: [
   813→                {
   814→                  label: "Forward pass",
   815→                  left: [
   816→                    "Inputs flow **left-to-right** through the network to produce a prediction",
   817→                    "Every intermediate activation is **stored** for later use",
   818→                  ],
   819→                },
   820→                {
   821→                  label: "Backward pass",
   822→                  left: [
   823→                    "Starting from the loss, gradients flow **right-to-left** using the chain rule",
   824→                    "Computes $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for **every** weight",
   825→                    "Update: every weight is then adjusted by gradient descent",
   826→                  ],
   827→                },
   828→              ],
   829→            },
   830→          ],
   831→        },
   832→        {
   833→          id: "u1-l5-s4",
   834→          title: "Complete worked example — 2-2-1 sigmoid network",
   835→          blocks: [
   836→            {
   837→              type: "widget",
   838→              widgetId: "u1-backprop-lab",
   839→              title: "Backpropagation lab — walk the exact numbers",
   840→              description: "Step through the forward pass, both backward passes and the weight update of the notes' 2-2-1 network. Change the inputs and watch every gradient recompute live.",
   841→            },
   842→            {
   843→              type: "example",
   844→              title: "Forward pass → backward pass → update (full calculation)",
   845→              given: [
   846→                "Network: 2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons (sigmoid) → 1 output neuron (sigmoid)",
   847→                "Inputs $x_1 = 0.5$, $x_2 = 0.3$ · Target = 1.0 · Learning rate $\\eta = 0.5$",
   848→                "Weights $w_1..w_6$ = 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, 0.5, 0.6 · Biases $b_{h1} = 0.25$, $b_{h2} = 0.20$, $b_o = 0.4$",
   849→                "Loss $L = \\frac{1}{2}(\\text{target} - \\text{output})^2$ · Sigmoid: $\\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$, $\\sigma'(z) = \\sigma(z)(1-\\sigma(z))$",
   850→              ],
   851→              steps: [
   852→                {
   853→                  label: "Step 1 — Forward pass",
   854→                  blocks: [
   855→                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_1^{in} = 0.5(0.2)+0.3(0.4)+0.25 = 0.4700 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_1^{out} = \\sigma(0.47) = 0.6154" },
   856→                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_2^{in} = 0.5(0.3)+0.3(0.1)+0.20 = 0.3800 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_2^{out} = \\sigma(0.38) = 0.5939" },

It is the fundamental building block of larger Multi-Layer Perceptrons.",
   129→            },

   133→            },

   182→          title: "The perceptron learning algorithm",
   183→          blocks: [
   184→            {
   185→              type: "text",
   186→              value: "Weights are learned iteratively so that the perceptron's output matches the desired target for every training example.",
   187→            },
   188→            {
   189→              type: "numbered",
   190→              items: [
   191→                "**Initialise** — set weights $w_i$ and bias $b$ to 0 (or small random values); choose a learning rate $\\eta$, $0 < \\eta \\le 1$.",
   192→                "**For every training pair $(x, t)$** — (a) compute the net input $z = \\sum w_ix_i + b$; (b) compute the predicted output $y = f(z)$; (c) compute the error $e = t - y$; (d) update every weight $w_i \\leftarrow w_i + \\eta \\cdot e \\cdot x_i$; (e) update the bias $b \\leftarrow b + \\eta \\cdot e$.",
   193→                "**Repeat** — one pass over all examples is one **epoch**. Repeat over multiple epochs until an entire epoch produces **zero errors** (convergence), or a maximum number of epochs is reached.",
   194→              ],
   195→            },
   196→            {
   197→              type: "formula",

   766→          blocks: [
   767→            {
   768→              type: "bullets",
   769→              items: [
   770→                "A single perceptron can only learn a **linear boundary**. Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) stack hidden layers to model **non-linear** relationships.",
   771→                "But the simple perceptron rule does not say how to update weights feeding **hidden neurons** — there is no direct target for a hidden neuron's output.",
   772→                "Backpropagation solves this: it propagates the output error **backward through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule**, to compute $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for every weight — including hidden-layer weights.",
   773→              ],
   774→            },
   775→          ],
   776→        },
   777→        {
   778→          id: "u1-l5-s2",
   779→          title: "The chain rule of differentiation",
   780→          blocks: [
   781→            {
   782→              type: "formula",
   783→              tex: "\\text{If } y = f(u) \\text{ and } u = g(x), \\quad \\text{then } \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy}{du}\\times\\frac{du}{dx}",
   784→            },
   785→            {
   786→              type: "example",
   787→              title: "Chain rule warm-up: y = (2x+1)² at x = 3",
   788→              steps: [
   789→                { label: "Substitute u = 2x+1", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "u = 2(3)+1 = 7, \\quad y = u^2 = 49" }] },
   790→                { label: "Local derivatives", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{du} = 2u = 14, \\qquad \\frac{du}{dx} = 2" }] },
   791→                { label: "Multiply", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{dx} = 14 \\times 2 = 28 \\;\\checkmark \\;(\\text{matches } 4(2x+1) = 28)" }] },
   792→                {
   793→                  label: "Significance",
   794→                  blocks: [
   795→                    {
   796→                      type: "text",
   797→                      value:
   798→                        "In a network, the Loss depends on a weight through a chain of nested functions (weight → net input → activation → … → Loss). Backpropagation is simply this chain rule applied repeatedly, one layer at a time.",
   799→                    },
   800→                  ],
   801→                },
   802→              ],
   803→            },
   804→          ],
   805→        },
   806→        {

   812→              pairs: [
   813→                {
   814→                  label: "Forward pass",
   815→                  left: [
   816→                    "Inputs flow **left-to-right** through the network to produce a prediction",
   817→                    "Every intermediate activation is **stored** for later use",
   818→                  ],
   819→                },

   848→                "Weights $w_1..w_6$ = 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, 0.5, 0.6 · Biases $b_{h1} = 0.25$, $b_{h2} = 0.20$, $b_o = 0.4$",
   849→                "Loss $L = \\frac{1}{2}(\\text{target} - \\text{output})^2$ · Sigmoid: $\\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$, $\\sigma'(z) = \\sigma(z)(1-\\sigma(z))$",

   856→                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_2^{in} = 0.5(0.3)+0.3(0.1)+0.20 = 0.3800 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_2^{out} = \\sigma(0.38) = 0.5939" },

   162→
   163→1. Introduction to Sequential Data and Recurrent Neural
   164→Networks
   165→
   166→1.1 What Is Sequential Data?
   167→     •    Sequential data is data in which order carries meaning — rearranging the elements changes (or
   168→          destroys) the meaning. This is different from ordinary tabular data, where the order of rows does
   169→          not matter.
   170→Common examples of sequential data:
   171→
   172→     •    Text / language — a sentence is a sequence of words; “dog bites man” ≠ “man bites dog”.
   173→     •    Speech / audio — a sequence of sound-pressure samples over time.
   174→     •    Time series — stock prices, weather readings, sensor logs: a sequence of numeric values indexed
   175→          by time.
   176→     •    Video — a sequence of image frames.
   177→     •    Biological sequences — DNA base pairs, protein amino-acid chains.
   178→Sequential data shares three properties that any model must respect:
   179→
   180→     •    It can be of variable length (sentences are not all the same number of words).
   181→     •    It is order-dependent (shuffling the elements changes the meaning).
   182→     •    It often has long-range dependencies — something at position 2 can affect the correct
   183→          interpretation of position 50.
   184→
   185→1.2 Why Feedforward Networks Struggle with Sequences
   186→A standard feedforward network (MLP) or a plain CNN expects one fixed-size input vector and produces
   187→one output, independently of any other input it has ever seen. This creates four concrete problems for
   188→sequence data:
   189→
   190→     •    Fixed input size. An MLP needs a fixed number of input features, but sentences and time series
   191→          vary in length.
   192→     •    No memory. Each input is processed in isolation; the network has no mechanism to “remember”
   193→          earlier inputs when processing the current one.
   194→     •    No parameter sharing across positions. If we tried to flatten a sequence into one long fixed
   195→          vector, the network would need separate weights for “word at position 5” versus “word at
   196→          position 50” — this does not generalise to lengths not seen in training and wastes parameters.
   197→     •    Violates the independence assumption. Standard supervised learning assumes examples are
   198→          independent; elements inside a sequence are, by definition, statistically dependent on their
   199→          neighbours.
   200→
   201→
   202→
   203→
   204→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                 Page 5 of 41
   205→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   206→
   207→
   208→
   209→
   210→  Figure 1. A feedforward network has no memory; a recurrent network feeds its hidden state back into itself, carrying
   211→                                     information from one time step to the next.
   212→
   213→
   214→Key Insight
   215→A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) fixes all four problems at once by introducing a hidden state that is
   216→updated at every time step using the same weights. This single idea — a feedback loop with shared
   217→parameters — is what allows one compact model to process sequences of any length.
   218→
   219→
   220→1.3 The Core Idea of a Recurrent Network
   221→      •   An RNN maintains a hidden state (also called the “context” or “memory”), denoted ht
   222→      •   At every time step t, the network reads the current input xt and combines it with the previous
   223→          hidden state ht−1 to produce a new hidden state ht.
   224→      •   The same weight matrices are reused at every time step (parameter sharing across time). This
   225→          is the single most important structural idea in this unit — it is what lets a fixed-size set of
   226→          parameters handle sequences of any length.
   227→      •   ht acts as a compressed summary of everything the network has read up to and including time t.
   228→      •   An output yt (a class label, a predicted next word, a predicted next value, etc.) can be produced
   229→          from ht at any time step where one is needed.
   230→                                     ht = f(xt, ht−1)   — general recurrence relation
   231→
   232→1.4 Notation Used Throughout This Unit
   233→The table below fixes the notation used in every section that follows, so that the same symbol always
   234→means the same thing.
   235→
   236→           Symbol                                                    Meaning
   237→
   238→ xt                              Input vector at time step t
   239→
   240→ ht                              Hidden state (memory) at time step t
   241→
   242→ yt                              Output produced at time step t
   243→
   244→ Wxh, Whh, Why                   Weight matrices: input→hidden, hidden→hidden, hidden→output
   245→
   246→
   247→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                          Page 6 of 41

   249→
   250→
   251→
   252→
   253→           Symbol                                                 Meaning
   254→
   255→ bh, by                          Bias vectors for the hidden and output layers
   256→
   257→ tanh, σ                         Hyperbolic-tangent and sigmoid activation functions
   258→
   259→ ⊙                               Element-wise (Hadamard) product
   260→
   261→ L                               Loss function
   262→
   263→ ∂L / ∂□                         Partial derivative of the loss with respect to □ (used in backpropagation)
   264→
   265→ T                               Length of the input sequence

   267→
   268→1.5 Applications of Recurrent Networks
   269→Because they can model dependencies across time, recurrent networks (and their gated variants, LSTM
   270→and GRU) have been used across a wide range of tasks:
   271→
   272→     •    Language modelling and text generation (predicting the next word/character).
   273→     •    Machine translation (sequence-to-sequence, encoder–decoder models).
   274→     •    Speech recognition (audio waveform → text).
   275→     •    Sentiment analysis and text classification.
   276→     •    Time-series forecasting — stock prices, electricity demand, weather.
   277→     •    Music and handwriting generation.
   278→     •    Video captioning and action recognition.
   279→     •    Chatbots and dialogue systems (largely superseded today by Transformers, but RNNs remain the
   280→          conceptual foundation and are still used in resource-constrained / streaming settings).
   281→
   282→
   283→
   284→
   285→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                      Page 7 of 41

   290→
   291→2. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
   292→
   293→2.1 Architecture
   294→     •    A simple (“vanilla”) RNN is a single cell that is applied repeatedly, once per time step, with the
   295→          same weights every time.
   296→     •    Drawing this repetition out explicitly over time steps is called unrolling the network — it turns
   297→          the recurrent (looped) picture into an ordinary, feedforward-looking computational graph that
   298→          we can apply standard backpropagation to.
   299→
   300→
   301→
   302→
   303→ Figure 2. An RNN drawn as a single folded cell (left) and unrolled across three time steps (right). Every column uses the
   304→                                      identical weight matrices Wxh, Whh, Why.
   305→
   306→     •    Zooming into a single time step shows exactly what happens inside the cell:
   307→
   308→
   309→
   310→
   311→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                            Page 8 of 41
   312→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                       Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   313→
   314→
   315→
   316→
   317→         Figure 3. Inside one RNN cell at time step t: the previous hidden state and the current input are each linearly
   318→                  transformed, summed with a bias, and squashed by tanh to produce the new hidden state.
   319→
   320→2.2 Forward-Pass Equations
   321→                                                     at = Wxh xt + Whh ht−1 + bh
   322→
   323→                                                           ht = tanh(at)
   324→
   325→                                                          yt = Why ht + by
   326→
   327→Significance of each term:
   328→
   329→     •     Wxh xt — brings in new information from the current input.
   330→     •     Whh ht−1 — brings forward everything remembered so far from the past.
   331→     •     tanh(·) — a nonlinearity that (a) lets the network represent non-linear relationships and (b)
   332→           squashes the state into (−1, 1), keeping it numerically bounded step after step.
   333→     •     Why ht + by — a read-out layer that turns the internal memory into whatever output the task
   334→           needs (a class score, a predicted value, next-word logits, …).
   335→
   336→2.3 Worked Example 1 — RNN Forward Pass, Step by Step
   337→Given
   338→Input sequence (T = 3, input size 2): x₁ = [1.0000, 0.5000], x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000], x₃ = [-0.5000,
   339→1.0000]
   340→Initial hidden state: h₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000] (hidden size 2)
   341→Wxh = [[0.5000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.4000]], Whh = [[0.1000, 0.4000], [-0.2000, 0.3000]], bh =
   342→[0.1000, -0.1000]
   343→Why = [[0.6000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.5000]], by = [0.1000, 0.2000]
   344→
   345→
   346→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                               Page 9 of 41
   347→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                 Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   348→
   349→
   350→
   351→Step 1 — Compute h₁ (process the first input)
   352→We need a1 = Wxh x1 + Whh h0 + bh. Since h0 = [0.0000, 0.0000], the recurrent term contributes nothing yet
   353→— this is the very first step, so there is no history to bring forward.
   354→Wxh x₁ = (0.5×1.0 + (−0.3)×0.5, 0.2×1.0 + 0.4×0.5) = (0.35, 0.40)
   355→
   356→a₁ = (0.35, 0.40) + (0, 0) + (0.1, −0.1) = [0.4500, 0.3000]
   357→
   358→h₁ = tanh([0.4500, 0.3000]) = [0.4219, 0.2913]
   359→
   360→Why this step matters
   361→tanh squashes each pre-activation into (−1, 1). Both components of a₁ were modest in size, so tanh has
   362→not saturated — the gradient through this step will still be healthy (we revisit this idea in Section 2.7).
   363→
   364→Step 2 — Compute h₂ (now the recurrence is active)
   365→Wxh x₂ = (0.5×0.5 + (−0.3)×(−1.0), 0.2×0.5 + 0.4×(−1.0)) = (0.5500, −0.3000)
   366→
   367→Whh h₁ = (0.1×0.4219 + 0.4×0.2913, −0.2×0.4219 + 0.3×0.2913) = (0.1587, 0.0030)
   368→
   369→a₂ = (0.5500, −0.3000) + (0.1587, 0.0030) + (0.1, −0.1) = [0.8087, -0.3970]
   370→
   371→h₂ = tanh([0.8087, -0.3970]) = [0.6689, -0.3774]
   372→
   373→     •    Notice that h₂ depends on x₂ and on h₁ (which itself depended on x₁). This is exactly how the RNN
   374→          carries information forward — h₂ already contains a trace of x₁.
   375→
   376→Step 3 — Compute h₃
   377→Wxh x₃ = (−0.5500, 0.3000),            Whh h₂ = (−0.0841, −0.2470)
   378→
   379→a₃ = [-0.5341, -0.0470]         ⇒      h₃ = tanh([-0.5341, -0.0470]) = [-0.4885, -0.0470]
   380→
   381→Step 4 — Produce the output y₃
   382→y₃ = Why h₃ + by = [[0.6000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.5000]] × [-0.4885, -0.0470] + [0.1000, 0.2000] = [-0.1790,
   383→0.0788]
   384→
   385→     •    This is a many-to-one read-out: we only needed an output at the final time step (e.g. classifying
   386→          the whole sequence). If a prediction were needed at every step, the same Why, by read-out
   387→          would be applied to h₁ and h₂ as well.
   388→                                            Table 1. Summary of Worked Example 1.
   389→
   390→     t             Input x_t                         Pre-activation a_t         Hidden state h_t = tanh(a_t)
   391→
   392→ 1         [1.0000, 0.5000]              [0.4500, 0.3000]                   [0.4219, 0.2913]
   393→
   394→ 2         [0.5000, -1.0000]             [0.8087, -0.3970]                  [0.6689, -0.3774]
   395→
   396→                                                                            [-0.4885, -0.0470] → y₃ = [-
   397→ 3         [-0.5000, 1.0000]             [-0.5341, -0.0470]
   398→                                                                            0.1790, 0.0788]
   399→

   401→
   402→

   407→
   408→2.4 Types of RNN Architectures
   409→The recurrence itself never changes; what changes from application to application is simply where inputs
   410→enter and where outputs are read out.
   411→
   412→
   413→
   414→
   415→                  Figure 4. Five standard input/output wiring patterns built from the same recurrent cell.
   416→
   417→     •    One-to-one — a single input maps to a single output; degenerates to a normal feedforward layer
   418→          (rarely used with recurrence, shown for completeness).
   419→     •    One-to-many — one input, a whole output sequence (e.g. image captioning: one image → a
   420→          sentence).
   421→     •    Many-to-one — a whole input sequence, one output (e.g. sentiment classification) — this is the
   422→          pattern used in Worked Example 1 above.
   423→     •    Many-to-many (aligned) — one output per input, same length (e.g. part-of-speech tagging).
   424→     •    Many-to-many (encoder–decoder) — an encoder RNN compresses the input into a context
   425→          vector; a separate decoder RNN generates the (possibly different-length) output sequence from
   426→          it (e.g. machine translation).
   427→
   428→2.5 Training an RNN: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT)
   429→     •    Idea: unroll the RNN for all T time steps (as in Figure 2), which turns it into one large feedforward
   430→          computational graph — then apply ordinary backpropagation to that graph.
   431→     •    Because the same weight matrix (say Whh) is reused at every time step, its total gradient is the
   432→          sum of the gradient contributed at every time step:
   433→                                              ∂L/∂Whh = Σₜ₌₁ᵀ ∂L/∂at ⊗ ht−1
   434→
   435→
   436→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                           Page 11 of 41
   437→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                               Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   438→
   439→
   440→
   441→     •    Each backward step from ht to ht−1 multiplies the incoming gradient by Whhᵀ and by the local tanh
   442→          derivative — this repeated multiplication is the root cause of the vanishing/exploding gradient
   443→          problem (Section 2.7).
   444→
   445→
   446→
   447→
   448→Figure 5. BPTT: the loss gradient flows backward through every copy of the network, moving from h3 back to h2, h1 and
   449→                                                          h0.
   450→
   451→2.6 Worked Example 2 — BPTT Gradient Computation
   452→Given
   453→Continue Worked Example 1. A target output target₃ = [1.0000, 0.0000] is supplied (one-hot encoding
   454→for class 0), and the squared-error loss is applied at the final time step only (a many-to-one setup):
   455→
   456→                 L = ½ ‖ y₃ − target₃ ‖² = ½ ‖ [-0.1790, 0.0788] − [1.0000, 0.0000] ‖² = 0.6981
   457→
   458→Step 1 — Gradient at the output
   459→∂L/∂y₃ = y₃ − target₃ = [-0.1790, 0.0788] − [1.0000, 0.0000] = [-1.1790, 0.0788]
   460→
   461→     •    For squared error, ∂L/∂y = predicted − target — the gradient simply points from the prediction
   462→          toward the target, scaled by the error.
   463→
   464→Step 2 — Backprop into h₃ through the output layer
   465→∂L/∂h₃ = Whyᵀ ∂L/∂y₃ = [[0.6000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.5000]]ᵀ × [-1.1790, 0.0788] = [-0.6916, 0.3931]
   466→
   467→Step 3 — Backprop through tanh at t = 3
   468→     •    The derivative of tanh is 1 − tanh²(a) = 1 − h², evaluated using the already-computed forward-
   469→          pass value — this is why we saved every h_t during the forward pass.
   470→∂L/∂a₃ = ∂L/∂h₃ ⊙ (1 − h₃²) = [-0.6916, 0.3931] ⊙ (1 − [-0.4885, -0.0470]²) = [-0.5266, 0.3922]
   471→
   472→
   473→
   474→
   475→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                      Page 12 of 41
   476→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   477→
   478→
   479→
   480→Step 4 — Gradient contribution to Whh from t = 3
   481→∂L/∂Whh |₃ = ∂L/∂a₃ ⊗ h₂ = [-0.5266, 0.3922] ⊗ [0.6689, -0.3774] = [[-0.3522, 0.1987], [0.2624, -
   482→0.1480]]
   483→
   484→     •    “⊗” here is an outer product: a gradient vector combined with the hidden state that was
   485→          multiplied by Whh on the forward pass — this is the standard rule for the gradient of a matrix
   486→          multiplication.
   487→
   488→Step 5 — Propagate the gradient back one more step, to h₂
   489→∂L/∂h₂ = Whhᵀ ∂L/∂a₃ = [[0.1000, 0.4000], [-0.2000, 0.3000]]ᵀ × [-0.5266, 0.3922] = [-0.1311, -0.0930]
   490→
   491→∂L/∂a₂ = [-0.1311, -0.0930] ⊙ (1 − [0.6689, -0.3774]²) = [-0.0725, -0.0797]
   492→
   493→∂L/∂Whh |₂ = [-0.0725, -0.0797] ⊗ [0.4219, 0.2913] = [[-0.0306, -0.0211], [-0.0336, -0.0232]]
   494→
   495→Step 6 — Propagate back to h₁, then to h₀
   496→∂L/∂h₁ = [[0.1000, 0.4000], [-0.2000, 0.3000]]ᵀ × [-0.0725, -0.0797] = [0.0087, -0.0529]           ⇒      ∂L/∂a₁ =
   497→[0.0072, -0.0484]
   498→
   499→∂L/∂Whh |₁ = [0.0072, -0.0484] ⊗ [0.0000, 0.0000] = [[0.0000, 0.0000], [0.0000, 0.0000]]
   500→
   501→Why this term is zero
   502→The contribution at t = 1 is multiplied by h₀ = (0, 0), the initial hidden state. With a zero initial state
   503→there is nothing for the very first step to “multiply against” for this particular weight, so its contribution
   504→vanishes.
   505→This is a special case of using a zero initial state, not a general property of BPTT: the gradient signal
   506→∂L/∂h₁ itself is still non-zero, so it correctly continues to update Wxh and bh through this step.
   507→
   508→Step 7 — Total gradient (sum over all time steps)
   509→                                 ∂L/∂Whh = ∂L/∂Whh|₁ + ∂L/∂Whh|₂ + ∂L/∂Whh|₃
   510→
   511→[[0.0000, 0.0000], [0.0000, 0.0000]] + [[-0.0306, -0.0211], [-0.0336, -0.0232]] + [[-0.3522, 0.1987],
   512→[0.2624, -0.1480]] = [[-0.3828, 0.1776], [0.2287, -0.1712]]
   513→
   514→     •    The same mechanism (chain rule + outer product with the relevant input, summed across time)
   515→          also gives ∂L/∂Wxh = [[0.2342, -0.4506], [-0.2844, 0.4478]] and ∂L/∂Why = [[0.5759, 0.0554], [-
   516→          0.0385, -0.0037]]; these are left as Practice Question 32.
   517→
   518→2.7 The Vanishing and Exploding Gradient Problem
   519→     •    Look again at Steps 5–6 above: every step back multiplies the gradient by Whhᵀ and by a tanh-
   520→          derivative factor that is always ≤ 1.
   521→     •    Over T time steps this becomes roughly a product of T such factors — informally, gradient ∝ λᵀ,
   522→          where λ reflects the typical size of Whhᵀ × tanh′.
   523→     •    If λ < 1: the product shrinks exponentially with T — the vanishing gradient problem. Early time
   524→          steps receive a near-zero learning signal, so the network effectively cannot learn long-range
   525→          dependencies.
   526→
   527→
   528→
   529→
   530→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 13 of 41
   531→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                    Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   532→
   533→
   534→
   535→      •    If λ > 1: the product grows exponentially — the exploding gradient problem. Weight updates
   536→           become huge and training diverges (loss becomes NaN / oscillates wildly).
   537→
   538→
   539→
   540→
   541→  Figure 6. Relative gradient magnitude after k backward steps, for three illustrative values of λ. Even a modest λ = 0.5
   542→                              leaves almost nothing after 10 steps; λ = 1.5 grows past 50×.
   543→
   544→                      Table 2. Illustrative decay/growth of |λ^k| with the number of backward steps k.
   545→
   546→          k (steps back)             λ = 0.5 (vanishing)          λ = 1.0 (stable)            λ = 1.5 (exploding)
   547→
   548→ 1                                         0.5000                       1.00                         1.5000
   549→
   550→ 2                                         0.2500                       1.00                         2.2500
   551→
   552→ 3                                         0.1250                       1.00                         3.3750
   553→
   554→ 5                                         0.03125                      1.00                         7.5938
   555→
   556→ 10                                       0.000977                      1.00                         57.665
   557→Standard mitigations used in practice:
   558→
   559→      •    Gradient clipping — rescale the gradient if its norm exceeds a threshold; a simple, effective fix
   560→           for exploding gradients.
   561→      •    Careful weight initialisation (e.g. orthogonal initialisation of Whh) — keeps λ close to 1 for
   562→           longer.
   563→      •    Truncated BPTT — limit how many steps gradients are propagated back through, trading long-
   564→           range learning for stability/speed.
   565→      •    Gated architectures — LSTM and GRU — redesign the recurrence itself so that gradients can
   566→           flow across many steps largely unimpeded. This is the main solution used in practice, and is the
   567→           subject of the next two sections.
   568→
   569→
   570→
   571→
   572→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                           Page 14 of 41
   573→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   574→
   575→
   576→
   577→
   578→3. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
   579→
   580→3.1 Motivation
   581→     •    Plain RNNs struggle to learn long-range dependencies because gradients shrink (or blow up)
   582→          exponentially as they are backpropagated through many time steps (Section 2.7).
   583→     •    LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) fixes this by giving the network a separate memory
   584→          channel — the cell state — that information can flow along with only minor, mostly linear
   585→          changes, instead of being repeatedly squashed through a matrix multiply and a tanh at every
   586→          step.
   587→     •    Three gates (small neural networks with sigmoid outputs in (0, 1)) learn when to write to, erase
   588→          from, and read from this memory.
   589→
   590→3.2 Architecture
   591→     •    Cell state Ct — the long-term memory “conveyor belt” running along the top of the diagram
   592→          below.
   593→     •    Forget gate ft — decides what fraction of the old cell state to keep.
   594→     •    Input gate it — decides how much of the new candidate information to write in.
   595→     •    Candidate c̃t — the new content proposed for the cell state (not yet gated).
   596→     •    Output gate ot — decides how much of the (updated) cell state to expose as the hidden state /
   597→          output.
   598→
   599→
   600→
   601→
   602→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 15 of 41
   603→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   604→
   605→
   606→
   607→
   608→ Figure 7. Internal structure of one LSTM cell. The cell state Ct runs along the top with only element-wise operations —
   609→                                     this is what protects the gradient from vanishing.
   610→
   611→3.3 Equations
   612→All four gates/candidates first form the same concatenated input, then apply their own weights:
   613→
   614→                    zₜ = [ hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ ]    (concatenate previous hidden state and current input)
   615→
   616→                                                        ft = σ(Wf zₜ + bf)
   617→
   618→                                                        it = σ(Wi zₜ + bi)
   619→
   620→                                                      c̃t = tanh(Wc zₜ + bc)
   621→
   622→                                                     Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t
   623→
   624→                                                       ot = σ(Wo zₜ + bo)
   625→
   626→                                                       ht = ot ⊙ tanh(Ct)
   627→
   628→Significance of each equation:
   629→
   630→     •    Forget gate — a sigmoid output near 0 erases that part of memory; near 1 preserves it
   631→          completely.
   632→     •    Input gate × candidate — the network only writes new information where the input gate allows
   633→          it, protecting unrelated parts of memory.
   634→
   635→
   636→
   637→
   638→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                         Page 16 of 41
   639→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   640→
   641→
   642→
   643→     •    Cell-state update — additive and element-wise (no matrix multiply, no squashing) — this is the
   644→          key structural difference from a plain RNN, and is what allows gradients to flow across many steps
   645→          largely unchanged (Section 3.5).
   646→     •    Output gate — the cell can hold information in Ct without necessarily exposing it in ht — memory
   647→          and “what to output right now” are decoupled.
   648→
   649→3.4 Worked Example 3 — LSTM Forward Pass, Step by Step
   650→Given
   651→Same two inputs as the RNN example, so the two architectures can be compared directly: x₁ = [1.0000,
   652→0.5000], x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000]
   653→Initial state: h₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000], C₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000]
   654→Wf = [[0.3,0.1,0.2,-0.1],[-0.2,0.4,0.1,0.3]], bf = [0.1000, 0.0000]
   655→Wi = [[0.2,-0.3,0.4,0.1],[0.1,0.2,-0.2,0.3]], bi = [0.0000, 0.1000]
   656→Wc = [[0.4,0.1,-0.3,0.2],[-0.1,0.3,0.2,0.1]], bc = [0.1000, -0.1000]
   657→Wo = [[0.3,0.2,0.1,-0.2],[0.2,-0.1,0.3,0.1]], bo = [0.0000, 0.2000]
   658→
   659→Time step t = 1
   660→Step 1.1 — Build the concatenated input: z₁ = [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 0, 1.0, 0.5]
   661→Step 1.2 — Forget gate: Wf z₁ + bf = (0.15, 0.25) + (0.1, 0.0) = (0.25, 0.25) ⇒ f₁ = σ(0.25, 0.25) =
   662→[0.5622, 0.5622]
   663→
   664→Step 1.3 — Input gate: Wi z₁ + bi = (0.45, −0.05) + (0.0, 0.1) = (0.45, 0.05) ⇒ i₁ = σ(0.45, 0.05) = [0.6106,
   665→0.5125]
   666→Step 1.4 — Candidate cell content: Wc z₁ + bc = (−0.3, 0.25) + (0.1, −0.1) = (−0.2, 0.15) ⇒ c̃₁ = tanh(−0.2,
   667→0.15) = [-0.0997, 0.1489]
   668→Step 1.5 — Update the cell state: C₁ = f₁⊙C₀ + i₁⊙c̃₁ = [0.5622, 0.5622]⊙[0.0000, 0.0000] + [0.6106,
   669→0.5125]⊙[-0.0997, 0.1489] = [0.0000, 0.0000] + [-0.0609, 0.0763] = [-0.0609, 0.0763]
   670→     •    Because C₀ = (0, 0), the forget gate has nothing to act on yet — the entire cell state at t = 1 comes
   671→          from the new candidate, scaled by the input gate.
   672→Step 1.6 — Output gate: Wo z₁ + bo = (0.0, 0.35) + (0.0, 0.2) = (0.0, 0.55) ⇒ o₁ = σ(0.0, 0.55) = [0.5000,
   673→0.6341]
   674→Step 1.7 — Hidden state: h₁ = o₁⊙tanh(C₁) = [0.5000, 0.6341]⊙tanh([-0.0609, 0.0763]) = [-0.0304,
   675→0.0483]
   676→
   677→Time step t = 2
   678→The identical six equations are applied again, now using h₁ and C₁ from the previous step and the new
   679→input x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000]: z₂ = [h₁ ; x₂] = [-0.0304, 0.0483, 0.5000, -1.0000]

   704→Compare with the plain RNN
   705→At t = 1 the plain RNN produced h₁ = [0.4219, 0.2913] (Worked Example 1); the LSTM produces h₁ = [-
   706→0.0304, 0.0483] from the
   707→same input. The values differ because the LSTM's gates are actively controlling how much new
   708→information enters the state — with these particular (untrained, illustrative) weights the gates happen
   709→to let relatively little through. After training on real data, the gates learn to open and close purposefully.
   710→
   711→
   712→3.5 Why LSTM Solves the Vanishing Gradient Problem
   713→     •    Recall from Section 2.7 that a plain RNN's gradient must pass through a matrix multiply by Whh
   714→          and a tanh derivative at every single step — repeated many times, this shrinks (or explodes)
   715→          exponentially.
   716→     •    The LSTM cell-state recurrence is Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + (new term) — this is additive, so ∂Ct/∂Ct−1 = ft
   717→          (an element-wise scaling, not a matrix multiply followed by a squashing nonlinearity).
   718→     •    If the forget gate learns to stay close to 1 for information that should be remembered, the
   719→          gradient can flow backward through many time steps with almost no shrinkage — an unimpeded
   720→          “gradient highway” along the cell state.
   721→     •    This does not eliminate vanishing gradients entirely (very long sequences can still be difficult, and
   722→          the hidden-state path through tanh still exists), but it dramatically extends how far back an RNN-
   723→          family model can learn useful dependencies — this is the single biggest reason LSTMs outperform
   724→          plain RNNs in practice.
   725→
   726→3.6 Advantages and Limitations
   727→     •    Advantages: learns long-range dependencies far better than a plain RNN; the gating mechanism
   728→          is learned end-to-end from data; remains a strong, well-understood baseline for sequence tasks.
   729→     •    Limitations: four sets of weights (forget, input, candidate, output) means roughly 4× the
   730→          parameters of a plain RNN of the same hidden size (Section 6); inherently sequential computation
   731→          makes it slower to train than fully parallel architectures such as Transformers; still not immune
   732→          to very long sequences (hundreds/thousands of steps).
   733→

   735→
   736→
