   742→
   743→4. Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)
   744→
   745→4.1 Motivation
   746→     •    Introduced by Cho et al. (2014), the GRU asks: can we get most of the benefit of LSTM's gating —
   747→          protection against vanishing gradients, learned control over memory — with a simpler cell?
   748→     •    GRU merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate, and removes the separate cell
   749→          state entirely — the hidden state itself carries long-term memory.
   750→     •    Fewer gates means fewer parameters (Section 6) and typically faster training, while remaining
   751→          competitive with LSTM on many tasks.
   752→
   753→4.2 Architecture
   754→     •    Update gate zt — decides how much of the old hidden state to keep versus how much of the new
   755→          candidate to mix in. It plays the combined role of LSTM's forget and input gates.
   756→     •    Reset gate rt — decides how much of the past hidden state to use when forming the new
   757→          candidate content.
   758→     •    Candidate hidden state h̃t — a proposed new hidden-state value, computed using the reset
   759→          (partially forgotten) past state.
   760→     •    No separate cell state — ht itself is the blend of old and new content.
   761→
   762→
   763→
   764→
   765→Figure 8. Internal structure of one GRU cell. The final blend node interpolates between the old hidden state and the new
   766→                                   candidate, controlled entirely by the update gate zt.
   767→
   768→
   769→
   770→
   771→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                         Page 19 of 41
   772→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                               Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   773→
   774→
   775→
   776→
   777→4.3 Equations
   778→                    zₜ = [ hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ ]    (concatenate previous hidden state and current input)
   779→
   780→                                                      zt = σ(Wz zₜ + bz)
   781→
   782→                                                       rt = σ(Wr zₜ + br)
   783→
   784→                                             h̃t = tanh(Wh [ rt ⊙ ht−1 ; xt ] + bh)
   785→
   786→                                                ht = (1 − zt) ⊙ ht−1 + zt ⊙ h̃t
   787→
   788→Significance of each equation:
   789→
   790→     •    Update gate — close to 0 keeps the old state almost unchanged; close to 1 replaces it almost
   791→          entirely with the new candidate.
   792→     •    Reset gate — close to 0 makes the candidate ignore the past and depend mostly on the current
   793→          input (useful when starting a new, unrelated chunk of a sequence, e.g. a new sentence).
   794→     •    Final blend — a convex combination (weights sum to 1) of old state and new candidate. Like the
   795→          LSTM cell-state update, this blend is dominated by simple arithmetic rather than repeated matrix
   796→          multiplication, which is what protects the gradient.
   797→
   798→4.4 Worked Example 4 — GRU Forward Pass, Step by Step
   799→Given
   800→Same two inputs again, for direct comparison with the RNN and LSTM examples: x₁ = [1.0000, 0.5000],
   801→x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000]
   802→Initial hidden state: h₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000]
   803→Wz = [[0.2,-0.1,0.3,0.1],[0.1,0.3,-0.2,0.2]], bz = [0.1000, 0.0000]
   804→Wr = [[0.4,0.2,-0.1,0.3],[-0.2,0.1,0.2,-0.3]], br = [0.0000, 0.1000]
   805→Wh = [[0.3,-0.2,0.4,0.1],[0.2,0.1,-0.3,0.2]], bh = [0.1000, -0.1000]
   806→
   807→Time step t = 1
   808→Step 1.1 — Build the concatenated input: z₁(input) = [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 0, 1.0, 0.5]
   809→Step 1.2 — Update gate: Wz·z₁ + bz = (0.35, −0.10) + (0.1, 0.0) = (0.45, −0.10) ⇒ z₁ = σ(0.45, −0.10) =
   810→[0.6106, 0.4750]
   811→Step 1.3 — Reset gate: Wr·z₁ + br = (0.05, 0.05) + (0.0, 0.1) = (0.05, 0.15) ⇒ r₁ = σ(0.05, 0.15) = [0.5125,
   812→0.5374]
   813→Step 1.4 — Apply the reset gate to the past state: r₁⊙h₀ = [0.5125, 0.5374]⊙[0.0000, 0.0000] = (0, 0)
   814→— with h₀ = 0 there is nothing to reset yet, so this step has no visible effect at t = 1 (its role becomes clear
   815→at t = 2).
   816→Step 1.5 — Candidate hidden state: Wh·[r₁⊙h₀ ; x₁] + bh = (0.45, −0.20) + (0.1, −0.1) = (0.55, −0.30) ⇒
   817→h̃ ₁ = tanh(0.55, −0.30) = [0.5005, -0.2913]
   818→Step 1.6 — Final blend (this is h₁): h₁ = (1−z₁)⊙h₀ + z₁⊙h̃ ₁ = (1−[0.6106, 0.4750])⊙[0.0000, 0.0000] +
   819→[0.6106, 0.4750]⊙[0.5005, -0.2913] = [0.3056, -0.1384]
   820→     •    Because h₀ = 0, the first term vanishes and h₁ is simply z₁ ⊙ h̃₁ — the update gate scales down
   821→          how much of the fresh candidate is accepted.
   822→

   830→z₂(input) = [h₁ ; x₂] = [0.3056, -0.1384, 0.5000, -1.0000]

   854→— this is Practice Question 21.
   855→
   856→4.5 GRU vs LSTM
   857→     •    GRU has no output gate — the full hidden state is always exposed (LSTM can hide part of its cell
   858→          state from the output via the output gate).
   859→     •    GRU has no separate cell state — memory and output are the same vector, which simplifies the
   860→          design but gives slightly less representational flexibility.
   861→     •    GRU uses one combined update gate where LSTM uses two independent gates (forget, input) —
   862→          fewer parameters, slightly less fine-grained control.
   863→     •    In practice, the two perform comparably on many tasks; GRU is often preferred when training
   864→          speed / parameter budget matters, LSTM when maximum modelling flexibility is preferred. Both
   865→          comfortably outperform a plain RNN on long sequences.

   875→
   876→5. Recurrent Neural Network Language Models
   877→
   878→5.1 What Is a Language Model?
   879→     •    A language model assigns a probability to sequences of words, or equivalently, predicts a
   880→          probability distribution over the next word given all the words seen so far.
   881→     •    Formally, for a sequence of words w1, …, wT, a language model estimates:
   882→                     P(w₁, …, wᵀ) = P(w₁) · P(w₂ | w₁) · P(w₃ | w₁, w₂) · ⋯ · P(wᵀ | w₁, …, wᵀ₋₁)
   883→
   884→     •    Language models power autocomplete, text generation, machine translation (as the decoder),
   885→          speech recognition (choosing the most fluent transcription), and are the training objective
   886→          behind today's large language models.
   887→
   888→5.2 An RNN as a Language Model — Architecture
   889→     •    Step 1 — Embedding: each word is converted from a discrete token into a dense vector (a row
   890→          of a learned embedding matrix E).
   891→     •    Step 2 — Recurrence: the embedding is fed into the RNN (or LSTM / GRU) exactly as in Sections
   892→          2–4; the hidden state accumulates context from every word seen so far.
   893→     •    Step 3 — Read-out: at every time step, the hidden state is projected to a vector of logits, one per
   894→          vocabulary word, and passed through softmax to obtain a probability distribution over the next
   895→          word.
   896→     •    Training: at each step, the true next word is compared against the predicted distribution using
   897→          cross-entropy loss; the same shared weights are updated via BPTT, exactly as in Section 2.5.
   898→
   899→
   900→
   901→
   902→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                      Page 22 of 41
   903→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                      Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   904→
   905→
   906→
   907→
   908→Figure 9. An RNN language model unrolled across two time steps. The same RNN weights from Section 2 are reused here
   909→             — only the input (word embeddings) and output (softmax over the vocabulary) layers are new.
   910→
   911→5.3 Equations
   912→                           eₜ = E[ wₜ ]   (look up the embedding row for the current word)
   913→
   914→                                      at = Wxh eₜ + Whh ht−1 + bh     ;      ht = tanh(at)
   915→
   916→                                                     logitst = Why ht + by
   917→
   918→                                           P(word | context) = softmax(logitsₜ)
   919→
   920→                          Lₜ = − log P(wₜ₊₁ = target | context)     (cross-entropy loss at step t)
   921→
   922→Significance:
   923→
   924→     •    Embedding lookup turns a discrete word into a point in continuous space, where similar words
   925→          can end up close together after training.
   926→     •    Softmax converts raw logits into a valid probability distribution (non-negative, sums to 1) over
   927→          the entire vocabulary.
   928→     •    Cross-entropy loss penalises the model in proportion to how surprised it was by the true next
   929→          word — a confident wrong prediction is penalised heavily; a confident correct prediction has
   930→          almost no loss.
   931→
   932→5.4 Worked Example 5 — Next-Word Prediction, Step by Step
   933→Given
   934→
   935→
   936→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                             Page 23 of 41
   937→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   938→
   939→
   940→
   941→Toy vocabulary (4 words): {I, love, deep, learning}, indices 0–3.
   942→Embedding table E (one row per word): I → [0.1000, 0.2000], love → [0.3000, -0.1000], deep → [-
   943→0.2000, 0.4000], learning → [0.5000, 0.1000]
   944→Recurrence weights: the same Wxh, Whh, bh from Worked Example 1 (Section 2.3) — re-used here to
   945→show that the recurrence itself is identical; only the surrounding embedding/read-out layers are new.
   946→Read-out weights: Why(lm) = [[0.2,0.1],[0.1,-0.2],[-0.3,0.4],[0.4,0.2]], by(lm) = [0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000,
   947→0.1000]
   948→Training sentence: “I love deep learning” → input/target pairs (I → love), (love → deep)
   949→
   950→Time step t = 1: input = “I”, target = “love”
   951→Step 1.1 — Embed the input word: e₁ = E[“I”] = [0.1000, 0.2000]
   952→Step 1.2 — Update the hidden state (identical recurrence to Section 2.3): a₁ = Wxh e₁ + Whh h₀ + bh =
   953→[0.0900, 0.0000] ⇒ h₁ = tanh([0.0900, 0.0000]) = [0.0898, 0.0000]
   954→Step 1.3 — Project to vocabulary-sized logits: logits₁ = Why(lm) h₁ + by(lm) = [0.0180, 0.0090, -0.0269,
   955→0.1359]
   956→Step 1.4 — Softmax → probability distribution over the 4 words: P = softmax([0.0180, 0.0090, -0.0269,
   957→0.1359]) = [I: 0.2456, love: 0.2434, deep: 0.2348, learning: 0.2763]
   958→Step 1.5 — Cross-entropy loss against the true next word “love”: L₁ = − log P(love) = − log(0.2434) =
   959→1.4132
   960→
   961→Reading the result
   962→All four probabilities came out close to 0.25 (i.e. close to uniform / random guessing) — unsurprising,
   963→since these are untrained, illustrative weights, not weights learned from real text. Training would push
   964→P(love) toward 1 for this context by adjusting every weight along the BPTT gradient path (Section 2.5–
   965→2.6).
   966→
   967→Time step t = 2: input = “love”, target = “deep”
   968→The hidden state now carries forward information from “I” as well:
   969→
   970→                      Quantity                                               Value
   971→
   972→ e₂ = E[“love”]                                      [0.3000, -0.1000]
   973→
   974→ a₂ = Wxh e₂ + Whh h₁ + bh                           [0.2890, -0.0980]
   975→
   976→ h₂ = tanh(a₂)                                       [0.2812, -0.0976]
   977→
   978→ logits₂ = Why(lm) h₂ + by(lm)                       [0.0465, 0.0476, -0.1234, 0.1929]
   979→
   980→ P (I, love, deep, learning)                         [0.2498, 0.2501, 0.2108, 0.2892]
   981→
   982→ L₂ = − log P(deep)                                  1.5569
   983→
   984→
   985→5.5 Perplexity
   986→     •    Perplexity is the standard way to report how well a language model predicts text; it converts the
   987→          average cross-entropy loss back onto an intuitive scale:
   988→                     Average loss = (L₁ + L₂ + ⋯) / T           Perplexity = exp(Average loss)
   989→
   990→
   991→
   992→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                     Page 24 of 41
   993→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                          Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
   994→
   995→
   996→
   997→For this example: Average loss = (1.4132 + 1.5569) / 2 = 1.4850 ⇒ Perplexity = exp(1.4850) = 4.4151
   998→     •    Interpretation: a perplexity of 4.42 means the model is, on average, about as “confused” as if it
   999→          were guessing uniformly at random among roughly 4.4 equally likely words — out of a 4-word
  1000→          vocabulary, that is only slightly better than pure guessing (perplexity 4.0), consistent with these
  1001→          being untrained weights.
  1002→     •    Lower perplexity = better model. A well-trained model on a large vocabulary typically achieves a
  1003→          perplexity far below the vocabulary size, because it learns to concentrate probability mass on
  1004→          plausible next words.
  1005→     •    Perplexity = 1 would mean the model is always 100% certain and always correct (the theoretical
  1006→          best); perplexity equal to the vocabulary size corresponds to uniform random guessing (the
  1007→          practical worst case for a sensible model).
  1008→
  1009→5.6 Beyond the Basics
  1010→     •    Teacher forcing — during training, the true previous word is fed as input at every step (as in
  1011→          Worked Example 5), even if the model's own previous prediction was wrong; this stabilises and
  1012→          speeds up training.
  1013→     •    Generation / sampling — at inference time there is no “true” next word, so the model's own
  1014→          output is fed back as the next input. Common strategies: greedy decoding (always pick the
  1015→          highest-probability word), sampling with temperature, and beam search.
  1016→     •    LSTM / GRU language models — in practice, the plain-RNN recurrence in this section is almost
  1017→          always replaced by an LSTM or GRU cell (Sections 3–4), since long documents need the improved
  1018→          long-range memory.
  1019→     •    Modern context — Transformer-based language models have largely superseded RNN-based
  1020→          ones for state-of-the-art results, but the evaluation concepts introduced here — next-word
  1021→          prediction, cross-entropy loss, and perplexity — remain exactly the same and are used to evaluate
  1022→          Transformer language models too.

  1070→
  1071→6.2 Parameter-Count Formulas
  1072→For input size d and hidden size h, counting every weight matrix and bias:
  1073→
  1074→    Architecture                  Parameter count formula                     Example: d = 100, h = 128
  1075→
  1076→ RNN                      h(d + h + 1)                              29,312
  1077→
  1078→ LSTM                     4 × h(d + h + 1)                          117,248 (= 4 × RNN)
  1079→
  1080→ GRU                      3 × h(d + h + 1)                          87,936 (= 3 × RNN)
  1081→     •    The “4×” and “3×” factors come directly from counting gates: LSTM has 4 sets of weights (forget,
  1082→          input, candidate, output), all sharing the same input shape (d + h) → h; GRU has 3 (update, reset,
  1083→          candidate). This is why, for a fixed parameter budget, a GRU can afford a larger hidden size than
  1084→          an LSTM.
  1085→
  1086→6.3 When to Use Which
  1087→     •    Plain RNN — short sequences, when simplicity/speed matters more than long-range memory, or
  1088→          as a teaching baseline. Rarely the best choice for real long-sequence tasks.
  1089→     •    LSTM — tasks needing the most reliable long-range memory and fine-grained control (separately
  1090→          tunable forget/input/output behaviour); a strong default when compute budget is not tight.
  1091→
  1092→
  1093→
  1094→
  1095→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                       Page 26 of 41
  1096→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1097→
  1098→
  1099→
  1100→     •    GRU — a strong default when training speed or parameter budget is constrained (e.g.
  1101→          mobile/embedded, very large hidden sizes, limited data); frequently matches LSTM accuracy with
  1102→          fewer resources.
  1103→     •    Neither, in modern large-scale NLP — Transformer-based architectures have largely replaced all
  1104→          three for state-of-the-art language tasks, because they parallelise across time (faster training)
  1105→          and use attention instead of a single recurrent bottleneck. RNN/LSTM/GRU remain important for
  1106→          streaming/online settings, resource-constrained devices, and as the conceptual foundation for
  1107→          sequence modelling.
  1108→

  1118→7. Practice Questions

  1120→This bank contains 50 questions covering every topic in this unit: 15 multiple-choice questions (Part A)
  1121→and 35 descriptive / numerical questions (Part B). Attempt each question before reading its solution.
  1122→
  1123→Part A — Multiple Choice Questions (Q1–Q15)
  1124→
  1125→Q1. Which of the following is NOT a defining property of sequential data? [1 mark]
  1126→     (A) Every sequence in the dataset must have exactly the same length. ✓ correct
  1127→     (B) The order of elements affects the meaning.
  1128→     (C) Later elements can depend on much earlier elements.
  1129→     (D) Elements are not statistically independent of their neighbours.
  1130→Answer: (A)
  1131→Solution:
  1132→Sequential data is explicitly allowed to be of variable length — sentences, audio clips and time series
  1133→routinely differ in length. This variability is precisely why ordinary feedforward networks (which need a
  1134→fixed-size input) struggle with sequences (Section 1.2), and why RNNs, which process one element at a
  1135→time and share weights across positions, are needed. Options B, C, and D all describe real properties of
  1136→sequential data (Section 1.1).
  1137→
  1138→Q2. What is the single most important structural idea that lets an RNN process sequences of any length
  1139→using a fixed number of parameters? [1 mark]
  1140→     (A) Using convolutional filters that slide over the input.
  1141→     (B) Increasing the hidden size whenever the sequence is longer.
  1142→     (C) Sharing the same weight matrices across all time steps. ✓ correct
  1143→     (D) Training a separate small network for every time step.
  1144→Answer: (C)
  1145→Solution:
  1146→Because Wxh, Whh, Why (and their biases) are reused, identically, at every time step, the total number
  1147→of parameters does not grow with sequence length — a 5-word sentence and a 500-word document are
  1148→processed by exactly the same set of weights, applied repeatedly (Section 1.3, Section 2.1). Option D is
  1149→effectively the opposite of parameter sharing and would not generalise to unseen lengths.
  1150→
  1151→Q3. In the standard update ht = tanh(Wxhxt + Whhht−1 + bh), every component of ht must lie in which
  1152→range? [1 mark]
  1153→     (A) (−1, 1) ✓ correct
  1154→     (B) (0, 1)
  1155→     (C) (−∞, ∞)
  1156→     (D) [0, ∞)
  1157→Answer: (A)
  1158→Solution:
  1159→tanh squashes any real-valued input into the open interval (−1, 1) (Section 2.2). (0, 1) is the range of the
  1160→sigmoid function instead, which is used inside LSTM/GRU gates, not the plain RNN hidden-state update.
  1161→
  1162→
  1163→
  1164→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 28 of 41
  1165→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1166→
  1167→
  1168→
  1169→Q4. If a pre-activation value a = 0, what are tanh(a) and its local derivative 1 − tanh²(a) at that point? [1
  1170→mark]
  1171→     (A) 0 and 0
  1172→     (B) 1 and 0
  1173→     (C) 1 and 1
  1174→     (D) 0 and 1 ✓ correct
  1175→Answer: (D)
  1176→Solution:
  1177→tanh(0) = 0, and 1 − tanh²(0) = 1 − 0 = 1. This is the largest possible value the tanh-derivative factor can
  1178→take (it is always ≤ 1) — so even in the best case, each backward step through tanh cannot amplify the
  1179→gradient, only preserve or shrink it. This is the local mechanism underlying the vanishing-gradient
  1180→discussion in Section 2.7.
  1181→
  1182→Q5. In BPTT for a plain RNN, the total gradient of the loss with respect to Whh is obtained by: [1 mark]
  1183→     (A) Summing the gradient contributions from every time step. ✓ correct
  1184→     (B) Using only the gradient contribution from the final time step.
  1185→     (C) Averaging the contributions from only the first and last time steps.
  1186→     (D) Taking the single largest contribution across all time steps.
  1187→Answer: (A)
  1188→Solution:
  1189→Because Whh is reused at every step, the multivariable chain rule requires summing its gradient
  1190→contribution from every time step it was used in: ∂L/∂Whh = Σₜ ∂L/∂aₜ ⊗ hₜ₋₁ (Section 2.5, demonstrated
  1191→numerically in Worked Example 2).
  1192→
  1193→Q6. The vanishing gradient problem in plain RNNs is primarily caused by: [1 mark]
  1194→     (A) Using too few hidden units.
  1195→     (B) Using too large a learning rate.
  1196→     (C) The softmax function saturating.
  1197→     (D) Repeated multiplication by Whhᵀ and a tanh-derivative factor (≤ 1) at every backward step. ✓
  1198→     correct
  1199→Answer: (D)
  1200→Solution:
  1201→Backpropagating through T time steps multiplies the gradient by roughly T copies of Whhᵀ and a tanh-
  1202→derivative factor. If the typical size of this product (informally λ) is less than 1, the gradient shrinks
  1203→exponentially with T (Section 2.7, Figure 6). This has nothing to do with learning rate (B) or softmax (C),
  1204→and too few hidden units (A) is a capacity problem, not a gradient-flow problem.
  1205→
  1206→Q7. Which technique is the standard, simplest fix specifically aimed at exploding gradients? [1 mark]
  1207→     (A) Gradient clipping ✓ correct
  1208→     (B) Dropout
  1209→     (C) Batch normalisation
  1210→     (D) Data augmentation
  1211→Answer: (A)
  1212→Solution:
  1213→
  1214→
  1215→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 29 of 41
  1216→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1217→
  1218→
  1219→
  1220→Gradient clipping directly rescales the gradient vector when its norm exceeds a chosen threshold, capping
  1221→the size of any single update — a direct, minimal-assumption fix for exploding gradients (Section 2.7).
  1222→Dropout and data augmentation address overfitting, not gradient explosion; batch normalisation targets
  1223→internal covariate shift in deep feedforward stacks.
  1224→
  1225→Q8. How many gate values does a standard LSTM cell compute at each time step? [1 mark]
  1226→     (A) 1
  1227→     (B) 3 ✓ correct
  1228→     (C) 2
  1229→     (D) 4
  1230→Answer: (B)
  1231→Solution:
  1232→An LSTM has exactly three gates: forget (fₜ), input (iₜ), and output (oₜ) — each a sigmoid, each genuinely
  1233→“gating” (scaling) something. The candidate c̃ₜ is also computed from the same weights but is not a gate:
  1234→it uses tanh and proposes new content rather than deciding how much of something to let through. This
  1235→distinction is a common point of confusion (Section 3.2–3.3).
  1236→
  1237→Q9. A forget-gate value ft close to 0 for a particular memory component means: [1 mark]
  1238→     (A) That component of the old cell state is almost entirely kept.
  1239→     (B) The input gate is automatically forced to 0.
  1240→     (C) That component of the old cell state is almost entirely erased. ✓ correct
  1241→     (D) The output gate closes for that component.
  1242→Answer: (C)
  1243→Solution:
  1244→Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + (new term); when ft ≈ 0 for a component, that component of Ct−1 is multiplied by ≈ 0
  1245→and is therefore erased from the running memory (Section 3.3). The forget and input gates are computed
  1246→independently (different weights), so (B) is false in general.
  1247→
  1248→Q10. The main reason the LSTM cell state protects gradients from vanishing is that its update rule is: [1
  1249→mark]
  1250→     (A) Multiplicative and passed through tanh at every step, like a plain RNN.
  1251→     (B) Computed only once, at the final time step.
  1252→     (C) Identical in form to the plain RNN's hidden-state update.
  1253→     (D) Additive and mostly element-wise, with no repeated matrix multiply on the main path. ✓ correct
  1254→Answer: (D)
  1255→Solution:
  1256→Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t is additive, so ∂Ct/∂Ct−1 = ft (an element-wise scaling), not a matrix multiplication
  1257→followed by a squashing nonlinearity. If ft stays near 1, gradients can flow across many steps with minimal
  1258→shrinkage — the “gradient highway” idea of Section 3.5.
  1259→
  1260→Q11. How many gates does a standard GRU have? [1 mark]
  1261→     (A) 1
  1262→     (B) 3
  1263→     (C) 2 ✓ correct
  1264→
  1265→
  1266→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 30 of 41
  1267→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1268→
  1269→
  1270→
  1271→     (D) 4
  1272→Answer: (C)
  1273→Solution:
  1274→A GRU has exactly two gates: the update gate zt and the reset gate rt (Section 4.2). This is one fewer gate-
  1275→type than LSTM's three, which is the direct source of GRU's smaller parameter count (≈ 3× a plain RNN,
  1276→versus ≈ 4× for LSTM — Section 6.2).
  1277→
  1278→Q12. Which statement about the GRU is correct? [1 mark]
  1279→     (A) GRU has a separate cell state distinct from its hidden state.
  1280→     (B) GRU merges the roles of LSTM's forget and input gates into a single update gate. ✓ correct
  1281→     (C) GRU has more parameters than an LSTM of the same hidden size.
  1282→     (D) GRU has an explicit output gate, exactly like LSTM.
  1283→Answer: (B)
  1284→Solution:
  1285→The update gate zt controls the blend ht = (1−zt)⊙ht−1 + zt⊙h̃t — z acting large plays the role of LSTM's
  1286→input gate (write new content), and (1−z) acting large plays the role of the forget gate (keep old content),
  1287→combined into one gate (Section 4.5). GRU has no separate cell state (A is false), fewer parameters than
  1288→LSTM (C is false), and no output gate (D is false).
  1289→
  1290→Q13. In an RNN language model, the softmax layer at each time step outputs: [1 mark]
  1291→     (A) The next hidden state directly.
  1292→     (B) The embedding vector of the input word.
  1293→     (C) A probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next word. ✓ correct
  1294→     (D) The scalar cross-entropy loss value.
  1295→Answer: (C)
  1296→Solution:
  1297→softmax(logitsₜ) converts the raw, unbounded logits into non-negative values that sum to 1 — a valid
  1298→probability distribution over every word in the vocabulary (Section 5.2–5.3). The loss (D) is computed
  1299→from this distribution afterward, using the true next word.
  1300→
  1301→Q14. If a language model's average cross-entropy loss on a test set is L, its perplexity is: [1 mark]
  1302→     (A) L²
  1303→     (B) 1 / L
  1304→     (C) log(L)
  1305→     (D) exp(L) ✓ correct
  1306→Answer: (D)
  1307→Solution:
  1308→Perplexity = exp(average cross-entropy loss) (Section 5.5). This maps loss = 0 (a perfect model) to
  1309→perplexity = 1, and increases perplexity exponentially as the average loss increases, giving a more intuitive
  1310→“effective number of choices” interpretation than the raw loss.
  1311→
  1312→Q15. For the same input size and hidden size, an LSTM has approximately how many times the number
  1313→of parameters of a plain RNN? [1 mark]
  1314→     (A) 1×
  1315→
  1316→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 31 of 41
  1317→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1318→
  1319→
  1320→
  1321→     (B) 4× ✓ correct
  1322→     (C) 2×
  1323→     (D) 3×
  1324→Answer: (B)
  1325→Solution:
  1326→A plain RNN has one set of weights of shape h×(d+h) plus a bias; an LSTM computes four such quantities
  1327→(forget, input, candidate, output) from the same input shape, so its parameter count is 4 × h(d+h+1)
  1328→versus h(d+h+1) for the RNN — exactly 4× (Section 6.2, Table “Parameter-Count Formulas”). GRU, with 3
  1329→such computations, is ≈ 3×.
  1330→
  1331→Part B — Descriptive and Numerical Questions (Q16–Q50)
  1332→Q16. List and briefly explain three properties that any model of sequential data must respect. [3 marks]
  1333→Solution:
  1334→     •    Variable length — sequences in a dataset are rarely all the same length (sentences, audio clips,
  1335→          etc.), so the model cannot assume a fixed-size input.
  1336→     •    Order-dependence — shuffling the elements changes (or destroys) the meaning; e.g. “dog bites
  1337→          man” ≠ “man bites dog”.
  1338→     •    Long-range dependencies — information at one position can affect the correct interpretation of
  1339→          a position much later in the sequence, so the model needs some form of memory (Section 1.1).
  1340→
  1341→Q17. Give two distinct reasons why a plain feedforward network (MLP) with a flattened input vector is
  1342→a poor choice for variable-length text classification. [2 marks]
  1343→Solution:
  1344→     •    Fixed input size: an MLP requires a predetermined number of input features. Flattening text of
  1345→          different lengths into one vector either forces truncation/padding to an arbitrary maximum
  1346→          length, or simply cannot be done consistently.
  1347→     •    No parameter sharing across positions: if position 5 and position 50 of the flattened vector each
  1348→          get their own weights, the network must separately learn what a given word means at every
  1349→          possible position, wasting parameters and failing to generalise to lengths/positions not seen
  1350→          during training (Section 1.2).
  1351→
  1352→Q18. Explain the difference between the “folded” and “unrolled” views of an RNN, and state why the
  1353→unrolled view is useful for training. [2 marks]
  1354→Solution:
  1355→     •    The folded view shows a single RNN cell with a self-loop (feedback arrow) — a compact picture
  1356→          of the recurrence rule itself.
  1357→     •    The unrolled view draws a separate copy of that same cell for every time step t = 1, …, T,
  1358→          connected in a chain, with the identical weights (Wxh, Whh, Why) used in every copy (Figure 2).
  1359→     •    The unrolled view is useful for training because it turns the recurrent (looped) computation into
  1360→          an ordinary directed acyclic graph, to which standard backpropagation can be applied directly —
  1361→          this is exactly what Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) does (Section 2.5).
  1362→
  1363→
  1364→
  1365→
  1366→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 32 of 41
  1367→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1368→
  1369→
  1370→
  1371→Q19. A plain RNN has input size 3 and hidden size 2. Given ht−1 = [0.1000, -0.2000], xt = [1, 0, −1], Wxh =
  1372→[[0.2000, 0.0000, -0.1000], [0.1000, 0.3000, 0.2000]], Whh = [[0.5000, -0.2000], [0.1000, 0.4000]], bh =
  1373→[0.0000, 0.1000], compute ht step by step. [4 marks]
  1374→Solution:
  1375→Step 1 — Input contribution: Wxh xₜ = [0.3000, -0.1000]
  1376→Step 2 — Recurrent contribution: Whh hₜ₋₁ = [0.0900, -0.0700]
  1377→Step 3 — Combine and add bias: aₜ = [0.3000, -0.1000] + [0.0900, -0.0700] + [0.0000, 0.1000] = [0.3900,
  1378→-0.0700]
  1379→Step 4 — Apply tanh: hₜ = tanh([0.3900, -0.0700]) = [0.3714, -0.0699]
  1380→
  1381→Q20. State the formula for the number of trainable parameters in a plain RNN with input size d and
  1382→hidden size h, and explain what each term counts. [3 marks]
  1383→Solution:
  1384→                     Total parameters = h×d (Wxh) + h×h (Whh) + h (bh) = h(d + h + 1)
  1385→
  1386→     •    h×d counts the entries of Wxh, which maps the d-dimensional input to the h-dimensional hidden
  1387→          update.
  1388→     •    h×h counts the entries of Whh, which maps the previous h-dimensional hidden state to its
  1389→          contribution to the new hidden state.
  1390→     •    h counts the entries of the bias vector bh (one bias per hidden unit). Note: this counts only the
  1391→          recurrent layer; a separate output layer Why, by would add h×(output size) + (output size) more.
  1392→
  1393→Q21. In Worked Examples 1, 3 and 4, the plain RNN, LSTM and GRU each processed the identical first
  1394→input x₁, yet produced three different values of h₁. Explain why, and identify which architecture's h₁
  1395→depends on x₁ alone versus which involve additional learned control. [3 marks]
  1396→Solution:
  1397→     •    Plain RNN: h₁ = tanh(Wxh x₁ + Whh h₀ + bh) is a direct, ungated transformation of x₁ (with h₀ = 0
  1398→          contributing nothing) — no learned gate decides how much of x₁ to accept.
  1399→     •    LSTM: h₁ = o₁ ⊙ tanh(C₁), where C₁ = i₁ ⊙ c̃₁ already involves the input gate i₁ deciding how much
  1400→          of the candidate c̃₁ to write in, and the output gate o₁ separately deciding how much of C₁ to
  1401→          expose — two extra learned filters between x₁ and h₁.
  1402→     •    GRU: h₁ = z₁ ⊙ h̃ ₁ (since h₀ = 0), where the update gate z₁ decides how much of the candidate to
  1403→          accept — one learned filter between x₁ and h₁.
  1404→     •    All three use the same raw input x₁, but the RNN applies no learned gating, while LSTM and GRU
  1405→          each pass the resulting candidate through one or more sigmoid gates before it becomes h₁ —
  1406→          with untrained (illustrative) weights these gates simply produce different numbers than the
  1407→          ungated RNN; after training, this gating is precisely what lets LSTM/GRU learn when to accept
  1408→          new information.
  1409→
  1410→Q22. A plain RNN (input size 2, hidden size 2) has Wxh = [[0.3000, 0.1000], [-0.1000, 0.2000]], Whh =
  1411→[[0.2000, 0.1000], [0.0500, -0.3000]], bh = [0.0000, 0.0000]. Given h₀ = [0, 0], x₁ = [0.2000, 0.8000], x₂ =
  1412→[-0.4000, 0.6000], compute h₁ and h₂. [5 marks]
  1413→Solution:
  1414→
  1415→
  1416→
  1417→
  1418→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 33 of 41
  1419→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1420→
  1421→
  1422→
  1423→Step 1 — t = 1: a₁ = Wxh x₁ + Whh h₀ + bh = [0.1400, 0.1400] ⇒ h₁ = tanh([0.1400, 0.1400]) = [0.1391,
  1424→0.1391]
  1425→Step 2 — t = 2: a₂ = Wxh x₂ + Whh h₁ + bh = [-0.0183, 0.1252] ⇒ h₂ = tanh([-0.0183, 0.1252]) = [-0.0183,
  1426→0.1246]

  1428→          chosen here — this is a coincidence of this question's data, not a general property of RNNs.
  1429→
  1430→Q23. Give one real-world example each (different from those already used in these notes) of a many-
  1431→to-one and a many-to-many (aligned) RNN application, and justify why each fits its category. [2 marks]
  1432→Solution:
  1433→     •    Many-to-one: spam-email detection — the model reads a whole sequence of words (the email
  1434→          body) but only needs to output a single decision (spam / not spam) at the end.
  1435→     •    Many-to-many (aligned): named-entity recognition — the model must output a label (e.g. Person
  1436→          / Organisation / Other) for every word in the input sentence, so input length and output length
  1437→          match exactly, one output per input position.
  1438→
  1439→Q24. Derive an expression for the Jacobian ∂ht/∂ht−1 of a plain RNN, and explain its role in BPTT. [4
  1440→marks]
  1441→Solution:
  1442→Step 1 — Write the recurrence: hₜ = tanh(aₜ), where aₜ = Wxh xₜ + Whh hₜ₋₁ + bh
  1443→Step 2 — Differentiate aₜ with respect to hₜ₋₁: ∂aₜ/∂hₜ₋₁ = Whh (the only term in aₜ that depends on hₜ₋₁)
  1444→Step 3 — Apply the chain rule through tanh: ∂hₜ/∂hₜ₋₁ = diag(1 − hₜ²) · Whh
  1445→     •    Here diag(1−hₜ²) is a diagonal matrix of the elementwise tanh-derivative values.
  1446→
  1447→Role in BPTT
  1448→This single-step Jacobian is exactly the factor that gets multiplied in, once per time step, when the
  1449→gradient is propagated backward from hₜ to hₜ₋₁ (Steps 5–6 of Worked Example 2). Its repeated
  1450→application — diag(1−h²)·Whh chained T times — is precisely the mechanism behind the
  1451→vanishing/exploding gradient problem of Section 2.7: if the dominant eigenvalue of this product has
  1452→magnitude < 1, gradients vanish; if > 1, they explode.
  1453→
  1454→Q25. Explain why the tanh derivative being maximised at a = 0 is relevant to the vanishing gradient
  1455→problem. [2 marks]
  1456→Solution:
  1457→     •    1 − tanh²(a) reaches its maximum value of 1 exactly at a = 0, and falls toward 0 as |a| grows (tanh
  1458→          saturates near ±1).
  1459→     •    Since each backward step through tanh multiplies the gradient by this factor, the best possible
  1460→          case at any single step is a multiplier of exactly 1 (no shrinkage) — it can never exceed 1. In
  1461→          practice, hidden units are rarely sitting at exactly a = 0, so the realistic per-step factor is usually
  1462→          noticeably below 1, which compounds multiplicatively over many time steps into the vanishing
  1463→          gradient problem (Section 2.7, and Q4 of Part A).
  1464→
  1465→Q26. A scalar (1-dimensional) RNN has Wxh = 0.5, Whh = 0.8, bh = 0.1, h₀ = 0. Inputs x₁ = 1, x₂ = 0.5. A
  1466→squared-error loss L = ½(h₂ − target)² is applied at t = 2 with target = 0.5. Compute ∂L/∂Whh. [6 marks]

  1475→Step 1 — Forward pass: a₁ = 0.5×1 + 0.8×0 + 0.1 = 0.6 ⇒ h₁ = tanh(0.6) = 0.537
  1476→a₂ = 0.5×0.5 + 0.8×0.537 + 0.1 = 0.7796 ⇒ h₂ = tanh(0.7796) = 0.6525
  1477→
  1478→Step 2 — Loss and output gradient: L = ½(0.6525 − 0.5)² = 0.0116       ∂L/∂h₂ = h₂ − target = 0.1525
  1479→Step 3 — Backprop through tanh at t = 2: ∂L/∂a₂ = 0.1525 × (1 − 0.6525²) = 0.0876
  1480→Step 4 — Contribution to Whh from t = 2: ∂L/∂Whh|₂ = ∂L/∂a₂ × h₁ = 0.0876 × 0.537 = 0.047
  1481→Step 5 — Propagate back to t = 1, contribution to Whh from t = 1: ∂L/∂h₁ = ∂L/∂a₂ × Whh = 0.0701 ⇒
  1482→∂L/∂a₁ = 0.0499 ⇒ ∂L/∂Whh|₁ = ∂L/∂a₁ × h₀ = ∂L/∂a₁ × 0 = 0
  1483→Step 6 — Total: ∂L/∂Whh = 0 + 0.047 = 0.047
  1484→
  1485→Q27. Explain the difference between the vanishing and exploding gradient problems in terms of the
  1486→quantity λ introduced in Section 2.7. [2 marks]
  1487→Solution:
  1488→     •    λ informally represents the typical magnitude of Whhᵀ combined with the local tanh-derivative
  1489→          factor, applied once per backward time step.
  1490→     •    If λ < 1, repeated multiplication across T steps produces λᵀ → 0 exponentially — the vanishing
  1491→          gradient problem; early time steps get almost no learning signal.
  1492→     •    If λ > 1, λᵀ grows exponentially — the exploding gradient problem; updates become huge and
  1493→          training destabilises. λ = 1 is the (unstable) knife-edge boundary between the two regimes.
  1494→
  1495→Q28. If λ = 0.8, compute the relative gradient magnitude λᵏ after k = 5 and k = 15 backward steps, and
  1496→comment on the result. [3 marks]
  1497→Solution:
  1498→Step 1: λ⁵ = 0.8⁵ = 0.32768
  1499→Step 2: λ¹⁵ = 0.8¹⁵ = 0.035184
  1500→     •    Even with a fairly mild λ = 0.8 (each step keeps 80% of the gradient), only about 32.8% survives
  1501→          after 5 steps, and a mere 3.52% survives after 15 steps — illustrating how quickly the vanishing
  1502→          gradient problem bites even without an extreme per-step shrinkage factor.
  1503→
  1504→Q29. List three standard mitigations for vanishing/exploding gradients in RNNs, and explain one of
  1505→them in detail. [3 marks]
  1506→Solution:
  1507→     •    Gradient clipping, careful (e.g. orthogonal) weight initialisation, truncated BPTT, and gated
  1508→          architectures (LSTM/GRU) are all standard mitigations (Section 2.7).
  1509→     •    Gradient clipping in detail: after computing the gradient for a batch, its norm ‖g‖ is compared
  1510→          against a threshold τ. If ‖g‖ > τ, the gradient is rescaled: g ← g × (τ/‖g‖), which preserves its
  1511→          direction but caps its magnitude. This is cheap to compute, requires no architecture change, and
  1512→          directly prevents the huge, destabilising updates caused by exploding gradients — though it does
  1513→          nothing to fix vanishing gradients.
  1514→
  1515→Q30. Explain what truncated BPTT is and what trade-off it makes. [2 marks]
  1516→Solution:
  1517→
  1518→
  1519→
  1520→
  1521→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 35 of 41
  1522→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1523→
  1524→
  1525→
  1526→     •    Truncated BPTT limits how many time steps the gradient is backpropagated through (e.g. only
  1527→          the most recent 20 steps), instead of all the way back to t = 1, even for very long sequences.
  1528→     •    Trade-off: it makes training faster and more memory-efficient, and avoids some numerical
  1529→          instability from very long gradient chains, but it means the model cannot learn dependencies that
  1530→          span more time steps than the truncation window — a direct trade-off between training
  1531→          efficiency/stability and the ability to learn long-range structure.
  1532→
  1533→Q31. In one line each, state the role of the forget gate, input gate, candidate, and output gate in an
  1534→LSTM cell. [4 marks]
  1535→Solution:
  1536→     •    Forget gate ft: decides what fraction of the old cell state Ct−1 to keep.
  1537→     •    Input gate it: decides how much of the new candidate content to write into the cell state.
  1538→     •    Candidate c̃t: proposes the new content itself (not a gate — uses tanh, not sigmoid).
  1539→     •    Output gate ot: decides how much of the (updated) cell state to expose as the hidden state ht.
  1540→
  1541→Q32. Continuing Worked Example 2 (Section 2.6), compute ∂L/∂Wxh and ∂L/∂Why. [6 marks]
  1542→Solution:
  1543→     •    ∂L/∂Wxh follows exactly the same pattern as ∂L/∂Whh (Section 2.6, Steps 4–7), but each time-
  1544→          step's contribution is an outer product with xₜ instead of hₜ₋₁:
  1545→t = 3 contribution: ∂L/∂Wxh|₃ = ∂L/∂a₃ ⊗ x₃ = [-0.5266, 0.3922] ⊗ [-0.5000, 1.0000] = [[0.2633, -0.5266],
  1546→[-0.1961, 0.3922]]
  1547→t = 2 contribution: ∂L/∂Wxh|₂ = ∂L/∂a₂ ⊗ x₂ = [-0.0725, -0.0797] ⊗ [0.5000, -1.0000] = [[-0.0362,
  1548→0.0725], [-0.0399, 0.0797]]
  1549→t = 1 contribution: ∂L/∂Wxh|₁ = ∂L/∂a₁ ⊗ x₁ = [0.0072, -0.0484] ⊗ [1.0000, 0.5000] = [[0.0072, 0.0036],
  1550→[-0.0484, -0.0242]] (non-zero here, unlike ∂L/∂Whh|₁, because x₁ ≠ 0 even though h₀ = 0)
  1551→Total: ∂L/∂Wxh = [[0.0072, 0.0036], [-0.0484, -0.0242]] + [[-0.0362, 0.0725], [-0.0399, 0.0797]] +
  1552→[[0.2633, -0.5266], [-0.1961, 0.3922]] = [[0.2342, -0.4506], [-0.2844, 0.4478]]
  1553→     •    ∂L/∂Why only involves the single time step where the output was read out (t = 3), so there is no
  1554→          sum over time — it is a plain feedforward-layer gradient:
  1555→∂L/∂Why = ∂L/∂y₃ ⊗ h₃ = [-1.1790, 0.0788] ⊗ [-0.4885, -0.0470] = [[0.5759, 0.0554], [-0.0385, -0.0037]]
  1556→
  1557→Q33. A scalar LSTM cell (input size 1, hidden size 1) has h₀ = 0, C₀ = 0, x₁ = 1.0, with weights (applied to z
  1558→= [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 1]): Wf = [0.5, 0.2], bf = 0; Wi = [0.3, −0.1], bi = 0.1; Wc = [0.6, 0.4], bc = 0; Wo = [0.2,
  1559→0.5], bo = 0.1. Compute f₁, i₁, c̃₁, C₁, o₁, h₁. [6 marks]
  1560→Solution:
  1561→Step 1 — Forget gate: f₁ = σ(0.5×0 + 0.2×1 + 0) = σ(0.2) = 0.5498
  1562→Step 2 — Input gate: i₁ = σ(0.3×0 + (−0.1)×1 + 0.1) = σ(0.0) = 0.5
  1563→Step 3 — Candidate: c̃₁ = tanh(0.6×0 + 0.4×1 + 0) = tanh(0.4) = 0.3799
  1564→Step 4 — Cell state (C₀ = 0, so the forget term vanishes): C₁ = 0.5498×0 + 0.5×0.3799 = 0.19
  1565→Step 5 — Output gate: o₁ = σ(0.2×0 + 0.5×1 + 0.1) = σ(0.6) = 0.6457
  1566→Step 6 — Hidden state: h₁ = o₁ × tanh(C₁) = 0.6457 × tanh(0.19) = 0.1212

  1574→Q34. Explain, using the forget-gate mechanism, why an LSTM can in principle remember information
  1575→for 100+ time steps, while a plain RNN struggles to. [3 marks]
  1576→Solution:
  1577→     •    If the forget gate learns a value close to 1 for a particular memory component, that component
  1578→          of the cell state is carried forward with almost no attenuation at every step: Ct = 1 × Ct−1 +
  1579→          (small/zero new term) ≈ Ct−1.
  1580→     •    Because this update is additive and element-wise (Section 3.5), the corresponding backward
  1581→          gradient ∂Ct/∂Ct−1 = ft ≈ 1 as well — so information (and its gradient) can survive many steps
  1582→          unchanged, in principle indefinitely.
  1583→     •    A plain RNN has no such mechanism: its hidden state is fully overwritten by tanh(…) at every step,
  1584→          and the corresponding gradient is repeatedly multiplied by Whhᵀ and a tanh-derivative < 1, which
  1585→          compounds toward zero (Section 2.7) — there is no learned way to “protect” a piece of
  1586→          information from this decay.
  1587→
  1588→Q35. Compute the number of trainable parameters in an LSTM layer with input size d = 50 and hidden
  1589→size h = 32. [2 marks]
  1590→Solution:
  1591→Step 1 — Recall the formula: Parameters = 4 × h(d + h + 1) (Section 6.2)
  1592→Step 2 — Substitute: = 4 × 32 × (50 + 32 + 1) = 4 × 32 × 83 = 10,624
  1593→
  1594→Q36. Why does LSTM keep the output gate separate from the cell-state update, instead of always
  1595→outputting the full cell state as the hidden state? [2 marks]
  1596→Solution:
  1597→     •    Decoupling means the cell can continue to store information in Ct (for possible future use)
  1598→          without being forced to expose that information in ht right now.
  1599→     •    This is useful when a piece of context is relevant for a later prediction but irrelevant to the
  1600→          immediate output — e.g. remembering the subject of a sentence while the immediate output
  1601→          should focus on a verb; the output gate lets the network learn when to reveal vs. withhold each
  1602→          memory component (Section 3.2).
  1603→
  1604→Q37. If a particular LSTM memory unit has a forget gate consistently equal to 0.99 and an input gate of
  1605→0 (no new writes) for 100 consecutive steps, what fraction of the original value in that memory unit
  1606→remains? [2 marks]
  1607→Solution:
  1608→With it = 0, the update reduces to Ct = ft × Ct−1 at every step, so after 100 steps: C₁₀₀ = (0.99)¹⁰⁰ × C₀ =
  1609→0.366 × C₀.
  1610→     •    About 36.6% of the original value survives — a forget gate very close to 1 is needed to preserve
  1611→          information over long spans; even f = 0.99 loses almost two-thirds of the signal over 100 steps,
  1612→          showing why training must push ft very close to 1 for genuinely long-range memories.
  1613→
  1614→Q38. What would happen, structurally, if the forget gate were removed and ft were fixed at 1 for every
  1615→unit at every step? [2 marks]
  1616→Solution:
  1617→
  1618→
  1619→
  1620→
  1621→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 37 of 41
  1622→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1623→
  1624→
  1625→
  1626→     •    The cell-state update would become Ct = Ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t — memory would only ever accumulate
  1627→          and could never be cleared or overwritten, since old content is never actively erased.
  1628→     •    This can cause the cell state to grow without bound over long sequences (in the worst case), and
  1629→          prevents the network from ever “resetting” its memory when the context genuinely changes (e.g.
  1630→          at a sentence boundary). This is essentially why the forget gate was added to the original LSTM
  1631→          design — without it, the earliest LSTM variant could exhibit unbounded cell-state growth on long
  1632→          sequences.
  1633→
  1634→Q39. In one line each, state the role of the reset gate and the update gate in a GRU cell. [2 marks]
  1635→Solution:
  1636→     •    Reset gate rt: decides how much of the previous hidden state to use when computing the new
  1637→          candidate content h̃ t.
  1638→     •    Update gate zt: decides the blend ratio between keeping the old hidden state and adopting the
  1639→          new candidate, ht = (1−zt)⊙ht−1 + zt⊙h̃ t.
  1640→
  1641→Q40. A scalar GRU cell (input size 1, hidden size 1) has h₀ = 0, x₁ = 1.0, with (applied to [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 1]):
  1642→Wz = [0.4, 0.1], bz = 0; Wr = [0.2, 0.3], br = 0.1; Wh = [0.5, −0.2], bh = 0.05. Compute z₁, r₁, h̃ ₁, and h₁. [5
  1643→marks]
  1644→Solution:
  1645→Step 1 — Update gate: z₁ = σ(0.4×0 + 0.1×1 + 0) = σ(0.1) = 0.525
  1646→Step 2 — Reset gate: r₁ = σ(0.2×0 + 0.3×1 + 0.1) = σ(0.4) = 0.5987
  1647→Step 3 — Apply reset gate to h₀ (which is already 0, so this has no numeric effect here): r₁ ⊙ h₀ = 0.5987
  1648→×0=0
  1649→Step 4 — Candidate hidden state: h̃ ₁ = tanh(0.5×0 + (−0.2)×1 + 0.05) = tanh(−0.15) = -0.1489
  1650→Step 5 — Final blend: h₁ = (1 − 0.525)×0 + 0.525×(-0.1489) = -0.0782
  1651→
  1652→Q41. Why does GRU not maintain a separate cell state, and what is the practical trade-off of this design
  1653→choice? [2 marks]
  1654→Solution:
  1655→     •    GRU's designers merged the memory and the exposed hidden state into a single vector, relying
  1656→          on the update gate alone to control how much of that single vector changes at each step — there
  1657→          is no second, separately-protected “conveyor belt” as in LSTM (Section 4.1–4.2).
  1658→     •    Trade-off: fewer parameters and a simpler cell (faster to train, Section 6), at the cost of slightly
  1659→          less representational flexibility — GRU cannot store a value in “private” memory while showing
  1660→          something different at the output, the way LSTM's output gate allows.
  1661→
  1662→Q42. Compute the number of trainable parameters in a GRU layer with input size d = 64 and hidden
  1663→size h = 48. [2 marks]
  1664→Solution:
  1665→Step 1 — Recall the formula: Parameters = 3 × h(d + h + 1) (Section 6.2)
  1666→Step 2 — Substitute: = 3 × 48 × (64 + 48 + 1) = 3 × 48 × 113 = 16,272

  1676→Q43. What does the GRU update reduce to when zt = 0 for all dimensions? What about when zt = 1? [2
  1677→marks]
  1678→Solution:
  1679→     •    zt = 0: ht = 1×ht−1 + 0×h̃ t = ht−1 — the hidden state is left completely unchanged; the new
  1680→          candidate is entirely ignored.
  1681→     •    zt = 1: ht = 0×ht−1 + 1×h̃ t = h̃ t — the old state is completely discarded and replaced by the new
  1682→          candidate.
  1683→     •    In practice zt learns intermediate values, blending the two continuously depending on the input.
  1684→
  1685→Q44. Give an intuitive example of when a GRU's reset gate would be useful with a value close to 0. [2
  1686→marks]
  1687→Solution:
  1688→     •    Consider a document that is a list of unrelated short product reviews concatenated together. At
  1689→          the start of a new review, the content of the previous review is no longer relevant context for
  1690→          interpreting the new one.
  1691→     •    A reset gate close to 0 at that boundary lets the candidate h̃ t be computed almost entirely from
  1692→          the current input (ignoring the stale ht−1), effectively letting the network “start fresh” without
  1693→          needing to wait for the update gate to slowly overwrite the old state (Section 4.3).
  1694→
  1695→Q45. Write the chain-rule factorisation of P(w₁, …, wᵀ) used by a language model, and explain in words
  1696→what each factor represents. [3 marks]
  1697→Solution:
  1698→                          P(w₁, …, wᵀ) = P(w₁) · P(w₂|w₁) · P(w₃|w₁,w₂) · ⋯ · P(wᵀ|w₁,…,wᵀ₋₁)
  1699→
  1700→     •    This is simply the probability chain rule applied to a sequence: the joint probability of the whole
  1701→          sequence equals the product of each word's probability conditioned on every word before it.
  1702→     •    An RNN language model approximates every conditional factor P(wₜ | w₁,…,wₜ₋₁) with a single
  1703→          softmax output at step t, whose entire dependence on the (arbitrarily long) history w₁,…,wₜ₋₁ is
  1704→          compressed into the fixed-size hidden state hₜ₋₁ (Section 5.1–5.2).
  1705→
  1706→Q46. A language model with vocabulary size 5 produces logits = [1.2000, 0.5000, -0.3000, 2.0000,
  1707→0.1000] at some time step. The true next word has index 3 (0-indexed). Compute the softmax
  1708→probabilities and the cross-entropy loss. [5 marks]
  1709→Solution:
  1710→Step 1 — Exponentiate each logit: exp([1.2000, 0.5000, -0.3000, 2.0000, 0.1000]) — compute e^1.2,
  1711→e^0.5, e^−0.3, e^2.0, e^0.1
  1712→Step 2 — Normalise (divide by the sum) to get softmax probabilities: P = [0.2337, 0.1161, 0.0522,
  1713→0.5202, 0.0778]
  1714→Step 3 — Cross-entropy loss uses only the probability assigned to the true index (3): L = − log P[3] = −
  1715→log(0.5202) = 0.6535
  1716→     •    Notice index 3 also has the largest logit (2.0) and correspondingly the largest probability (≈ 0.52)
  1717→          — since this is also the target, the loss is relatively small, reflecting a fairly confident, correct
  1718→          prediction.

  1728→Q47. A language model achieves an average cross-entropy loss of 2.3 nats per word on a test set.
  1729→Compute its perplexity. [2 marks]
  1730→Solution:
  1731→Perplexity = exp(average loss) = exp(2.3) = 9.9742
  1732→     •    A perplexity of ≈ 10 means the model's uncertainty at each step is comparable to choosing
  1733→          uniformly among about 10 equally likely words, regardless of how large the true vocabulary is.
  1734→
  1735→Q48. Explain teacher forcing and describe one problem it can cause at inference (generation) time. [3
  1736→marks]
  1737→Solution:
  1738→     •    Teacher forcing: during training, the model is always fed the true previous word as input at each
  1739→          step, regardless of what the model itself would have predicted (Section 5.6).
  1740→     •    Problem — exposure bias: at generation time there is no ground truth to feed back in, so the
  1741→          model must feed in its own (possibly imperfect) previous prediction. Since the model never
  1742→          practised recovering from its own mistakes during training, small errors can compound as
  1743→          generation proceeds, leading to increasingly poor output quality — a mismatch between the
  1744→          training and inference conditions.
  1745→
  1746→Q49. Give one application example each for plain RNN, LSTM, and GRU, and briefly justify each choice.
  1747→[3 marks]
  1748→Solution:
  1749→     •    Plain RNN: a short, fixed-pattern signal classifier (e.g. detecting a simple gesture from a few
  1750→          dozen accelerometer readings) — the sequences are short enough that vanishing gradients are
  1751→          not a serious concern, so the simplicity and speed of a plain RNN is an acceptable trade-off.
  1752→     •    LSTM: long-document sentiment analysis or long-range time-series forecasting (e.g. multi-week
  1753→          demand forecasting) — the long-range memory and fine-grained gating are worth the extra
  1754→          parameters when dependencies span long distances.
  1755→     •    GRU: on-device / mobile keyboard next-word prediction — a tight compute and memory budget
  1756→          favours GRU's roughly 25% parameter saving over LSTM, while still comfortably outperforming a
  1757→          plain RNN.
  1758→
  1759→Q50. Summarise, in a short set of bullet points, the historical progression from RNN → LSTM → GRU →
  1760→Transformer, giving the main motivation behind each step. [4 marks]
  1761→Solution:
  1762→     •    RNN: introduced parameter sharing across time via a recurrent hidden state, solving the fixed-
  1763→          input-size and no-memory problems of feedforward networks (Section 1–2).
  1764→     •    → LSTM: added gated, additive memory (the cell state) specifically to fix the vanishing gradient
  1765→          problem that crippled plain RNNs on long sequences (Section 2.7 → Section 3).
  1766→     •    → GRU: simplified LSTM's gating (2 gates instead of 3, no separate cell state) to reduce
  1767→          parameters and training cost while keeping most of the long-range-memory benefit (Section 4).
  1768→     •    → Transformer (beyond this unit): replaced recurrence entirely with self-attention, allowing
  1769→          every position to directly attend to every other position. This removes the sequential step-by-
  1770→          step bottleneck (enabling full parallelisation across time during training) and provides a more
  1771→          direct path for gradients/information between distant positions than even LSTM/GRU can offer.
  1772→
  1773→
  1774→Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 40 of 41
  1775→CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks
  1776→
  1777→
  1778→
  1779→     •    Each step's motivation was the same underlying goal: let information from arbitrarily far back in
  1780→          a sequence influence the current prediction, as efficiently as possible.

   129→   129→            },

   133→   133→            },
   134→   134→            {

   136→   136→              tex: "z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \\dots + w_nx_n + b = \\sum_i w_ix_i + b",

   187→   187→            },

   190→   190→              items: [
   191→   191→                "**Initialise** — set weights $w_i$ and bias $b$ to 0 (or small random values); choose a learning rate $\\eta$, $0 < \\eta \\le 1$.",
   192→   192→                "**For every training pair $(x, t)$** — (a) compute the net input $z = \\sum w_ix_i + b$; (b) compute the predicted output $y = f(z)$; (c) compute the error $e = t - y$; (d) update every weight $w_i \\leftarrow w_i + \\eta \\cdot e \\cdot x_i$; (e) update the bias $b \\leftarrow b + \\eta \\cdot e$.",
   193→   193→                "**Repeat** — one pass over all examples is one **epoch**. Repeat over multiple epochs until an entire epoch produces **zero errors** (convergence), or a maximum number of epochs is reached.",
   194→   194→              ],

   758→   758→      id: "u1-l5",
   759→   759→      title: "Backpropagation",
   760→   760→      subtitle: "The chain rule, applied layer by layer — with the complete 2-2-1 network worked example.",
   761→   761→      minutes: 16,
   762→   762→      sections: [
   763→   763→        {
   764→   764→          id: "u1-l5-s1",
   765→   765→          title: "Why is backpropagation needed?",
   766→   766→          blocks: [
   767→   767→            {
   768→   768→              type: "bullets",
   769→   769→              items: [
   770→   770→                "A single perceptron can only learn a **linear boundary**. Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) stack hidden layers to model **non-linear** relationships.",
   771→   771→                "But the simple perceptron rule does not say how to update weights feeding **hidden neurons** — there is no direct target for a hidden neuron's output.",
   772→   772→                "Backpropagation solves this: it propagates the output error **backward through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule**, to compute $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for every weight — including hidden-layer weights.",
   773→   773→              ],
   774→   774→            },
   775→   775→          ],
   776→   776→        },
   777→   777→        {
   778→   778→          id: "u1-l5-s2",
   779→   779→          title: "The chain rule of differentiation",
   780→   780→          blocks: [
   781→   781→            {
   782→   782→              type: "formula",
   783→   783→              tex: "\\text{If } y = f(u) \\text{ and } u = g(x), \\quad \\text{then } \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy}{du}\\times\\frac{du}{dx}",
   784→   784→            },
   785→   785→            {
   786→   786→              type: "example",
   787→   787→              title: "Chain rule warm-up: y = (2x+1)² at x = 3",
   788→   788→              steps: [
   789→   789→                { label: "Substitute u = 2x+1", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "u = 2(3)+1 = 7, \\quad y = u^2 = 49" }] },
   790→   790→                { label: "Local derivatives", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{du} = 2u = 14, \\qquad \\frac{du}{dx} = 2" }] },
   791→   791→                { label: "Multiply", blocks: [{ type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{dy}{dx} = 14 \\times 2 = 28 \\;\\checkmark \\;(\\text{matches } 4(2x+1) = 28)" }] },
   792→   792→                {
   793→   793→                  label: "Significance",
   794→   794→                  blocks: [
   795→   795→                    {
   796→   796→                      type: "text",
   797→   797→                      value:
   798→   798→                        "In a network, the Loss depends on a weight through a chain of nested functions (weight → net input → activation → … → Loss). Backpropagation is simply this chain rule applied repeatedly, one layer at a time.",
   799→   799→                    },
   800→   800→                  ],
   801→   801→                },
   802→   802→              ],
   803→   803→            },
   804→   804→          ],
   805→   805→        },
   806→   806→        {
   807→   807→          id: "u1-l5-s3",
   808→   808→          title: "Forward pass and backward pass",
   809→   809→          blocks: [
   810→   810→            {
   811→   811→              type: "compare",
   812→   812→              pairs: [
   813→   813→                {
   814→   814→                  label: "Forward pass",
   815→   815→                  left: [
   816→   816→                    "Inputs flow **left-to-right** through the network to produce a prediction",
   817→   817→                    "Every intermediate activation is **stored** for later use",
   818→   818→                  ],
   819→   819→                },
   820→   820→                {
   821→   821→                  label: "Backward pass",
   822→   822→                  left: [
   823→   823→                    "Starting from the loss, gradients flow **right-to-left** using the chain rule",
   824→   824→                    "Computes $\\partial L/\\partial w$ for **every** weight",
   825→   825→                    "Update: every weight is then adjusted by gradient descent",
   826→   826→                  ],
   827→   827→                },
   828→   828→              ],
   829→   829→            },
   830→   830→          ],
   831→   831→        },
   832→   832→        {
   833→   833→          id: "u1-l5-s4",
   834→   834→          title: "Complete worked example — 2-2-1 sigmoid network",
   835→   835→          blocks: [
   836→   836→            {
   837→   837→              type: "widget",
   838→   838→              widgetId: "u1-backprop-lab",
   839→   839→              title: "Backpropagation lab — walk the exact numbers",
   840→   840→              description: "Step through the forward pass, both backward passes and the weight update of the notes' 2-2-1 network. Change the inputs and watch every gradient recompute live.",
   841→   841→            },
   842→   842→            {
   843→   843→              type: "example",
   844→   844→              title: "Forward pass → backward pass → update (full calculation)",
   845→   845→              given: [
   846→   846→                "Network: 2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons (sigmoid) → 1 output neuron (sigmoid)",
   847→   847→                "Inputs $x_1 = 0.5$, $x_2 = 0.3$ · Target = 1.0 · Learning rate $\\eta = 0.5$",
   848→   848→                "Weights $w_1..w_6$ = 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, 0.5, 0.6 · Biases $b_{h1} = 0.25$, $b_{h2} = 0.20$, $b_o = 0.4$",
   849→   849→                "Loss $L = \\frac{1}{2}(\\text{target} - \\text{output})^2$ · Sigmoid: $\\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$, $\\sigma'(z) = \\sigma(z)(1-\\sigma(z))$",
   850→   850→              ],
   851→   851→              steps: [
   852→   852→                {
   853→   853→                  label: "Step 1 — Forward pass",
   854→   854→                  blocks: [
   855→   855→                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_1^{in} = 0.5(0.2)+0.3(0.4)+0.25 = 0.4700 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_1^{out} = \\sigma(0.47) = 0.6154" },
   856→   856→                    { type: "formula", tex: "h_2^{in} = 0.5(0.3)+0.3(0.1)+0.20 = 0.3800 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; h_2^{out} = \\sigma(0.38) = 0.5939" },
   857→   857→                    { type: "formula", tex: "o_{in} = 0.6154(0.5)+0.5939(0.6)+0.4 = 1.0640 \\;\\Rightarrow\\; o_{out} = \\sigma(1.064) = 0.7435" },
   858→   858→                    { type: "formula", tex: "L = \\tfrac{1}{2}(1 - 0.7435)^2 = \\tfrac{1}{2}(0.2565)^2 = 0.0329" },
   859→   859→                  ],
   860→   860→                },
   861→   861→                {
   862→   862→                  label: "Step 2 — Backward pass: output layer",
   863→   863→                  blocks: [
   864→   864→                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial o_{out}} = -(1 - 0.7435) = -0.2565" },
   865→   865→                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial o_{out}}{\\partial o_{in}} = 0.7435(1-0.7435) = 0.1907 \\;(\\text{sigmoid derivative})" },
   866→   866→                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\delta_o = -0.2565 \\times 0.1907 = -0.0489" },
   867→   867→                    { type: "formula", tex: "\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial w_5} = \\delta_o \\times h_1^{out} = -0.0301, \\qquad \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial w_6} = \\delta_o \\times h_2^{out} = -0.0291" },
   868→   868→                    {
   869→   869→                      type: "text",
   870→   870→                      value:

    69→
    70→1. Introduction to Deep Unsupervised Learning
    71→
    72→1.1 What is Unsupervised Learning?
    73→  ● Learning from data x that has no labels y — only the inputs are given, no “correct answer” is
    74→    supplied.
    75→  ● Goal: discover hidden structure, patterns, or the underlying probability distribution p(x) that
    76→    generated the data.
    77→  ● Classical examples: k-means clustering, PCA, hierarchical clustering — these use shallow, hand-
    78→    designed feature spaces.
    79→  ● Contrast with supervised learning: no loss like cross-entropy against a ground-truth label; the
    80→    “supervision” instead comes from the data itself (e.g. reconstruct the input, distinguish real vs.
    81→    fake, model the data density).
    82→
    83→1.2 Why “Deep” Unsupervised Learning?
    84→  ● Classical methods (PCA, k-means) can only capture linear / shallow structure.
    85→  ● Real data (images, speech, text) lies on complex, non-linear low-dimensional manifolds inside a
    86→    high-dimensional space.
    87→  ● Deep neural networks, stacked in multiple layers, learn a hierarchy of features — simple patterns
    88→    in early layers combine into abstract concepts in later layers — exactly what is needed to model
    89→    such manifolds.
    90→  ● This hierarchy is learned automatically from unlabelled data, which is abundant, instead of
    91→    requiring expensive manual labelling.
    92→
    93→1.3 Why do we care? (Applications)
    94→  ● Representation / feature learning for downstream supervised tasks (pre-training).
    95→  ● Data generation — synthesizing realistic images, audio, text (GANs, VAEs).
    96→  ● Dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection (autoencoders).
    97→  ● Density estimation — learning p(x) explicitly to compute likelihoods, detect outliers (RBM, DBN,
    98→    DBM).
    99→  ● Data compression and efficient coding (autoencoders, RBMs).
   100→
   101→1.4 Roadmap: The Model Families in this Unit
   102→
   103→
   104→
   105→
   106→                                     Page 3 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
   107→CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                   Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning
   108→
   109→
   110→
   111→
   112→          Fig. 1.1 — The deep unsupervised learning models covered in this unit, grouped by how they learn p(x).
   113→
   114→
   115→  Key idea that unifies this whole unit
   116→     ● Every model in this unit answers the same question differently: “How do I learn a good model
   117→       of p(x) using only unlabelled data?”
   118→     ● Autoencoder / VAE: learn by compressing and reconstructing x through a bottleneck.
   119→     ● GAN: learn by playing a two-player minimax game between a generator and a discriminator.
   120→     ● Maximum Entropy: choose the least-biased distribution consistent with known constraints —
   121→       the theoretical justification behind many of these models.
   122→     ● RBM / DBN / DBM / ConvBM: define an energy function over (visible, hidden) units and learn
   123→       its parameters so that observed data has low energy (high probability).
   124→
   125→
   126→
   127→
   128→                                           Page 4 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
   129→CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning
   130→
   131→
   132→2. Autoencoders
   133→
   134→2.1 Concept and Motivation
   135→  ● An autoencoder is a neural network trained to copy its input to its output, through a narrow
   136→    bottleneck.
   137→  ● Because it is forced through a bottleneck, it cannot just memorise — it must learn a compressed,
   138→    useful representation of the data.
   139→  ● It is trained with no labels — the “label” for input x is x itself. This is called self-supervised learning.
   140→  ● Two parts, trained jointly, end-to-end, by gradient descent:
   141→        ◦ Encoder f: maps input x to a latent code z (compression)
   142→        ◦ Decoder g: maps the code z back to a reconstruction x̂ (decompression)
   143→
   144→2.2 Architecture
   145→
   146→
   147→
   148→
   149→              Fig. 2.1 — Autoencoder: input is compressed to a low-dimensional code z, then reconstructed.
   150→
   151→
   152→2.3 Mathematical Formulation
   153→For input x ∈ ℝⁿ:
   154→
   155→                                        Encoder:        z = f(x) = σ(Wx + b)
   156→
   157→                                       Decoder:        x̂ = g(z) = σ(W′z + b′)
   158→
   159→where σ is a non-linear activation (sigmoid / ReLU / tanh), and W, b, W′, b′ are learned weights and
   160→biases.
   161→
   162→Training minimises the reconstruction loss between x and x̂, most commonly Mean Squared Error:
   163→
   164→                                          L(x, x̂) = (1) / (n) Σi=1n (xi − x̂i)2
   165→
   166→                                          Page 5 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
   167→CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning
   168→
   169→  ● Significance: minimising this loss is exactly what forces the bottleneck to keep only the most
   170→    important information needed to reconstruct x — unimportant/noisy variation is discarded.
   171→
   172→
   173→✎ Worked Example 2.1 — Forward Pass Through a Small Autoencoder
   174→Given input x = [0.8, 0.3] (n = 2), a 1-unit bottleneck, sigmoid activation, encoder weights W = [0.5, −0.3],
   175→bias b = 0.1, decoder weights W′ = [0.6, 0.4]ᵀ, bias b′ = [0, 0]. Find the reconstruction and the loss.
   176→
   177→  ● Step 1 — Encoder pre-activation (weighted sum of inputs). This is the encoder deciding how much
   178→    each input contributes to the compressed code:
   179→
   180→                        z_pre = (0.5)(0.8) + (−0.3)(0.3) + 0.1 = 0.40 − 0.09 + 0.10 = 0.41
   181→
   182→  ● Step 2 — Apply activation. The sigmoid squashes the code into (0,1) and adds the non-linearity that
   183→    lets the network represent more than a linear projection (unlike PCA):
   184→
   185→                                       z = σ(0.41) = 1 / (1 + e−0.41) = 0.6011
   186→
   187→  ● Step 3 — Decoder pre-activations. The single code value z is expanded back out to 2 numbers, one
   188→    per output unit:
   189→
   190→                        x̂1,pre = (0.6)(0.6011) = 0.3606,       x̂2,pre = (0.4)(0.6011) = 0.2404
   191→
   192→  ● Step 4 — Apply activation to get the reconstruction:
   193→
   194→                                 x̂ = [σ(0.3606), σ(0.2404)] = [0.5892, 0.5598]
   195→
   196→  ● Step 5 — Reconstruction loss (MSE). This single number is the training signal — backpropagation
   197→    adjusts W, b, W′, b′ to reduce it:
   198→
   199→            L = (1) / (2)[(0.8 − 0.5892)2 + (0.3 − 0.5598)2] = (1) / (2)[0.0444 + 0.0675] = 0.0560
   200→
   201→
   202→
   203→  ℹ Interpretation: the code z = 0.6011 is a single number that had to summarise both 0.8 and 0.3. The
   204→  loss (0.056) tells us how much information was lost in that compression — with only 1 bottleneck
   205→  unit for 2 inputs, some loss is expected.
   206→
   207→
   208→
   209→2.4 Types of Autoencoders
   210→
   211→          Type                      Key Idea                             Mechanism                         Typical Use
   212→
   213→                                                           Forces compression; simplest,           Dimensionality reduction,
   214→ Undercomplete            Bottleneck dim < input dim
   215→                                                           most common form                        feature learning
   216→
   217→                                                                                                   Used only combined with
   218→                                                           Needs an extra constraint (below)
   219→ Overcomplete             Bottleneck dim ≥ input dim                                               sparsity/noise/contractive
   220→                                                           or it just learns identity
   221→                                                                                                   penalty
   222→
   223→                          Penalise number of ‘active’      Adds sparsity penalty (e.g. KL-         Learn interpretable,
   224→ Sparse
   225→                          hidden units                     divergence) on hidden activations       disentangled features
   226→

   228→
   229→
   230→                                          Page 6 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
   231→CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                    Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning
   232→
   233→
   234→          Type                       Key Idea                              Mechanism                         Typical Use
   235→
   236→                                                             Input is corrupted (noise/masking)
   237→                           Reconstruct clean x from                                                 Robust features, noise
   238→ Denoising (DAE)                                             before encoding; target is original
   239→                           corrupted x̃                                                             removal
   240→                                                             x
   241→
   242→                                                             Adds ‖∂h/∂x‖² penalty (Jacobian        Robust, locally-invariant
   243→ Contractive (CAE)         Penalise sensitivity to input
   244→                                                             norm) to loss                          representations
   245→
   246→
   247→
   248→Sparse Autoencoder — the sparsity penalty
   249→Let ρ be the desired (small) target sparsity, e.g. 0.05, and ρ̂ⱼ the average activation of hidden unit j over
   250→the training batch. The sparsity penalty for unit j is the KL-divergence between two Bernoulli
   251→distributions:
   252→
   253→                              KL(ρ ‖ ρ̂j) = ρ log((ρ) / (ρ̂j)) + (1−ρ) log((1−ρ) / (1−ρ̂j))
   254→
   255→
   256→✎ Worked Example 2.2 — Sparsity Penalty Computation
   257→Given target sparsity ρ = 0.05 and observed average activation ρ̂ = 0.20, find the KL penalty (natural log).
   258→
   259→  ● Step 1 — First term (penalises unit being “on” too often relative to target):
   260→
   261→                        0.05 × ln(0.05/0.20) = 0.05 × ln(0.25) = 0.05 × (−1.3863) = −0.0693
   262→
   263→  ● Step 2 — Second term (penalises the “off” probability mismatch):
   264→
   265→                        0.95 × ln(0.95/0.80) = 0.95 × ln(1.1875) = 0.95 × 0.1718 = 0.1632
   266→
   267→  ● Step 3 — Sum:
   268→
   269→                                KL(0.05 ‖ 0.20) = −0.0693 + 0.1632 = 0.0939 nats
   270→
   271→ℹ Since ρ̂ (0.20) is far above the target ρ (0.05), the penalty is clearly positive; it would be exactly 0 if ρ̂ =
   272→ρ, and gradient descent pushes ρ̂ back toward ρ, i.e. towards a sparser (mostly-off) hidden layer.
   273→
   274→
   275→
   276→2.5 Applications
   277→  ● Dimensionality reduction (a non-linear generalisation of PCA).
   278→  ● Image denoising and inpainting.
   279→  ● Anomaly / fraud detection (anomalies have high reconstruction error).
   280→  ● Pre-training deep networks layer-by-layer before supervised fine-tuning.
   281→  ● Learned code z used as a compact feature vector for retrieval, clustering, or as input to another
   282→    model (e.g. the encoder of a VAE, Section 3).
   283→
