11.4 Quick Glossary
  ● Feature map: the output produced by convolving one filter over the input.
  ● Receptive field: the region of the original input that influences a given output value.
  ● Stride: the number of pixels the filter moves between applications.
  ● Padding: extra border pixels (usually zeros) added around the input.
  ● Epoch: one full pass of the training algorithm over the entire training dataset.
  ● Overfitting: a model that fits the training data very well but generalizes poorly to new data.
  ● Regularization: any technique (dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, ...) used to reduce
    overfitting.
  ● Backpropagation: the chain-rule algorithm used to compute ∂L/∂w for every weight in the
    network.
  ● Logits: the raw, un-normalized output scores of the final layer, before softmax.
  ● Global Average Pooling (GAP): pools an entire feature map down to a single number per channel;
    commonly replaces large FC stacks.

This question bank covers the complete unit: Section A contains 15 multiple-choice questions, and

Section A -- Multiple Choice Questions (15)



Q1. What is the primary reason a convolution layer needs far fewer parameters than a fully-connected
layer on the same image?
      (A) It uses fewer layers overall
      (B) Weight sharing and local connectivity -- the same small filter is reused at every position
      (C) It only works on grayscale images
      (D) It does not use any activation function
      ✓ Answer: (B) Local connectivity means each neuron only looks at a small patch, and parameter
      sharing means the same filter weights are reused across every position -- see Example 1.1 (≈4000×
      fewer parameters).


Q2. An input of size 7×7 is convolved with a 3×3 filter, stride 1, no padding. What is the output size?
      (A) 3×3
      (B) 4×4
      (C) 5×5
      (D) 6×6
      ✓ Answer: (C) O = (N−F)/S + 1 = (7−3)/1 + 1 = 5, so the output is 5×5.


Q3. What is a 'feature map' in a CNN?
      (A) The raw input image
      (B) The learnable filter itself
      (C) The output produced by convolving one filter over the input
      (D) The final softmax probability vector
      ✓ Answer: (C) A feature map (activation map) is the 2-D result of sliding one specific filter across
      the input; a layer with K filters produces K feature maps.


Q4. For 'same' padding with stride 1 and a filter size F = 5, what padding P is required?
      (A) P = 1
      (B) P = 2
      (C) P = 3
      (D) P = 4
      ✓ Answer: (B) P = (F−1)/2 = (5−1)/2 = 2.

                                         Page 30 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                             Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks


Q5. N = 11, F = 3, S = 2, P = 0. What is the output size?
      (A) 4
      (B) 5
      (C) 6
      (D) 7
      ✓ Answer: (B) O = ⌊(N−F)/S⌋ + 1 = ⌊(11−3)/2⌋ + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5.


Q6. Which statement about pooling layers is TRUE?
      (A) Pooling layers have learnable weights, just like conv layers
      (B) Max pooling must always use stride 1
      (C) Pooling layers have no learnable parameters at all
      (D) Average pooling cannot be used as the final layer of a CNN
      ✓ Answer: (C) Pooling is a fixed mathematical operation (max or mean) -- it has no weights or
      biases to learn. Global Average Pooling is, in fact, commonly used as the final layer in modern
      architectures.


Q7. A 2×2 max-pooling window contains the values {3, 7, 2, 5}. What value does it output?
      (A) 2
      (B) 3
      (C) 5
      (D) 7
      ✓ Answer: (D) Max pooling outputs the largest value in the window: max(3,7,2,5) = 7.


Q8. Backpropagation computes gradients efficiently by repeatedly applying which mathematical rule?
      (A) The product rule
      (B) The chain rule
      (C) The quotient rule
      (D) L'Hopital's rule
      ✓ Answer: (B) Backprop decomposes ∂L/∂w (for a weight buried deep in the network) into a
      product of simple local derivatives via the chain rule, working backward from the output.


Q9. Initializing every weight in a network to exactly zero causes which problem?
      (A) Vanishing gradients only, nothing else
      (B) Exploding gradients
      (C) The symmetry problem -- every neuron in a layer updates identically forever
      (D) Overfitting
      ✓ Answer: (C) With identical weights, every neuron in a layer computes the same output and
      receives the same gradient, so they never differentiate from one another -- the layer can never use
      its full capacity.

                                      Page 31 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks


Q10. He initialization sets the variance of the weights to:
      (A) 1 / n_in
      (B) 2 / n_in
      (C) 1 / (n_in + n_out)
      (D) n_in / 2
      ✓ Answer: (B) He init uses Var(W) = 2/n_in -- double Xavier's variance -- to compensate for ReLU
      zeroing out roughly half its inputs on average.


Q11. Immediately after the 'normalize' step of Batch Normalization (before scale-and-shift), the batch of
values has:
      (A) Mean = 1, Variance = 0
      (B) Mean = 0, Variance = 1
      (C) Mean = 0, Variance = 0
      (D) It depends on γ and β
      ✓ Answer: (B) Step 3 of BN (z_i = (x_i−μ)/√(σ²+ε)) is defined precisely so the normalized values
      have mean 0 and variance 1, by construction, before γ and β are applied in Step 4.


Q12. In inverted dropout, the surviving (non-dropped) activations are scaled, during training, by a factor
of:
      (A) p
      (B) 1 − p
      (C) 1 / (1 − p)
      (D) 1 / p
      ✓ Answer: (C) Surviving activations are divided by the keep-probability (1−p), i.e. multiplied by
      1/(1−p), so the expected total signal matches what the next layer will see at test time (when
      nothing is dropped).


Q13. Which hyperparameter search strategy scales worst as the number of hyperparameters grows?
      (A) Random Search
      (B) Grid Search
      (C) Bayesian Optimization
      (D) Manual tuning by an expert
      ✓ Answer: (B) Grid search tries every combination, so its cost grows multiplicatively with each
      new hyperparameter (Example 9.1) -- random search and Bayesian optimization scale far more
      gracefully.


Q14. Which architecture first introduced residual (skip) connections?
      (A) AlexNet
      (B) VGG
      (C) GoogLeNet
                                     Page 32 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

      (D) ResNet
      ✓ Answer: (D) ResNet (He et al., 2015) introduced the residual block H(x) = F(x) + x, using identity
      shortcuts to solve the degradation problem in very deep networks.


Q15. In an Inception module, the 1×1 convolutions are primarily used to:
      (A) Increase the spatial (height/width) size of the feature map
      (B) Reduce the channel depth before the expensive 3×3 / 5×5 convolutions run
      (C) Add colour information
      (D) Replace the need for any pooling branch
      ✓ Answer: (B) These 'bottleneck' 1×1 convolutions cut the number of channels first, so the
      following 3×3/5×5 convolutions operate on far fewer channels -- see Example 10.1 for the ≈10×
      parameter saving this produces.

13. Practice Questions -- Section B

35 short-answer, numerical, and descriptive questions with fully worked solutions, organised by topic.

Topic: Introduction to CNN

Q1. [Short Answer] Explain why weight sharing in a convolution layer leads to translation invariance.
Illustrate with a simple vertical-edge filter.
Solution
  ● In a convolution layer, the same filter (the same set of weights) is slid across every position of the
    input -- the filter is not re-learned for each location.
  ● Suppose a filter has learned to respond strongly to vertical edges. Because that exact filter is
    applied everywhere, a vertical edge will produce a strong activation whether it appears in the top-
    left of the image or the bottom-right.
  ● Result: if an object shifts position within the frame, the same feature (a vertical edge, a curve, a
    colour blob) is still detected -- just at a shifted location in the output feature map. This shift-
    equivariance of individual feature maps, combined with pooling, is what gives CNNs their practical
    translation invariance.


Q2. [Descriptive] Describe the complete pipeline of a CNN for image classification, explaining the specific
role of each layer type in transforming a raw image into a class prediction.
Solution
  ● Input: a raw image, e.g. 32×32×3 (height × width × colour channels).
  ● Convolution + ReLU (repeated): each convolution layer slides learnable filters over its input to
    produce feature maps that highlight local patterns (edges → textures → parts → objects, from early
    to late layers); ReLU then adds the non-linearity needed to model complex functions.
  ● Pooling (interspersed): down-samples the feature maps, reducing spatial size and computation
    while keeping the strongest signals, and adding mild translation invariance.
  ● Flatten: once the spatial size has been reduced enough, the final 3-D feature volume is reshaped
    into a 1-D vector.
  ● Fully Connected layers: combine all the extracted high-level features to reason about the image as
    a whole.
  ● Softmax output: converts the final layer's raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution over the
    classes, and the class with the highest probability is the network's prediction.
This exact pipeline is illustrated in Figure 1.1 of the notes.

Topic: The Convolution Operation

Q3. [Numerical] A 5×5 input is convolved with the 3×3 'plus-shaped' filter below, stride 1, no padding.
Compute the complete 3×3 output feature map. Input = [[0,1,2,1,0], [1,2,1,0,1], [2,1,0,1,2], [1,0,1,2,1],
[0,1,2,1,0]] Filter = [[0,1,0], [1,1,1], [0,1,0]]

                                       Page 34 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

Solution
The filter only has 1's in the centre 'plus' positions, so at each window we simply add the top, left,
centre, right and bottom cell of the 3×3 patch (the four corners are ignored, since they are multiplied by
0).

         Position               5 relevant cells (top, left, centre, right, bottom)                Sum

 (0,0)                  1, 1, 2, 1, 1                                                         6

 (0,1)                  2, 2, 1, 0, 0                                                         5

 (0,2)                  1, 1, 0, 1, 1                                                         4

 (1,0)                  2, 2, 1, 0, 0                                                         5

 (1,1)                  1, 1, 0, 1, 1                                                         4

 (1,2)                  0, 0, 1, 2, 2                                                         5

 (2,0)                  1, 1, 0, 1, 1                                                         4

 (2,1)                  0, 0, 1, 2, 2                                                         5

 (2,2)                  1, 1, 2, 1, 1                                                         6


Final output feature map: [[6, 5, 4], [5, 4, 5], [4, 5, 6]]

Significance: notice the output is symmetric (top-left equals bottom-right, etc.) -- a direct consequence
of the input and filter both being symmetric. Sanity-checking symmetry like this is a quick way to catch
arithmetic mistakes.


Q4. [Numerical] An input volume of size 64×64×3 is passed through a convolution layer with 16 filters of
size 3×3, stride 1, no padding. Find (a) the number of learnable parameters, and (b) the output volume
shape.
Solution
Step 1 -- Parameters per filter (each filter's true depth automatically matches the input's 3 channels,
plus 1 bias):

                                               (3×3×3) + 1 = 27 + 1 = 28

Step 2 -- Total parameters for 16 filters:

                                                      28 × 16 = 448

Step 3 -- Output spatial size (N=64, F=3, S=1, P=0):

                                                 O = (64−3)/1 + 1 = 62

Step 4 -- Output volume: spatial 62×62, depth = number of filters = 16, so the output volume is 62 × 62 ×
16.

Significance: only 448 parameters are needed regardless of how large the 64×64 image is -- this
parameter count would be identical even for a 1000×1000 input.


                                           Page 35 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                               Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks


Q5. [Numerical] A 28×28×1 image feeds into (a) a fully-connected layer of 500 neurons, or (b) a
convolution layer of 8 filters, size 5×5. Compute the parameter count for both and their ratio.
Solution
Step 1 -- Fully connected layer:

                        Params = (28×28×1)×500 + 500 = 784×500 + 500 = 392,500

Step 2 -- Convolution layer:

                                    Params = (5×5×1 + 1)×8 = 26×8 = 208

Step 3 -- Ratio:

                                              392,500 / 208 ≈ 1887

Significance: the dense layer needs almost 1900× more parameters than the convolution layer to
process the very same image -- reinforcing Example 1.1's point on a second, independent set of
numbers.


Q6. [Short Answer] Explain the difference between a 'filter' and a 'feature map', and how the two are
related.
Solution
  ● A filter (kernel) is a small grid of learnable weights -- it is a parameter of the model, learned during
    training, and stays fixed once training ends.
  ● A feature map (activation map) is the output produced when a specific filter is convolved across an
    input -- it is data that is computed fresh for every new input image, not a stored parameter.
  ● Relationship: one filter, applied to one input, produces exactly one feature map. A convolution
    layer with K filters therefore produces K feature maps, stacked into an output volume of depth K.


Q7. [Numerical] An input volume is 16×16×3. Layer 1 applies 8 filters of size 3×3, stride 1, 'same' padding
(P=1). Layer 2 then applies 16 filters of size 3×3, stride 2, padding P=1, directly on Layer 1's output. Find
the output volume shape after each layer.
Solution
Layer 1 -- N=16, F=3, S=1, P=1:

                                     O = (16 + 2×1 − 3)/1 + 1 = 15 + 1 = 16

Output volume after Layer 1: 16 × 16 × 8 (spatial size unchanged, confirming 'same' padding; depth = 8
filters).

Layer 2 -- N=16, F=3, S=2, P=1 (applied to the 16×16×8 volume from Layer 1):

                               O = ⌊(16 + 2×1 − 3)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊15/2⌋ + 1 = 7 + 1 = 8

Output volume after Layer 2: 8 × 8 × 16.




                                        Page 36 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

Significance: notice Layer 2's input depth (8) does not appear anywhere in the output-size formula --
depth never affects the spatial output size, only the number of filters does (and only via the output's
depth, not its height/width).

Topic: Padding and Stride

Q8. [Numerical] Find the padding P required to achieve 'same' output size, given filter size F=7 and stride
S=1.
Solution

                                         P = (F − 1)/2 = (7 − 1)/2 = 3

Significance: a 7×7 filter needs a 3-pixel zero border on every side to preserve spatial size -- larger filters
always need proportionally more padding for 'same' output.


Q9. [Numerical] Compute the output size for N=15, F=5, S=2, P=2.
Solution

                             O = ⌊(15 + 2×2 − 5)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊14/2⌋ + 1 = 7 + 1 = 8

The output is 8×8.


Q10. [Numerical] A network stacks three convolution layers (stride 1 throughout): Layer 1 is 3×3, Layer 2
is 3×3, Layer 3 is 5×5. (a) Find the final receptive field. (b) Compare the total parameter count (for C
input/output channels per layer) against a single convolution with the same receptive field.
Solution
Step 1 -- Receptive field after each layer (RF grows by F−1 each time, stride 1):

  ● After Layer 1 (3×3): RF = 3
  ● After Layer 2 (3×3): RF = 3 + (3−1) = 5
  ● After Layer 3 (5×5): RF = 5 + (5−1) = 9
Step 2 -- Parameter cost of the 3-layer stack (per C input/output channels):

                                (3×3 + 3×3 + 5×5) × C² = (9+9+25)C² = 43C²

Step 3 -- A single convolution with the same 9×9 receptive field:

                                                 9×9×C² = 81C²

Step 4 -- With C=64: 43×64² = 176,128 vs. 81×64² = 331,776 -- a reduction of about 47%.

Significance: the same receptive field (9×9) is reached with roughly half the parameters by stacking
smaller filters -- the same principle behind Example 3.3 and the design of VGG.


Q11. [Short Answer] Explain, with a concrete example, why 'valid' (no) padding causes information near
the image border to be under-used.
Solution


                                       Page 37 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                    Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● With no padding, a filter can only be centred on interior pixels -- it can never be centred exactly on
    a corner or edge pixel, since part of the window would fall outside the image.
  ● Concrete example: for a 5×5 input and a 3×3 filter, the very corner pixel (0,0) is covered by the
    filter only once (when the window is at position (0,0)); a centre pixel such as (2,2) is covered up to 9
    times as the filter slides through every position that overlaps it.
  ● This means border pixels contribute to far fewer output values than centre pixels do, so the
    network effectively 'sees' border information less often -- padding (Section 3.1) directly corrects
    this imbalance.

Q14. [Numerical] Find the pooling output size for N=13, F=3, S=2 (no padding).
Solution

                                O = ⌊(13−3)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊10/2⌋ + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6

Q15. [Short Answer] Explain why Global Average Pooling (GAP) reduces overfitting risk compared to a
large fully-connected layer, referencing parameter counts.
Solution
  ● GAP has zero learnable parameters -- it simply averages each channel down to one number --
    whereas a Flatten+Dense combination on the same feature map can need over a hundred million
    parameters (see Example 4.2: 102,764,544 vs. 513,000).
  ● Fewer parameters mean fewer opportunities for the model to memorise noise or idiosyncrasies
    specific to the training set, which is the essence of overfitting.
  ● GAP also forces each channel to summarise 'how much of this feature is present, on average,
    anywhere in the image', which is a more robust, spatially-invariant signal than a large set of
    position-specific dense weights.

Topic: Training a ConvNet

Q16. [Numerical] A single sigmoid neuron has x=3, w=0.4, b=−0.2, target y=0, learning rate η=0.05.
Perform one complete forward pass, compute the loss (MSE), then perform backpropagation and update
both w and b.
Solution
STEP 1 -- Forward pass:

                               z = wx + b = (0.4)(3) + (−0.2) = 1.2 − 0.2 = 1.0

                              a = σ(1.0) = 1/(1+e−1) = 1/(1+0.3679) ≈ 0.7311

STEP 2 -- Loss (MSE):

                                  L = 0.5(y−a)2 = 0.5(0−0.7311)2 ≈ 0.2672

STEP 3 -- Backward pass (chain rule):

  ● ∂L/∂a = −(y−a) = −(0−0.7311) = 0.7311

                                        Page 39 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● ∂a/∂z = a(1−a) = 0.7311×0.2689 ≈ 0.1966
  ● ∂z/∂w = x = 3, ∂z/∂b = 1

                               (∂L) / (∂w) = 0.7311 × 0.1966 × 3 ≈ 0.4312

                                (∂L) / (∂b) = 0.7311 × 0.1966 × 1 ≈ 0.1437

STEP 4 -- Update:

                                    wnew = 0.4 − 0.05(0.4312) ≈ 0.3784

                                  bnew = −0.2 − 0.05(0.1437) ≈ −0.2072

Significance: since the target was y=0 but the network predicted a=0.7311 (too high), both updates
nudge w and b downward -- exactly the direction that would reduce the prediction, and hence the loss.


Q17. [Numerical] A weight w=1.2 has gradient ∂L/∂w=0.35. Using learning rate η=0.2, compute the
updated weight.
Solution

                        wnew = w − η(∂L/∂w) = 1.2 − (0.2)(0.35) = 1.2 − 0.07 = 1.13


Q18. [Short Answer] Why is backpropagation described as an application of the chain rule? Relate your
answer to the layered structure of a CNN.
Solution
  ● A CNN is a composition of functions -- the output of Layer 1 feeds into Layer 2, whose output feeds
    into Layer 3, and so on. Mathematically, the network computes a nested function like
    L(fn(fn−1(...f1(x)...))).
  ● The chain rule states that the derivative of a composition of functions is the product of their
    individual derivatives. Backprop applies exactly this: it computes ∂L/∂w for a deeply buried weight
    by multiplying together the local derivative at every layer between that weight and the final loss.
  ● This lets each layer be programmed to know only its own simple local derivative; the overall
    complex gradient emerges automatically by chaining these simple pieces together, layer by layer,
    backward from the loss.


Q19. [Descriptive] Explain the forward pass, loss computation, and backward pass as one coherent
training loop, and explain why mini-batches are used in practice rather than the full dataset or a single
example.
Solution
  ● Forward pass: a batch of inputs is pushed through every layer to produce predictions.
  ● Loss computation: the predictions are compared against the true labels using a loss function (e.g.
    cross-entropy), giving a single number that measures how wrong the network currently is.
  ● Backward pass: the chain rule is applied layer by layer, backward from the loss, to compute ∂L/∂w
    for every weight.



                                     Page 40 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● Update: every weight takes a small step opposite to its gradient (gradient descent), and the loop
    repeats.
  ● Why mini-batches: using the full dataset per update (batch GD) gives a very stable gradient
    direction but is slow and memory-heavy; using a single example (SGD) is fast but extremely noisy. A
    mini-batch (e.g. 32-256 examples) strikes a practical balance -- stable enough gradients, while still
    allowing many updates per epoch and fitting comfortably in GPU memory.

Topic: Weight Initialization

Q20. [Numerical] A layer has n_in = 512 incoming connections. Compute the standard deviation used by
(a) Xavier initialization and (b) He initialization.
Solution
(a) Xavier:

                                     std(W) = √((1) / (512)) ≈ 0.0442

(b) He:

                           std(W) = √((2) / (512)) = √(1/256) = 1/16 = 0.0625

Significance: He's std-dev (0.0625) is √2 times larger than Xavier's (0.0442), consistent with He using
exactly double the variance.


Q21. [Short Answer] Why does pairing Xavier initialization with ReLU activations tend to make activations
shrink toward zero in deep networks?
Solution
  ● ReLU sets all negative inputs to exactly 0, so on average only about half of a ReLU layer's outputs
    are non-zero.
  ● Xavier initialization was derived assuming a (roughly) symmetric activation like tanh, which does
    not zero out half its output -- it does not account for this halving effect.
  ● As a result, when Xavier init is combined with ReLU, the variance of activations roughly halves at
    every layer, so after enough layers the signal shrinks toward zero -- this is exactly why He
    initialization doubles the variance, to compensate.


Q22. [Descriptive] Explain the symmetry problem caused by zero-initialization in detail, including why it
persists through every iteration of gradient descent (not just the first).
Solution
  ● Suppose every weight feeding into a layer's neurons is initialized to exactly 0 (or any other single
    shared constant). Every neuron in that layer then computes the exact same weighted sum of the
    inputs, and therefore the exact same output after activation.
  ● During backpropagation, the gradient flowing to each of these neurons also depends only on the
    (identical) forward computation and the (identical) downstream gradient -- so every neuron in the
    layer receives an identical gradient too.


                                     Page 41 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                 Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● Why it persists: since every neuron starts identical AND receives an identical update at every step,
    they remain identical to each other forever, no matter how many iterations of gradient descent are
    run. The layer is permanently stuck behaving as if it had only one distinct neuron, however many it
    actually contains.
  ● Randomizing the initial weights breaks this symmetry from the very first step, since different
    neurons then start with different weights, compute different outputs, and receive different
    gradients -- allowing them to specialise.

Topic: Batch Normalization

Q23. [Numerical] Apply Batch Normalization to the mini-batch x = [10, 12, 14, 16], with learnable
parameters γ=0.5, β=0 (ignore ε).
Solution
Step 1 -- Mean:

                                      μ = (10+12+14+16)/4 = 52/4 = 13

Step 2 -- Variance:

                        σ2 = [(10−13)2+(12−13)2+(14−13)2+(16−13)2]/4 = [9+1+1+9]/4 = 5

Step 3 -- Normalize (√5 ≈ 2.2361):

         z = [(10−13), (12−13), (14−13), (16−13)] / 2.2361 ≈ [−1.3416, −0.4472, 0.4472, 1.3416]

Step 4 -- Scale by γ=0.5, shift by β=0:

                                    y ≈ [−0.6708, −0.2236, 0.2236, 0.6708]

Significance: with γ=0.5 (less than 1), BN is choosing to compress the spread of this batch's normalized
values back down -- a good illustration of γ and β letting the network partially or fully undo the raw
normalization when useful.


Q24. [Short Answer] Explain what happens with Batch Normalization at test time, when there may be no
'batch' to compute statistics from.
Solution
  ● During training, BN keeps a running (exponential moving) average of the mean and variance it sees
    across all the mini-batches processed.
  ● At test time, this stored running average is used directly in place of a freshly computed batch
    mean/variance -- so a single test example can be normalized deterministically, without needing a
    batch at all.


Q25. [Descriptive] Discuss internal covariate shift and explain how Batch Normalization's four steps
address it, including the role of the learnable γ and β parameters.
Solution




                                          Page 42 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                 Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● Internal covariate shift: as training proceeds, the weights of every earlier layer keep changing,
    which means the statistical distribution of inputs arriving at any given later layer keeps shifting too.
    Each layer must continually re-adapt to this moving target, which slows convergence and forces
    small, cautious learning rates.
  ● How BN addresses it: by explicitly re-centring and re-scaling each layer's activations (Steps 1-3:
    compute batch mean, compute batch variance, normalize to zero-mean/unit-variance) at every
    layer, on every mini-batch, BN guarantees the distribution reaching the next layer stays stable and
    well-behaved, regardless of how the earlier layers' weights have changed.
  ● Role of γ, β (Step 4): forcing every layer to strictly zero-mean/unit-variance could actually limit
    what the network can represent (e.g. sigmoid works best with a wider input range in some cases). γ
    and β are learnable, so the network can rescale/shift the normalized values to whatever
    distribution is actually optimal -- including learning to undo the normalization entirely if that were
    ever the best choice.

Topic: Dropout

Q26. [Numerical] A layer has 6 neuron activations [0.2, 0.6, 0.4, 0.9, 0.5, 0.7]. Dropout rate p=0.5 is
applied, and the random mask happens to be [0,1,0,1,1,0] (1=keep, 0=drop). Compute the layer's output
after inverted dropout.
Solution
Step 1 -- Apply the mask (element-wise multiply):

                        [0.2×0, 0.6×1, 0.4×0, 0.9×1, 0.5×1, 0.7×0] = [0, 0.6, 0, 0.9, 0.5, 0]

Step 2 -- Scale surviving values by 1/(1−p) = 1/0.5 = 2:

                                                [0, 1.2, 0, 1.8, 1.0, 0]

Significance: 3 of the 6 neurons were dropped (p=0.5, matching the expected ≈50%), and the 3 survivors
were doubled so the expected total signal (sum) is preserved compared to using all 6 neurons unscaled.


Q27. [Short Answer] Why is activation scaling needed during training in inverted dropout, but not needed
at test time?
Solution
  ● During training, a fraction p of neurons are zeroed out, which shrinks the total signal reaching the
    next layer. Scaling the survivors by 1/(1−p) compensates for this, keeping the expected total signal
    the same as it would be with no dropout at all.
  ● At test time, the full (un-thinned) network is used -- no neurons are dropped, so the total signal
    already matches what was targeted during training. Since the scaling was already applied during
    training, no further adjustment is needed at test time; the network is simply used as-is.


Q28. [Descriptive] Explain how dropout can be interpreted as implicitly training an ensemble of sub-
networks.
Solution


                                          Page 43 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                             Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● Every time a forward pass is run during training, a different random subset of neurons is dropped --
    so, in effect, a different, smaller 'thinned' sub-network is being trained on that particular batch.
  ● Because weights are shared across all these thinned sub-networks (the same underlying weight
    matrix is used every time, just with some entries temporarily zeroed), training with dropout is
    similar to training a huge collection of different networks simultaneously, all tied together by
    shared parameters.
  ● At test time, using the full network (with inverted-dropout scaling already applied) approximates
    averaging the predictions of this entire ensemble of thinned sub-networks -- a cheap
    approximation to a well-known and powerful technique (model ensembling), obtained here almost
    for free.

Topic: Hyperparameter Optimization

Q29. [Numerical] A grid search is planned over 5 learning rates × 4 batch sizes × 2 optimizers. Each
training run takes 1.5 hours. Compute the total number of combinations and the total compute time.
Solution

                                      Combinations = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40

                                  Total time = 40 × 1.5 hours = 60 hours

Significance: 60 hours (2.5 days) on a single machine, for a fairly modest 3-hyperparameter grid --
illustrating again why grid search is only practical for small search spaces.


Q30. [Short Answer] If only 2 of 6 hyperparameters in a search actually have a meaningful effect on
performance, explain why random search tends to outperform grid search for the same compute
budget.
Solution
  ● Grid search spends its budget on every combination of all 6 hyperparameters equally -- for the 4
    hyperparameters that don't matter, it is repeatedly re-testing essentially the same effective
    configuration, wasting trials.
  ● Random search samples each hyperparameter independently across its full range on every trial. For
    the 2 hyperparameters that do matter, this means random search still explores many distinct
    values of exactly those 2 dimensions, using its budget far more efficiently on the dimensions that
    actually matter.
  ● In practice this means random search can find a comparably good (or better) setting with far fewer
    total trials than grid search, whenever only a small subset of hyperparameters are truly influential -
    - which is very often the case.


Q31. [Descriptive] Explain learning-rate scheduling and why using a single fixed learning rate for all of
training is often suboptimal.
Solution




                                      Page 44 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks

  ● The trade-off with a fixed rate: a learning rate large enough for fast early progress is often too
    large later on, causing oscillation around the minimum instead of settling into it; a rate small
    enough for fine, stable convergence late in training is painfully slow at the start.
  ● Learning-rate scheduling resolves this by changing η over the course of training -- typically starting
    relatively large and decreasing it as training progresses. Common schedules include step decay
    (drop η by a fixed factor every few epochs), exponential decay, and cosine annealing (smoothly
    decreasing η following a cosine curve).
  ● Net effect: fast, coarse progress early in training, followed by careful, precise fine-tuning as the
    model approaches a good solution -- generally reaching a better final result than any single fixed
    learning rate could.

Topic: CNN Architectures

Q32. [Numerical] An input volume is 14×14×256. A 3×3 convolution producing 64 output channels is
needed. Compare the parameter cost of (a) applying the 3×3 convolution directly, versus (b) first using a
1×1 bottleneck to reduce 256→32 channels, then applying the 3×3 convolution (32→64).
Solution
(a) Direct 3×3 convolution:

                                    Params = 3×3×256×64 = 147,456

(b) With a 1×1 bottleneck:

                                     1×1 conv: 1×1×256×32 = 8,192

                                     3×3 conv: 3×3×32×64 = 18,432

                                    Total = 8,192 + 18,432 = 26,624

Step -- Compare: 147,456 / 26,624 ≈ 5.54, i.e. roughly an 82% reduction.

Significance: even with different numbers from Example 10.1, the same pattern holds: a 1×1 bottleneck
cuts parameters by roughly 5-10× for a typical channel count -- this is a general, reliable rule of thumb,
not a one-off coincidence.


Q33. [Short Answer] Why does GoogLeNet have far fewer parameters than VGG, despite being a deeper
network (22 layers vs. 16)?
Solution
  ● GoogLeNet uses 1×1 bottleneck convolutions throughout its Inception modules to shrink channel
    depth before the expensive 3×3/5×5 convolutions run, cutting their parameter cost by roughly 5-
    10× (Example 10.1 / Question 32).
  ● GoogLeNet replaces the huge Flatten+Dense stack at the end of the network with Global Average
    Pooling, which has zero learnable parameters, whereas VGG's dense layers alone account for the
    vast majority of its ≈138 million parameters (Example 4.2).
  ● Together, these two design choices let GoogLeNet reach 22 layers of depth using only ≈5 million
    parameters, versus VGG's 16 layers and ≈138 million parameters.

                                     Page 45 of 46 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                 Unit: Convolutional Neural Networks


Q34. [Descriptive] Compare AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet, and ResNet in terms of depth, parameter count,
and key innovation, and explain the evolutionary logic connecting them.
Solution

        Architecture             Depth                Parameters                    Key Innovation

 AlexNet (2012)             8 layers              ≈60M                    ReLU, Dropout, GPU training

 VGG-16 (2014)              16 layers             ≈138M                   Deep stack of small 3×3 filters

                                                                          Inception module + 1×1
 GoogLeNet (2014)           22 layers             ≈5M
                                                                          bottlenecks + GAP

 ResNet-152 (2015)          152 layers            ≈60M                    Residual / skip connections


  ● AlexNet first proved deep CNNs trained on GPUs could dramatically beat traditional computer
    vision -- opening the door to everything that followed.
  ● VGG pushed depth further using small, uniform filters, showing depth reliably helps -- but at a
    heavy parameter cost, mostly in its dense layers.
  ● GoogLeNet showed that clever, efficient module design (multi-scale filters + bottlenecks + GAP) can
    beat brute-force scaling -- more accurate than VGG with about 27× fewer parameters.
  ● ResNet then solved the degradation problem that had capped how deep any of the earlier designs
    could practically go, using residual connections -- unlocking networks over 100 layers deep as
    genuinely trainable.


Q35. [Descriptive] Explain the degradation problem observed in very deep plain (non-residual) networks,
and explain -- referencing H(x) = F(x) + x -- how residual connections solve it.
Solution
  ● The degradation problem: beyond a certain depth, simply stacking more layers onto a plain CNN
    makes both training and test accuracy get worse, not better. Crucially, this is not overfitting (test
    error alone getting worse while training error improves) -- training error itself rises, showing that
    the extra layers are making the network strictly harder to optimize, via vanishing/exploding
    gradients compounding across so many layers.
  ● The residual fix: instead of asking a block of layers to learn the full, possibly complex mapping H(x)
    directly, ResNet re-parameterizes the problem: the block learns only the residual F(x) = H(x) − x,
    and its actual output is computed as F(x) + x, adding the original input back in via an identity
    shortcut.
  ● Why this helps optimization: if the ideal mapping for a given block turns out to be close to the
    identity function, it is trivial for the block to learn F(x)≈0 (push its weights toward zero) rather than
    having to learn to reproduce H(x)=x exactly from scratch through several non-linear layers. More
    importantly, during backpropagation, the '+x' shortcut carries the gradient straight through with a
    local derivative of exactly 1, giving every layer a direct, unimpeded path back to the loss -- so
    gradients no longer have to survive an unbroken chain of many multiplications through non-linear
    layers, which is precisely what allows networks over 100 layers deep to train successfully.

1. Introduction to Sequential Data and Recurrent Neural
Networks

1.1 What Is Sequential Data?
     •    Sequential data is data in which order carries meaning — rearranging the elements changes (or
          destroys) the meaning. This is different from ordinary tabular data, where the order of rows does
          not matter.
Common examples of sequential data:

     •    Text / language — a sentence is a sequence of words; “dog bites man” ≠ “man bites dog”.
     •    Speech / audio — a sequence of sound-pressure samples over time.
     •    Time series — stock prices, weather readings, sensor logs: a sequence of numeric values indexed
          by time.
     •    Video — a sequence of image frames.
     •    Biological sequences — DNA base pairs, protein amino-acid chains.
Sequential data shares three properties that any model must respect:

     •    It can be of variable length (sentences are not all the same number of words).
     •    It is order-dependent (shuffling the elements changes the meaning).
     •    It often has long-range dependencies — something at position 2 can affect the correct
          interpretation of position 50.

1.2 Why Feedforward Networks Struggle with Sequences
A standard feedforward network (MLP) or a plain CNN expects one fixed-size input vector and produces
one output, independently of any other input it has ever seen. This creates four concrete problems for
sequence data:

     •    Fixed input size. An MLP needs a fixed number of input features, but sentences and time series
          vary in length.
     •    No memory. Each input is processed in isolation; the network has no mechanism to “remember”
          earlier inputs when processing the current one.
     •    No parameter sharing across positions. If we tried to flatten a sequence into one long fixed
          vector, the network would need separate weights for “word at position 5” versus “word at
          position 50” — this does not generalise to lengths not seen in training and wastes parameters.
     •    Violates the independence assumption. Standard supervised learning assumes examples are
          independent; elements inside a sequence are, by definition, statistically dependent on their
          neighbours.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                 Page 5 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




  Figure 1. A feedforward network has no memory; a recurrent network feeds its hidden state back into itself, carrying
                                     information from one time step to the next.


Key Insight
A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) fixes all four problems at once by introducing a hidden state that is
updated at every time step using the same weights. This single idea — a feedback loop with shared
parameters — is what allows one compact model to process sequences of any length.


1.3 The Core Idea of a Recurrent Network
      •   An RNN maintains a hidden state (also called the “context” or “memory”), denoted ht
      •   At every time step t, the network reads the current input xt and combines it with the previous
          hidden state ht−1 to produce a new hidden state ht.
      •   The same weight matrices are reused at every time step (parameter sharing across time). This
          is the single most important structural idea in this unit — it is what lets a fixed-size set of
          parameters handle sequences of any length.
      •   ht acts as a compressed summary of everything the network has read up to and including time t.
      •   An output yt (a class label, a predicted next word, a predicted next value, etc.) can be produced
          from ht at any time step where one is needed.
                                     ht = f(xt, ht−1)   — general recurrence relation

1.4 Notation Used Throughout This Unit
The table below fixes the notation used in every section that follows, so that the same symbol always
means the same thing.

           Symbol                                                    Meaning

 xt                              Input vector at time step t

 ht                              Hidden state (memory) at time step t

 yt                              Output produced at time step t

 Wxh, Whh, Why                   Weight matrices: input→hidden, hidden→hidden, hidden→output


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                          Page 6 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




           Symbol                                                 Meaning

 bh, by                          Bias vectors for the hidden and output layers

 tanh, σ                         Hyperbolic-tangent and sigmoid activation functions

 ⊙                               Element-wise (Hadamard) product

 L                               Loss function

 ∂L / ∂□                         Partial derivative of the loss with respect to □ (used in backpropagation)

 T                               Length of the input sequence


1.5 Applications of Recurrent Networks
Because they can model dependencies across time, recurrent networks (and their gated variants, LSTM
and GRU) have been used across a wide range of tasks:

     •    Language modelling and text generation (predicting the next word/character).
     •    Machine translation (sequence-to-sequence, encoder–decoder models).
     •    Speech recognition (audio waveform → text).
     •    Sentiment analysis and text classification.
     •    Time-series forecasting — stock prices, electricity demand, weather.
     •    Music and handwriting generation.
     •    Video captioning and action recognition.
     •    Chatbots and dialogue systems (largely superseded today by Transformers, but RNNs remain the
          conceptual foundation and are still used in resource-constrained / streaming settings).




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                      Page 7 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                    Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




2. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)

2.1 Architecture
     •    A simple (“vanilla”) RNN is a single cell that is applied repeatedly, once per time step, with the
          same weights every time.
     •    Drawing this repetition out explicitly over time steps is called unrolling the network — it turns
          the recurrent (looped) picture into an ordinary, feedforward-looking computational graph that
          we can apply standard backpropagation to.




 Figure 2. An RNN drawn as a single folded cell (left) and unrolled across three time steps (right). Every column uses the
                                      identical weight matrices Wxh, Whh, Why.

     •    Zooming into a single time step shows exactly what happens inside the cell:




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                            Page 8 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                       Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




         Figure 3. Inside one RNN cell at time step t: the previous hidden state and the current input are each linearly
                  transformed, summed with a bias, and squashed by tanh to produce the new hidden state.

2.2 Forward-Pass Equations
                                                     at = Wxh xt + Whh ht−1 + bh

                                                           ht = tanh(at)

                                                          yt = Why ht + by

Significance of each term:

     •     Wxh xt — brings in new information from the current input.
     •     Whh ht−1 — brings forward everything remembered so far from the past.
     •     tanh(·) — a nonlinearity that (a) lets the network represent non-linear relationships and (b)
           squashes the state into (−1, 1), keeping it numerically bounded step after step.
     •     Why ht + by — a read-out layer that turns the internal memory into whatever output the task
           needs (a class score, a predicted value, next-word logits, …).

2.3 Worked Example 1 — RNN Forward Pass, Step by Step
Given
Input sequence (T = 3, input size 2): x₁ = [1.0000, 0.5000], x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000], x₃ = [-0.5000,
1.0000]
Initial hidden state: h₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000] (hidden size 2)
Wxh = [[0.5000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.4000]], Whh = [[0.1000, 0.4000], [-0.2000, 0.3000]], bh =
[0.1000, -0.1000]
Why = [[0.6000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.5000]], by = [0.1000, 0.2000]


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                               Page 9 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                 Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Step 1 — Compute h₁ (process the first input)
We need a1 = Wxh x1 + Whh h0 + bh. Since h0 = [0.0000, 0.0000], the recurrent term contributes nothing yet
— this is the very first step, so there is no history to bring forward.
Wxh x₁ = (0.5×1.0 + (−0.3)×0.5, 0.2×1.0 + 0.4×0.5) = (0.35, 0.40)

a₁ = (0.35, 0.40) + (0, 0) + (0.1, −0.1) = [0.4500, 0.3000]

h₁ = tanh([0.4500, 0.3000]) = [0.4219, 0.2913]

Why this step matters
tanh squashes each pre-activation into (−1, 1). Both components of a₁ were modest in size, so tanh has
not saturated — the gradient through this step will still be healthy (we revisit this idea in Section 2.7).

Step 2 — Compute h₂ (now the recurrence is active)
Wxh x₂ = (0.5×0.5 + (−0.3)×(−1.0), 0.2×0.5 + 0.4×(−1.0)) = (0.5500, −0.3000)

Whh h₁ = (0.1×0.4219 + 0.4×0.2913, −0.2×0.4219 + 0.3×0.2913) = (0.1587, 0.0030)

a₂ = (0.5500, −0.3000) + (0.1587, 0.0030) + (0.1, −0.1) = [0.8087, -0.3970]

h₂ = tanh([0.8087, -0.3970]) = [0.6689, -0.3774]

     •    Notice that h₂ depends on x₂ and on h₁ (which itself depended on x₁). This is exactly how the RNN
          carries information forward — h₂ already contains a trace of x₁.

Step 3 — Compute h₃
Wxh x₃ = (−0.5500, 0.3000),            Whh h₂ = (−0.0841, −0.2470)

a₃ = [-0.5341, -0.0470]         ⇒      h₃ = tanh([-0.5341, -0.0470]) = [-0.4885, -0.0470]

Step 4 — Produce the output y₃
y₃ = Why h₃ + by = [[0.6000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.5000]] × [-0.4885, -0.0470] + [0.1000, 0.2000] = [-0.1790,
0.0788]

     •    This is a many-to-one read-out: we only needed an output at the final time step (e.g. classifying
          the whole sequence). If a prediction were needed at every step, the same Why, by read-out
          would be applied to h₁ and h₂ as well.
                                            Table 1. Summary of Worked Example 1.

     t             Input x_t                         Pre-activation a_t         Hidden state h_t = tanh(a_t)

 1         [1.0000, 0.5000]              [0.4500, 0.3000]                   [0.4219, 0.2913]

 2         [0.5000, -1.0000]             [0.8087, -0.3970]                  [0.6689, -0.3774]

                                                                            [-0.4885, -0.0470] → y₃ = [-
 3         [-0.5000, 1.0000]             [-0.5341, -0.0470]
                                                                            0.1790, 0.0788]

2.4 Types of RNN Architectures
The recurrence itself never changes; what changes from application to application is simply where inputs
enter and where outputs are read out.




                  Figure 4. Five standard input/output wiring patterns built from the same recurrent cell.

     •    One-to-one — a single input maps to a single output; degenerates to a normal feedforward layer
          (rarely used with recurrence, shown for completeness).
     •    One-to-many — one input, a whole output sequence (e.g. image captioning: one image → a
          sentence).
     •    Many-to-one — a whole input sequence, one output (e.g. sentiment classification) — this is the
          pattern used in Worked Example 1 above.
     •    Many-to-many (aligned) — one output per input, same length (e.g. part-of-speech tagging).
     •    Many-to-many (encoder–decoder) — an encoder RNN compresses the input into a context
          vector; a separate decoder RNN generates the (possibly different-length) output sequence from
          it (e.g. machine translation).

2.5 Training an RNN: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT)
     •    Idea: unroll the RNN for all T time steps (as in Figure 2), which turns it into one large feedforward
          computational graph — then apply ordinary backpropagation to that graph.
     •    Because the same weight matrix (say Whh) is reused at every time step, its total gradient is the
          sum of the gradient contributed at every time step:
                                              ∂L/∂Whh = Σₜ₌₁ᵀ ∂L/∂at ⊗ ht−1


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                           Page 11 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                               Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     •    Each backward step from ht to ht−1 multiplies the incoming gradient by Whhᵀ and by the local tanh
          derivative — this repeated multiplication is the root cause of the vanishing/exploding gradient
          problem (Section 2.7).




Figure 5. BPTT: the loss gradient flows backward through every copy of the network, moving from h3 back to h2, h1 and
                                                          h0.

2.6 Worked Example 2 — BPTT Gradient Computation
Given
Continue Worked Example 1. A target output target₃ = [1.0000, 0.0000] is supplied (one-hot encoding
for class 0), and the squared-error loss is applied at the final time step only (a many-to-one setup):

                 L = ½ ‖ y₃ − target₃ ‖² = ½ ‖ [-0.1790, 0.0788] − [1.0000, 0.0000] ‖² = 0.6981

Step 1 — Gradient at the output
∂L/∂y₃ = y₃ − target₃ = [-0.1790, 0.0788] − [1.0000, 0.0000] = [-1.1790, 0.0788]

     •    For squared error, ∂L/∂y = predicted − target — the gradient simply points from the prediction
          toward the target, scaled by the error.

Step 2 — Backprop into h₃ through the output layer
∂L/∂h₃ = Whyᵀ ∂L/∂y₃ = [[0.6000, -0.3000], [0.2000, 0.5000]]ᵀ × [-1.1790, 0.0788] = [-0.6916, 0.3931]

Step 3 — Backprop through tanh at t = 3
     •    The derivative of tanh is 1 − tanh²(a) = 1 − h², evaluated using the already-computed forward-
          pass value — this is why we saved every h_t during the forward pass.
∂L/∂a₃ = ∂L/∂h₃ ⊙ (1 − h₃²) = [-0.6916, 0.3931] ⊙ (1 − [-0.4885, -0.0470]²) = [-0.5266, 0.3922]




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                      Page 12 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Step 4 — Gradient contribution to Whh from t = 3
∂L/∂Whh |₃ = ∂L/∂a₃ ⊗ h₂ = [-0.5266, 0.3922] ⊗ [0.6689, -0.3774] = [[-0.3522, 0.1987], [0.2624, -
0.1480]]

     •    “⊗” here is an outer product: a gradient vector combined with the hidden state that was
          multiplied by Whh on the forward pass — this is the standard rule for the gradient of a matrix
          multiplication.

Step 5 — Propagate the gradient back one more step, to h₂
∂L/∂h₂ = Whhᵀ ∂L/∂a₃ = [[0.1000, 0.4000], [-0.2000, 0.3000]]ᵀ × [-0.5266, 0.3922] = [-0.1311, -0.0930]

∂L/∂a₂ = [-0.1311, -0.0930] ⊙ (1 − [0.6689, -0.3774]²) = [-0.0725, -0.0797]

∂L/∂Whh |₂ = [-0.0725, -0.0797] ⊗ [0.4219, 0.2913] = [[-0.0306, -0.0211], [-0.0336, -0.0232]]

Step 6 — Propagate back to h₁, then to h₀
∂L/∂h₁ = [[0.1000, 0.4000], [-0.2000, 0.3000]]ᵀ × [-0.0725, -0.0797] = [0.0087, -0.0529]           ⇒      ∂L/∂a₁ =
[0.0072, -0.0484]

∂L/∂Whh |₁ = [0.0072, -0.0484] ⊗ [0.0000, 0.0000] = [[0.0000, 0.0000], [0.0000, 0.0000]]

Why this term is zero
The contribution at t = 1 is multiplied by h₀ = (0, 0), the initial hidden state. With a zero initial state
there is nothing for the very first step to “multiply against” for this particular weight, so its contribution
vanishes.
This is a special case of using a zero initial state, not a general property of BPTT: the gradient signal
∂L/∂h₁ itself is still non-zero, so it correctly continues to update Wxh and bh through this step.

Step 7 — Total gradient (sum over all time steps)
                                 ∂L/∂Whh = ∂L/∂Whh|₁ + ∂L/∂Whh|₂ + ∂L/∂Whh|₃

[[0.0000, 0.0000], [0.0000, 0.0000]] + [[-0.0306, -0.0211], [-0.0336, -0.0232]] + [[-0.3522, 0.1987],
[0.2624, -0.1480]] = [[-0.3828, 0.1776], [0.2287, -0.1712]]

     •    The same mechanism (chain rule + outer product with the relevant input, summed across time)
          also gives ∂L/∂Wxh = [[0.2342, -0.4506], [-0.2844, 0.4478]] and ∂L/∂Why = [[0.5759, 0.0554], [-
          0.0385, -0.0037]]; these are left as Practice Question 32.

2.7 The Vanishing and Exploding Gradient Problem
     •    Look again at Steps 5–6 above: every step back multiplies the gradient by Whhᵀ and by a tanh-
          derivative factor that is always ≤ 1.
     •    Over T time steps this becomes roughly a product of T such factors — informally, gradient ∝ λᵀ,
          where λ reflects the typical size of Whhᵀ × tanh′.
     •    If λ < 1: the product shrinks exponentially with T — the vanishing gradient problem. Early time
          steps receive a near-zero learning signal, so the network effectively cannot learn long-range
          dependencies.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 13 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                    Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



      •    If λ > 1: the product grows exponentially — the exploding gradient problem. Weight updates
           become huge and training diverges (loss becomes NaN / oscillates wildly).




  Figure 6. Relative gradient magnitude after k backward steps, for three illustrative values of λ. Even a modest λ = 0.5
                              leaves almost nothing after 10 steps; λ = 1.5 grows past 50×.

                      Table 2. Illustrative decay/growth of |λ^k| with the number of backward steps k.

          k (steps back)             λ = 0.5 (vanishing)          λ = 1.0 (stable)            λ = 1.5 (exploding)

 1                                         0.5000                       1.00                         1.5000

 2                                         0.2500                       1.00                         2.2500

 3                                         0.1250                       1.00                         3.3750

 5                                         0.03125                      1.00                         7.5938

 10                                       0.000977                      1.00                         57.665
Standard mitigations used in practice:

      •    Gradient clipping — rescale the gradient if its norm exceeds a threshold; a simple, effective fix
           for exploding gradients.
      •    Careful weight initialisation (e.g. orthogonal initialisation of Whh) — keeps λ close to 1 for
           longer.
      •    Truncated BPTT — limit how many steps gradients are propagated back through, trading long-
           range learning for stability/speed.
      •    Gated architectures — LSTM and GRU — redesign the recurrence itself so that gradients can
           flow across many steps largely unimpeded. This is the main solution used in practice, and is the
           subject of the next two sections.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                           Page 14 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




3. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

3.1 Motivation
     •    Plain RNNs struggle to learn long-range dependencies because gradients shrink (or blow up)
          exponentially as they are backpropagated through many time steps (Section 2.7).
     •    LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) fixes this by giving the network a separate memory
          channel — the cell state — that information can flow along with only minor, mostly linear
          changes, instead of being repeatedly squashed through a matrix multiply and a tanh at every
          step.
     •    Three gates (small neural networks with sigmoid outputs in (0, 1)) learn when to write to, erase
          from, and read from this memory.

3.2 Architecture
     •    Cell state Ct — the long-term memory “conveyor belt” running along the top of the diagram
          below.
     •    Forget gate ft — decides what fraction of the old cell state to keep.
     •    Input gate it — decides how much of the new candidate information to write in.
     •    Candidate c̃t — the new content proposed for the cell state (not yet gated).
     •    Output gate ot — decides how much of the (updated) cell state to expose as the hidden state /
          output.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 15 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




 Figure 7. Internal structure of one LSTM cell. The cell state Ct runs along the top with only element-wise operations —
                                     this is what protects the gradient from vanishing.

3.3 Equations
All four gates/candidates first form the same concatenated input, then apply their own weights:

                    zₜ = [ hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ ]    (concatenate previous hidden state and current input)

                                                        ft = σ(Wf zₜ + bf)

                                                        it = σ(Wi zₜ + bi)

                                                      c̃t = tanh(Wc zₜ + bc)

                                                     Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t

                                                       ot = σ(Wo zₜ + bo)

                                                       ht = ot ⊙ tanh(Ct)

Significance of each equation:

     •    Forget gate — a sigmoid output near 0 erases that part of memory; near 1 preserves it
          completely.
     •    Input gate × candidate — the network only writes new information where the input gate allows
          it, protecting unrelated parts of memory.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                         Page 16 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     •    Cell-state update — additive and element-wise (no matrix multiply, no squashing) — this is the
          key structural difference from a plain RNN, and is what allows gradients to flow across many steps
          largely unchanged (Section 3.5).
     •    Output gate — the cell can hold information in Ct without necessarily exposing it in ht — memory
          and “what to output right now” are decoupled.

3.4 Worked Example 3 — LSTM Forward Pass, Step by Step
Given
Same two inputs as the RNN example, so the two architectures can be compared directly: x₁ = [1.0000,
0.5000], x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000]
Initial state: h₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000], C₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000]
Wf = [[0.3,0.1,0.2,-0.1],[-0.2,0.4,0.1,0.3]], bf = [0.1000, 0.0000]
Wi = [[0.2,-0.3,0.4,0.1],[0.1,0.2,-0.2,0.3]], bi = [0.0000, 0.1000]
Wc = [[0.4,0.1,-0.3,0.2],[-0.1,0.3,0.2,0.1]], bc = [0.1000, -0.1000]
Wo = [[0.3,0.2,0.1,-0.2],[0.2,-0.1,0.3,0.1]], bo = [0.0000, 0.2000]

Time step t = 1
Step 1.1 — Build the concatenated input: z₁ = [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 0, 1.0, 0.5]
Step 1.2 — Forget gate: Wf z₁ + bf = (0.15, 0.25) + (0.1, 0.0) = (0.25, 0.25) ⇒ f₁ = σ(0.25, 0.25) =
[0.5622, 0.5622]

Step 1.3 — Input gate: Wi z₁ + bi = (0.45, −0.05) + (0.0, 0.1) = (0.45, 0.05) ⇒ i₁ = σ(0.45, 0.05) = [0.6106,
0.5125]
Step 1.4 — Candidate cell content: Wc z₁ + bc = (−0.3, 0.25) + (0.1, −0.1) = (−0.2, 0.15) ⇒ c̃₁ = tanh(−0.2,
0.15) = [-0.0997, 0.1489]
Step 1.5 — Update the cell state: C₁ = f₁⊙C₀ + i₁⊙c̃₁ = [0.5622, 0.5622]⊙[0.0000, 0.0000] + [0.6106,
0.5125]⊙[-0.0997, 0.1489] = [0.0000, 0.0000] + [-0.0609, 0.0763] = [-0.0609, 0.0763]
     •    Because C₀ = (0, 0), the forget gate has nothing to act on yet — the entire cell state at t = 1 comes
          from the new candidate, scaled by the input gate.
Step 1.6 — Output gate: Wo z₁ + bo = (0.0, 0.35) + (0.0, 0.2) = (0.0, 0.55) ⇒ o₁ = σ(0.0, 0.55) = [0.5000,
0.6341]
Step 1.7 — Hidden state: h₁ = o₁⊙tanh(C₁) = [0.5000, 0.6341]⊙tanh([-0.0609, 0.0763]) = [-0.0304,
0.0483]

Time step t = 2
The identical six equations are applied again, now using h₁ and C₁ from the previous step and the new
input x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000]: z₂ = [h₁ ; x₂] = [-0.0304, 0.0483, 0.5000, -1.0000]

                   Quantity                              Pre-activation (Wz + b)          After activation

 Forget gate f₂                                      —                             [0.5734, 0.4441]

 Input gate i₂                                       —                             [0.5198, 0.4272]

 Candidate c̃₂                                       —                             [-0.2518, -0.0823]


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                         Page 17 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




                   Quantity                              Pre-activation (Wz + b)          After activation

 Cell state C₂ = f₂⊙C₁ + i₂⊙c̃₂                                                    [-0.1658, -0.0013]

 Output gate o₂                                      —                             [0.5623, 0.5595]

 Hidden state h₂ = o₂⊙tanh(C₂)                                                     [-0.0924, -0.0007]

Compare with the plain RNN
At t = 1 the plain RNN produced h₁ = [0.4219, 0.2913] (Worked Example 1); the LSTM produces h₁ = [-
0.0304, 0.0483] from the
same input. The values differ because the LSTM's gates are actively controlling how much new
information enters the state — with these particular (untrained, illustrative) weights the gates happen
to let relatively little through. After training on real data, the gates learn to open and close purposefully.


3.5 Why LSTM Solves the Vanishing Gradient Problem
     •    Recall from Section 2.7 that a plain RNN's gradient must pass through a matrix multiply by Whh
          and a tanh derivative at every single step — repeated many times, this shrinks (or explodes)
          exponentially.
     •    The LSTM cell-state recurrence is Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + (new term) — this is additive, so ∂Ct/∂Ct−1 = ft
          (an element-wise scaling, not a matrix multiply followed by a squashing nonlinearity).
     •    If the forget gate learns to stay close to 1 for information that should be remembered, the
          gradient can flow backward through many time steps with almost no shrinkage — an unimpeded
          “gradient highway” along the cell state.
     •    This does not eliminate vanishing gradients entirely (very long sequences can still be difficult, and
          the hidden-state path through tanh still exists), but it dramatically extends how far back an RNN-
          family model can learn useful dependencies — this is the single biggest reason LSTMs outperform
          plain RNNs in practice.

3.6 Advantages and Limitations
     •    Advantages: learns long-range dependencies far better than a plain RNN; the gating mechanism
          is learned end-to-end from data; remains a strong, well-understood baseline for sequence tasks.
     •    Limitations: four sets of weights (forget, input, candidate, output) means roughly 4× the
          parameters of a plain RNN of the same hidden size (Section 6); inherently sequential computation
          makes it slower to train than fully parallel architectures such as Transformers; still not immune
          to very long sequences (hundreds/thousands of steps).




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                         Page 18 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




4. Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)

4.1 Motivation
     •    Introduced by Cho et al. (2014), the GRU asks: can we get most of the benefit of LSTM's gating —
          protection against vanishing gradients, learned control over memory — with a simpler cell?
     •    GRU merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate, and removes the separate cell
          state entirely — the hidden state itself carries long-term memory.
     •    Fewer gates means fewer parameters (Section 6) and typically faster training, while remaining
          competitive with LSTM on many tasks.

4.2 Architecture
     •    Update gate zt — decides how much of the old hidden state to keep versus how much of the new
          candidate to mix in. It plays the combined role of LSTM's forget and input gates.
     •    Reset gate rt — decides how much of the past hidden state to use when forming the new
          candidate content.
     •    Candidate hidden state h̃t — a proposed new hidden-state value, computed using the reset
          (partially forgotten) past state.
     •    No separate cell state — ht itself is the blend of old and new content.




Figure 8. Internal structure of one GRU cell. The final blend node interpolates between the old hidden state and the new
                                   candidate, controlled entirely by the update gate zt.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                         Page 19 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                               Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




4.3 Equations
                    zₜ = [ hₜ₋₁ ; xₜ ]    (concatenate previous hidden state and current input)

                                                      zt = σ(Wz zₜ + bz)

                                                       rt = σ(Wr zₜ + br)

                                             h̃t = tanh(Wh [ rt ⊙ ht−1 ; xt ] + bh)

                                                ht = (1 − zt) ⊙ ht−1 + zt ⊙ h̃t

Significance of each equation:

     •    Update gate — close to 0 keeps the old state almost unchanged; close to 1 replaces it almost
          entirely with the new candidate.
     •    Reset gate — close to 0 makes the candidate ignore the past and depend mostly on the current
          input (useful when starting a new, unrelated chunk of a sequence, e.g. a new sentence).
     •    Final blend — a convex combination (weights sum to 1) of old state and new candidate. Like the
          LSTM cell-state update, this blend is dominated by simple arithmetic rather than repeated matrix
          multiplication, which is what protects the gradient.

4.4 Worked Example 4 — GRU Forward Pass, Step by Step
Given
Same two inputs again, for direct comparison with the RNN and LSTM examples: x₁ = [1.0000, 0.5000],
x₂ = [0.5000, -1.0000]
Initial hidden state: h₀ = [0.0000, 0.0000]
Wz = [[0.2,-0.1,0.3,0.1],[0.1,0.3,-0.2,0.2]], bz = [0.1000, 0.0000]
Wr = [[0.4,0.2,-0.1,0.3],[-0.2,0.1,0.2,-0.3]], br = [0.0000, 0.1000]
Wh = [[0.3,-0.2,0.4,0.1],[0.2,0.1,-0.3,0.2]], bh = [0.1000, -0.1000]

Time step t = 1
Step 1.1 — Build the concatenated input: z₁(input) = [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 0, 1.0, 0.5]
Step 1.2 — Update gate: Wz·z₁ + bz = (0.35, −0.10) + (0.1, 0.0) = (0.45, −0.10) ⇒ z₁ = σ(0.45, −0.10) =
[0.6106, 0.4750]
Step 1.3 — Reset gate: Wr·z₁ + br = (0.05, 0.05) + (0.0, 0.1) = (0.05, 0.15) ⇒ r₁ = σ(0.05, 0.15) = [0.5125,
0.5374]
Step 1.4 — Apply the reset gate to the past state: r₁⊙h₀ = [0.5125, 0.5374]⊙[0.0000, 0.0000] = (0, 0)
— with h₀ = 0 there is nothing to reset yet, so this step has no visible effect at t = 1 (its role becomes clear
at t = 2).
Step 1.5 — Candidate hidden state: Wh·[r₁⊙h₀ ; x₁] + bh = (0.45, −0.20) + (0.1, −0.1) = (0.55, −0.30) ⇒
h̃ ₁ = tanh(0.55, −0.30) = [0.5005, -0.2913]
Step 1.6 — Final blend (this is h₁): h₁ = (1−z₁)⊙h₀ + z₁⊙h̃ ₁ = (1−[0.6106, 0.4750])⊙[0.0000, 0.0000] +
[0.6106, 0.4750]⊙[0.5005, -0.2913] = [0.3056, -0.1384]
     •    Because h₀ = 0, the first term vanishes and h₁ is simply z₁ ⊙ h̃₁ — the update gate scales down
          how much of the fresh candidate is accepted.

— this is Practice Question 21.

4.5 GRU vs LSTM
     •    GRU has no output gate — the full hidden state is always exposed (LSTM can hide part of its cell
          state from the output via the output gate).
     •    GRU has no separate cell state — memory and output are the same vector, which simplifies the
          design but gives slightly less representational flexibility.
     •    GRU uses one combined update gate where LSTM uses two independent gates (forget, input) —
          fewer parameters, slightly less fine-grained control.
     •    In practice, the two perform comparably on many tasks; GRU is often preferred when training
          speed / parameter budget matters, LSTM when maximum modelling flexibility is preferred. Both
          comfortably outperform a plain RNN on long sequences.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                     Page 21 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                               Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




5. Recurrent Neural Network Language Models

5.1 What Is a Language Model?
     •    A language model assigns a probability to sequences of words, or equivalently, predicts a
          probability distribution over the next word given all the words seen so far.
     •    Formally, for a sequence of words w1, …, wT, a language model estimates:
                     P(w₁, …, wᵀ) = P(w₁) · P(w₂ | w₁) · P(w₃ | w₁, w₂) · ⋯ · P(wᵀ | w₁, …, wᵀ₋₁)

     •    Language models power autocomplete, text generation, machine translation (as the decoder),
          speech recognition (choosing the most fluent transcription), and are the training objective
          behind today's large language models.

5.2 An RNN as a Language Model — Architecture
     •    Step 1 — Embedding: each word is converted from a discrete token into a dense vector (a row
          of a learned embedding matrix E).
     •    Step 2 — Recurrence: the embedding is fed into the RNN (or LSTM / GRU) exactly as in Sections
          2–4; the hidden state accumulates context from every word seen so far.
     •    Step 3 — Read-out: at every time step, the hidden state is projected to a vector of logits, one per
          vocabulary word, and passed through softmax to obtain a probability distribution over the next
          word.
     •    Training: at each step, the true next word is compared against the predicted distribution using
          cross-entropy loss; the same shared weights are updated via BPTT, exactly as in Section 2.5.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                      Page 22 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                      Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks




Figure 9. An RNN language model unrolled across two time steps. The same RNN weights from Section 2 are reused here
             — only the input (word embeddings) and output (softmax over the vocabulary) layers are new.

5.3 Equations
                           eₜ = E[ wₜ ]   (look up the embedding row for the current word)

                                      at = Wxh eₜ + Whh ht−1 + bh     ;      ht = tanh(at)

                                                     logitst = Why ht + by

                                           P(word | context) = softmax(logitsₜ)

                          Lₜ = − log P(wₜ₊₁ = target | context)     (cross-entropy loss at step t)

Significance:

     •    Embedding lookup turns a discrete word into a point in continuous space, where similar words
          can end up close together after training.
     •    Softmax converts raw logits into a valid probability distribution (non-negative, sums to 1) over
          the entire vocabulary.
     •    Cross-entropy loss penalises the model in proportion to how surprised it was by the true next
          word — a confident wrong prediction is penalised heavily; a confident correct prediction has
          almost no loss.

5.4 Worked Example 5 — Next-Word Prediction, Step by Step
Given


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                             Page 23 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Toy vocabulary (4 words): {I, love, deep, learning}, indices 0–3.
Embedding table E (one row per word): I → [0.1000, 0.2000], love → [0.3000, -0.1000], deep → [-
0.2000, 0.4000], learning → [0.5000, 0.1000]
Recurrence weights: the same Wxh, Whh, bh from Worked Example 1 (Section 2.3) — re-used here to
show that the recurrence itself is identical; only the surrounding embedding/read-out layers are new.
Read-out weights: Why(lm) = [[0.2,0.1],[0.1,-0.2],[-0.3,0.4],[0.4,0.2]], by(lm) = [0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000,
0.1000]
Training sentence: “I love deep learning” → input/target pairs (I → love), (love → deep)

Time step t = 1: input = “I”, target = “love”
Step 1.1 — Embed the input word: e₁ = E[“I”] = [0.1000, 0.2000]
Step 1.2 — Update the hidden state (identical recurrence to Section 2.3): a₁ = Wxh e₁ + Whh h₀ + bh =
[0.0900, 0.0000] ⇒ h₁ = tanh([0.0900, 0.0000]) = [0.0898, 0.0000]
Step 1.3 — Project to vocabulary-sized logits: logits₁ = Why(lm) h₁ + by(lm) = [0.0180, 0.0090, -0.0269,
0.1359]
Step 1.4 — Softmax → probability distribution over the 4 words: P = softmax([0.0180, 0.0090, -0.0269,
0.1359]) = [I: 0.2456, love: 0.2434, deep: 0.2348, learning: 0.2763]
Step 1.5 — Cross-entropy loss against the true next word “love”: L₁ = − log P(love) = − log(0.2434) =
1.4132

Reading the result
All four probabilities came out close to 0.25 (i.e. close to uniform / random guessing) — unsurprising,
since these are untrained, illustrative weights, not weights learned from real text. Training would push
P(love) toward 1 for this context by adjusting every weight along the BPTT gradient path (Section 2.5–
2.6).

Time step t = 2: input = “love”, target = “deep”
The hidden state now carries forward information from “I” as well:
