5.5 Perplexity
     •    Perplexity is the standard way to report how well a language model predicts text; it converts the
          average cross-entropy loss back onto an intuitive scale:
                     Average loss = (L₁ + L₂ + ⋯) / T           Perplexity = exp(Average loss)



Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                     Page 24 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                          Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



For this example: Average loss = (1.4132 + 1.5569) / 2 = 1.4850 ⇒ Perplexity = exp(1.4850) = 4.4151
     •    Interpretation: a perplexity of 4.42 means the model is, on average, about as “confused” as if it
          were guessing uniformly at random among roughly 4.4 equally likely words — out of a 4-word
          vocabulary, that is only slightly better than pure guessing (perplexity 4.0), consistent with these
          being untrained weights.
     •    Lower perplexity = better model. A well-trained model on a large vocabulary typically achieves a
          perplexity far below the vocabulary size, because it learns to concentrate probability mass on
          plausible next words.
     •    Perplexity = 1 would mean the model is always 100% certain and always correct (the theoretical
          best); perplexity equal to the vocabulary size corresponds to uniform random guessing (the
          practical worst case for a sensible model).

5.6 Beyond the Basics
     •    Teacher forcing — during training, the true previous word is fed as input at every step (as in
          Worked Example 5), even if the model's own previous prediction was wrong; this stabilises and
          speeds up training.
     •    Generation / sampling — at inference time there is no “true” next word, so the model's own
          output is fed back as the next input. Common strategies: greedy decoding (always pick the
          highest-probability word), sampling with temperature, and beam search.
     •    LSTM / GRU language models — in practice, the plain-RNN recurrence in this section is almost
          always replaced by an LSTM or GRU cell (Sections 3–4), since long documents need the improved
          long-range memory.
     •    Modern context — Transformer-based language models have largely superseded RNN-based
          ones for state-of-the-art results, but the evaluation concepts introduced here — next-word
          prediction, cross-entropy loss, and perplexity — remain exactly the same and are used to evaluate
          Transformer language models too.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                 Page 25 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                                Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks

6.2 Parameter-Count Formulas
For input size d and hidden size h, counting every weight matrix and bias:

    Architecture                  Parameter count formula                     Example: d = 100, h = 128

 RNN                      h(d + h + 1)                              29,312

 LSTM                     4 × h(d + h + 1)                          117,248 (= 4 × RNN)

 GRU                      3 × h(d + h + 1)                          87,936 (= 3 × RNN)
     •    The “4×” and “3×” factors come directly from counting gates: LSTM has 4 sets of weights (forget,
          input, candidate, output), all sharing the same input shape (d + h) → h; GRU has 3 (update, reset,
          candidate). This is why, for a fixed parameter budget, a GRU can afford a larger hidden size than
          an LSTM.

6.3 When to Use Which
     •    Plain RNN — short sequences, when simplicity/speed matters more than long-range memory, or
          as a teaching baseline. Rarely the best choice for real long-sequence tasks.
     •    LSTM — tasks needing the most reliable long-range memory and fine-grained control (separately
          tunable forget/input/output behaviour); a strong default when compute budget is not tight.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                       Page 26 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     •    GRU — a strong default when training speed or parameter budget is constrained (e.g.
          mobile/embedded, very large hidden sizes, limited data); frequently matches LSTM accuracy with
          fewer resources.
     •    Neither, in modern large-scale NLP — Transformer-based architectures have largely replaced all
          three for state-of-the-art language tasks, because they parallelise across time (faster training)
          and use attention instead of a single recurrent bottleneck. RNN/LSTM/GRU remain important for
          streaming/online settings, resource-constrained devices, and as the conceptual foundation for
          sequence modelling.

7. Practice Questions

This bank contains 50 questions covering every topic in this unit: 15 multiple-choice questions (Part A)
and 35 descriptive / numerical questions (Part B). Attempt each question before reading its solution.

Part A — Multiple Choice Questions (Q1–Q15)

Q1. Which of the following is NOT a defining property of sequential data? [1 mark]
     (A) Every sequence in the dataset must have exactly the same length. ✓ correct
     (B) The order of elements affects the meaning.
     (C) Later elements can depend on much earlier elements.
     (D) Elements are not statistically independent of their neighbours.
Answer: (A)
Solution:
Sequential data is explicitly allowed to be of variable length — sentences, audio clips and time series
routinely differ in length. This variability is precisely why ordinary feedforward networks (which need a
fixed-size input) struggle with sequences (Section 1.2), and why RNNs, which process one element at a
time and share weights across positions, are needed. Options B, C, and D all describe real properties of
sequential data (Section 1.1).

Q2. What is the single most important structural idea that lets an RNN process sequences of any length
using a fixed number of parameters? [1 mark]
     (A) Using convolutional filters that slide over the input.
     (B) Increasing the hidden size whenever the sequence is longer.
     (C) Sharing the same weight matrices across all time steps. ✓ correct
     (D) Training a separate small network for every time step.
Answer: (C)
Solution:
Because Wxh, Whh, Why (and their biases) are reused, identically, at every time step, the total number
of parameters does not grow with sequence length — a 5-word sentence and a 500-word document are
processed by exactly the same set of weights, applied repeatedly (Section 1.3, Section 2.1). Option D is
effectively the opposite of parameter sharing and would not generalise to unseen lengths.

Q3. In the standard update ht = tanh(Wxhxt + Whhht−1 + bh), every component of ht must lie in which
range? [1 mark]
     (A) (−1, 1) ✓ correct
     (B) (0, 1)
     (C) (−∞, ∞)
     (D) [0, ∞)
Answer: (A)
Solution:
tanh squashes any real-valued input into the open interval (−1, 1) (Section 2.2). (0, 1) is the range of the
sigmoid function instead, which is used inside LSTM/GRU gates, not the plain RNN hidden-state update.



Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 28 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Q4. If a pre-activation value a = 0, what are tanh(a) and its local derivative 1 − tanh²(a) at that point? [1
mark]
     (A) 0 and 0
     (B) 1 and 0
     (C) 1 and 1
     (D) 0 and 1 ✓ correct
Answer: (D)
Solution:
tanh(0) = 0, and 1 − tanh²(0) = 1 − 0 = 1. This is the largest possible value the tanh-derivative factor can
take (it is always ≤ 1) — so even in the best case, each backward step through tanh cannot amplify the
gradient, only preserve or shrink it. This is the local mechanism underlying the vanishing-gradient
discussion in Section 2.7.

Q5. In BPTT for a plain RNN, the total gradient of the loss with respect to Whh is obtained by: [1 mark]
     (A) Summing the gradient contributions from every time step. ✓ correct
     (B) Using only the gradient contribution from the final time step.
     (C) Averaging the contributions from only the first and last time steps.
     (D) Taking the single largest contribution across all time steps.
Answer: (A)
Solution:
Because Whh is reused at every step, the multivariable chain rule requires summing its gradient
contribution from every time step it was used in: ∂L/∂Whh = Σₜ ∂L/∂aₜ ⊗ hₜ₋₁ (Section 2.5, demonstrated
numerically in Worked Example 2).

Q6. The vanishing gradient problem in plain RNNs is primarily caused by: [1 mark]
     (A) Using too few hidden units.
     (B) Using too large a learning rate.
     (C) The softmax function saturating.
     (D) Repeated multiplication by Whhᵀ and a tanh-derivative factor (≤ 1) at every backward step. ✓
     correct
Answer: (D)
Solution:
Backpropagating through T time steps multiplies the gradient by roughly T copies of Whhᵀ and a tanh-
derivative factor. If the typical size of this product (informally λ) is less than 1, the gradient shrinks
exponentially with T (Section 2.7, Figure 6). This has nothing to do with learning rate (B) or softmax (C),
and too few hidden units (A) is a capacity problem, not a gradient-flow problem.

Q7. Which technique is the standard, simplest fix specifically aimed at exploding gradients? [1 mark]
     (A) Gradient clipping ✓ correct
     (B) Dropout
     (C) Batch normalisation
     (D) Data augmentation
Answer: (A)
Solution:


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 29 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Gradient clipping directly rescales the gradient vector when its norm exceeds a chosen threshold, capping
the size of any single update — a direct, minimal-assumption fix for exploding gradients (Section 2.7).
Dropout and data augmentation address overfitting, not gradient explosion; batch normalisation targets
internal covariate shift in deep feedforward stacks.

Q8. How many gate values does a standard LSTM cell compute at each time step? [1 mark]
     (A) 1
     (B) 3 ✓ correct
     (C) 2
     (D) 4
Answer: (B)
Solution:
An LSTM has exactly three gates: forget (fₜ), input (iₜ), and output (oₜ) — each a sigmoid, each genuinely
“gating” (scaling) something. The candidate c̃ₜ is also computed from the same weights but is not a gate:
it uses tanh and proposes new content rather than deciding how much of something to let through. This
distinction is a common point of confusion (Section 3.2–3.3).

Q9. A forget-gate value ft close to 0 for a particular memory component means: [1 mark]
     (A) That component of the old cell state is almost entirely kept.
     (B) The input gate is automatically forced to 0.
     (C) That component of the old cell state is almost entirely erased. ✓ correct
     (D) The output gate closes for that component.
Answer: (C)
Solution:
Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + (new term); when ft ≈ 0 for a component, that component of Ct−1 is multiplied by ≈ 0
and is therefore erased from the running memory (Section 3.3). The forget and input gates are computed
independently (different weights), so (B) is false in general.

Q10. The main reason the LSTM cell state protects gradients from vanishing is that its update rule is: [1
mark]
     (A) Multiplicative and passed through tanh at every step, like a plain RNN.
     (B) Computed only once, at the final time step.
     (C) Identical in form to the plain RNN's hidden-state update.
     (D) Additive and mostly element-wise, with no repeated matrix multiply on the main path. ✓ correct
Answer: (D)
Solution:
Ct = ft ⊙ Ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t is additive, so ∂Ct/∂Ct−1 = ft (an element-wise scaling), not a matrix multiplication
followed by a squashing nonlinearity. If ft stays near 1, gradients can flow across many steps with minimal
shrinkage — the “gradient highway” idea of Section 3.5.

Q11. How many gates does a standard GRU have? [1 mark]
     (A) 1
     (B) 3
     (C) 2 ✓ correct


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 30 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     (D) 4
Answer: (C)
Solution:
A GRU has exactly two gates: the update gate zt and the reset gate rt (Section 4.2). This is one fewer gate-
type than LSTM's three, which is the direct source of GRU's smaller parameter count (≈ 3× a plain RNN,
versus ≈ 4× for LSTM — Section 6.2).

Q12. Which statement about the GRU is correct? [1 mark]
     (A) GRU has a separate cell state distinct from its hidden state.
     (B) GRU merges the roles of LSTM's forget and input gates into a single update gate. ✓ correct
     (C) GRU has more parameters than an LSTM of the same hidden size.
     (D) GRU has an explicit output gate, exactly like LSTM.
Answer: (B)
Solution:
The update gate zt controls the blend ht = (1−zt)⊙ht−1 + zt⊙h̃t — z acting large plays the role of LSTM's
input gate (write new content), and (1−z) acting large plays the role of the forget gate (keep old content),
combined into one gate (Section 4.5). GRU has no separate cell state (A is false), fewer parameters than
LSTM (C is false), and no output gate (D is false).

Q13. In an RNN language model, the softmax layer at each time step outputs: [1 mark]
     (A) The next hidden state directly.
     (B) The embedding vector of the input word.
     (C) A probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next word. ✓ correct
     (D) The scalar cross-entropy loss value.
Answer: (C)
Solution:
softmax(logitsₜ) converts the raw, unbounded logits into non-negative values that sum to 1 — a valid
probability distribution over every word in the vocabulary (Section 5.2–5.3). The loss (D) is computed
from this distribution afterward, using the true next word.

Q14. If a language model's average cross-entropy loss on a test set is L, its perplexity is: [1 mark]
     (A) L²
     (B) 1 / L
     (C) log(L)
     (D) exp(L) ✓ correct
Answer: (D)
Solution:
Perplexity = exp(average cross-entropy loss) (Section 5.5). This maps loss = 0 (a perfect model) to
perplexity = 1, and increases perplexity exponentially as the average loss increases, giving a more intuitive
“effective number of choices” interpretation than the raw loss.

Q15. For the same input size and hidden size, an LSTM has approximately how many times the number
of parameters of a plain RNN? [1 mark]
     (A) 1×

Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 31 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     (B) 4× ✓ correct
     (C) 2×
     (D) 3×
Answer: (B)
Solution:
A plain RNN has one set of weights of shape h×(d+h) plus a bias; an LSTM computes four such quantities
(forget, input, candidate, output) from the same input shape, so its parameter count is 4 × h(d+h+1)
versus h(d+h+1) for the RNN — exactly 4× (Section 6.2, Table “Parameter-Count Formulas”). GRU, with 3
such computations, is ≈ 3×.

Part B — Descriptive and Numerical Questions (Q16–Q50)
Q16. List and briefly explain three properties that any model of sequential data must respect. [3 marks]
Solution:
     •    Variable length — sequences in a dataset are rarely all the same length (sentences, audio clips,
          etc.), so the model cannot assume a fixed-size input.
     •    Order-dependence — shuffling the elements changes (or destroys) the meaning; e.g. “dog bites
          man” ≠ “man bites dog”.
     •    Long-range dependencies — information at one position can affect the correct interpretation of
          a position much later in the sequence, so the model needs some form of memory (Section 1.1).

Q17. Give two distinct reasons why a plain feedforward network (MLP) with a flattened input vector is
a poor choice for variable-length text classification. [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    Fixed input size: an MLP requires a predetermined number of input features. Flattening text of
          different lengths into one vector either forces truncation/padding to an arbitrary maximum
          length, or simply cannot be done consistently.
     •    No parameter sharing across positions: if position 5 and position 50 of the flattened vector each
          get their own weights, the network must separately learn what a given word means at every
          possible position, wasting parameters and failing to generalise to lengths/positions not seen
          during training (Section 1.2).

Q18. Explain the difference between the “folded” and “unrolled” views of an RNN, and state why the
unrolled view is useful for training. [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    The folded view shows a single RNN cell with a self-loop (feedback arrow) — a compact picture
          of the recurrence rule itself.
     •    The unrolled view draws a separate copy of that same cell for every time step t = 1, …, T,
          connected in a chain, with the identical weights (Wxh, Whh, Why) used in every copy (Figure 2).
     •    The unrolled view is useful for training because it turns the recurrent (looped) computation into
          an ordinary directed acyclic graph, to which standard backpropagation can be applied directly —
          this is exactly what Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) does (Section 2.5).




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 32 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Q19. A plain RNN has input size 3 and hidden size 2. Given ht−1 = [0.1000, -0.2000], xt = [1, 0, −1], Wxh =
[[0.2000, 0.0000, -0.1000], [0.1000, 0.3000, 0.2000]], Whh = [[0.5000, -0.2000], [0.1000, 0.4000]], bh =
[0.0000, 0.1000], compute ht step by step. [4 marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Input contribution: Wxh xₜ = [0.3000, -0.1000]
Step 2 — Recurrent contribution: Whh hₜ₋₁ = [0.0900, -0.0700]
Step 3 — Combine and add bias: aₜ = [0.3000, -0.1000] + [0.0900, -0.0700] + [0.0000, 0.1000] = [0.3900,
-0.0700]
Step 4 — Apply tanh: hₜ = tanh([0.3900, -0.0700]) = [0.3714, -0.0699]

Q20. State the formula for the number of trainable parameters in a plain RNN with input size d and
hidden size h, and explain what each term counts. [3 marks]
Solution:
                     Total parameters = h×d (Wxh) + h×h (Whh) + h (bh) = h(d + h + 1)

     •    h×d counts the entries of Wxh, which maps the d-dimensional input to the h-dimensional hidden
          update.
     •    h×h counts the entries of Whh, which maps the previous h-dimensional hidden state to its
          contribution to the new hidden state.
     •    h counts the entries of the bias vector bh (one bias per hidden unit). Note: this counts only the
          recurrent layer; a separate output layer Why, by would add h×(output size) + (output size) more.

Q21. In Worked Examples 1, 3 and 4, the plain RNN, LSTM and GRU each processed the identical first
input x₁, yet produced three different values of h₁. Explain why, and identify which architecture's h₁
depends on x₁ alone versus which involve additional learned control. [3 marks]
Solution:
     •    Plain RNN: h₁ = tanh(Wxh x₁ + Whh h₀ + bh) is a direct, ungated transformation of x₁ (with h₀ = 0
          contributing nothing) — no learned gate decides how much of x₁ to accept.
     •    LSTM: h₁ = o₁ ⊙ tanh(C₁), where C₁ = i₁ ⊙ c̃₁ already involves the input gate i₁ deciding how much
          of the candidate c̃₁ to write in, and the output gate o₁ separately deciding how much of C₁ to
          expose — two extra learned filters between x₁ and h₁.
     •    GRU: h₁ = z₁ ⊙ h̃ ₁ (since h₀ = 0), where the update gate z₁ decides how much of the candidate to
          accept — one learned filter between x₁ and h₁.
     •    All three use the same raw input x₁, but the RNN applies no learned gating, while LSTM and GRU
          each pass the resulting candidate through one or more sigmoid gates before it becomes h₁ —
          with untrained (illustrative) weights these gates simply produce different numbers than the
          ungated RNN; after training, this gating is precisely what lets LSTM/GRU learn when to accept
          new information.

Q22. A plain RNN (input size 2, hidden size 2) has Wxh = [[0.3000, 0.1000], [-0.1000, 0.2000]], Whh =
[[0.2000, 0.1000], [0.0500, -0.3000]], bh = [0.0000, 0.0000]. Given h₀ = [0, 0], x₁ = [0.2000, 0.8000], x₂ =
[-0.4000, 0.6000], compute h₁ and h₂. [5 marks]
Solution:




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 33 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Step 1 — t = 1: a₁ = Wxh x₁ + Whh h₀ + bh = [0.1400, 0.1400] ⇒ h₁ = tanh([0.1400, 0.1400]) = [0.1391,
0.1391]
Step 2 — t = 2: a₂ = Wxh x₂ + Whh h₁ + bh = [-0.0183, 0.1252] ⇒ h₂ = tanh([-0.0183, 0.1252]) = [-0.0183,
0.1246]
     •    Note that both components of a₁ are equal (0.14, 0.14) purely because of the specific numbers
          chosen here — this is a coincidence of this question's data, not a general property of RNNs.

Q23. Give one real-world example each (different from those already used in these notes) of a many-
to-one and a many-to-many (aligned) RNN application, and justify why each fits its category. [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    Many-to-one: spam-email detection — the model reads a whole sequence of words (the email
          body) but only needs to output a single decision (spam / not spam) at the end.
     •    Many-to-many (aligned): named-entity recognition — the model must output a label (e.g. Person
          / Organisation / Other) for every word in the input sentence, so input length and output length
          match exactly, one output per input position.

Q24. Derive an expression for the Jacobian ∂ht/∂ht−1 of a plain RNN, and explain its role in BPTT. [4
marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Write the recurrence: hₜ = tanh(aₜ), where aₜ = Wxh xₜ + Whh hₜ₋₁ + bh
Step 2 — Differentiate aₜ with respect to hₜ₋₁: ∂aₜ/∂hₜ₋₁ = Whh (the only term in aₜ that depends on hₜ₋₁)
Step 3 — Apply the chain rule through tanh: ∂hₜ/∂hₜ₋₁ = diag(1 − hₜ²) · Whh
     •    Here diag(1−hₜ²) is a diagonal matrix of the elementwise tanh-derivative values.

Role in BPTT
This single-step Jacobian is exactly the factor that gets multiplied in, once per time step, when the
gradient is propagated backward from hₜ to hₜ₋₁ (Steps 5–6 of Worked Example 2). Its repeated
application — diag(1−h²)·Whh chained T times — is precisely the mechanism behind the
vanishing/exploding gradient problem of Section 2.7: if the dominant eigenvalue of this product has
magnitude < 1, gradients vanish; if > 1, they explode.

Q25. Explain why the tanh derivative being maximised at a = 0 is relevant to the vanishing gradient
problem. [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    1 − tanh²(a) reaches its maximum value of 1 exactly at a = 0, and falls toward 0 as |a| grows (tanh
          saturates near ±1).
     •    Since each backward step through tanh multiplies the gradient by this factor, the best possible
          case at any single step is a multiplier of exactly 1 (no shrinkage) — it can never exceed 1. In
          practice, hidden units are rarely sitting at exactly a = 0, so the realistic per-step factor is usually
          noticeably below 1, which compounds multiplicatively over many time steps into the vanishing
          gradient problem (Section 2.7, and Q4 of Part A).

Q26. A scalar (1-dimensional) RNN has Wxh = 0.5, Whh = 0.8, bh = 0.1, h₀ = 0. Inputs x₁ = 1, x₂ = 0.5. A
squared-error loss L = ½(h₂ − target)² is applied at t = 2 with target = 0.5. Compute ∂L/∂Whh. [6 marks]
Solution:


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                   Page 34 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Step 1 — Forward pass: a₁ = 0.5×1 + 0.8×0 + 0.1 = 0.6 ⇒ h₁ = tanh(0.6) = 0.537
a₂ = 0.5×0.5 + 0.8×0.537 + 0.1 = 0.7796 ⇒ h₂ = tanh(0.7796) = 0.6525

Step 2 — Loss and output gradient: L = ½(0.6525 − 0.5)² = 0.0116       ∂L/∂h₂ = h₂ − target = 0.1525
Step 3 — Backprop through tanh at t = 2: ∂L/∂a₂ = 0.1525 × (1 − 0.6525²) = 0.0876
Step 4 — Contribution to Whh from t = 2: ∂L/∂Whh|₂ = ∂L/∂a₂ × h₁ = 0.0876 × 0.537 = 0.047
Step 5 — Propagate back to t = 1, contribution to Whh from t = 1: ∂L/∂h₁ = ∂L/∂a₂ × Whh = 0.0701 ⇒
∂L/∂a₁ = 0.0499 ⇒ ∂L/∂Whh|₁ = ∂L/∂a₁ × h₀ = ∂L/∂a₁ × 0 = 0
Step 6 — Total: ∂L/∂Whh = 0 + 0.047 = 0.047

Q27. Explain the difference between the vanishing and exploding gradient problems in terms of the
quantity λ introduced in Section 2.7. [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    λ informally represents the typical magnitude of Whhᵀ combined with the local tanh-derivative
          factor, applied once per backward time step.
     •    If λ < 1, repeated multiplication across T steps produces λᵀ → 0 exponentially — the vanishing
          gradient problem; early time steps get almost no learning signal.
     •    If λ > 1, λᵀ grows exponentially — the exploding gradient problem; updates become huge and
          training destabilises. λ = 1 is the (unstable) knife-edge boundary between the two regimes.

Q28. If λ = 0.8, compute the relative gradient magnitude λᵏ after k = 5 and k = 15 backward steps, and
comment on the result. [3 marks]
Solution:
Step 1: λ⁵ = 0.8⁵ = 0.32768
Step 2: λ¹⁵ = 0.8¹⁵ = 0.035184
     •    Even with a fairly mild λ = 0.8 (each step keeps 80% of the gradient), only about 32.8% survives
          after 5 steps, and a mere 3.52% survives after 15 steps — illustrating how quickly the vanishing
          gradient problem bites even without an extreme per-step shrinkage factor.

Q29. List three standard mitigations for vanishing/exploding gradients in RNNs, and explain one of
them in detail. [3 marks]
Solution:
     •    Gradient clipping, careful (e.g. orthogonal) weight initialisation, truncated BPTT, and gated
          architectures (LSTM/GRU) are all standard mitigations (Section 2.7).
     •    Gradient clipping in detail: after computing the gradient for a batch, its norm ‖g‖ is compared
          against a threshold τ. If ‖g‖ > τ, the gradient is rescaled: g ← g × (τ/‖g‖), which preserves its
          direction but caps its magnitude. This is cheap to compute, requires no architecture change, and
          directly prevents the huge, destabilising updates caused by exploding gradients — though it does
          nothing to fix vanishing gradients.

Q30. Explain what truncated BPTT is and what trade-off it makes. [2 marks]
Solution:




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 35 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     •    Truncated BPTT limits how many time steps the gradient is backpropagated through (e.g. only
          the most recent 20 steps), instead of all the way back to t = 1, even for very long sequences.
     •    Trade-off: it makes training faster and more memory-efficient, and avoids some numerical
          instability from very long gradient chains, but it means the model cannot learn dependencies that
          span more time steps than the truncation window — a direct trade-off between training
          efficiency/stability and the ability to learn long-range structure.

Q31. In one line each, state the role of the forget gate, input gate, candidate, and output gate in an
LSTM cell. [4 marks]
Solution:
     •    Forget gate ft: decides what fraction of the old cell state Ct−1 to keep.
     •    Input gate it: decides how much of the new candidate content to write into the cell state.
     •    Candidate c̃t: proposes the new content itself (not a gate — uses tanh, not sigmoid).
     •    Output gate ot: decides how much of the (updated) cell state to expose as the hidden state ht.

Q32. Continuing Worked Example 2 (Section 2.6), compute ∂L/∂Wxh and ∂L/∂Why. [6 marks]
Solution:
     •    ∂L/∂Wxh follows exactly the same pattern as ∂L/∂Whh (Section 2.6, Steps 4–7), but each time-
          step's contribution is an outer product with xₜ instead of hₜ₋₁:
t = 3 contribution: ∂L/∂Wxh|₃ = ∂L/∂a₃ ⊗ x₃ = [-0.5266, 0.3922] ⊗ [-0.5000, 1.0000] = [[0.2633, -0.5266],
[-0.1961, 0.3922]]
t = 2 contribution: ∂L/∂Wxh|₂ = ∂L/∂a₂ ⊗ x₂ = [-0.0725, -0.0797] ⊗ [0.5000, -1.0000] = [[-0.0362,
0.0725], [-0.0399, 0.0797]]
t = 1 contribution: ∂L/∂Wxh|₁ = ∂L/∂a₁ ⊗ x₁ = [0.0072, -0.0484] ⊗ [1.0000, 0.5000] = [[0.0072, 0.0036],
[-0.0484, -0.0242]] (non-zero here, unlike ∂L/∂Whh|₁, because x₁ ≠ 0 even though h₀ = 0)
Total: ∂L/∂Wxh = [[0.0072, 0.0036], [-0.0484, -0.0242]] + [[-0.0362, 0.0725], [-0.0399, 0.0797]] +
[[0.2633, -0.5266], [-0.1961, 0.3922]] = [[0.2342, -0.4506], [-0.2844, 0.4478]]
     •    ∂L/∂Why only involves the single time step where the output was read out (t = 3), so there is no
          sum over time — it is a plain feedforward-layer gradient:
∂L/∂Why = ∂L/∂y₃ ⊗ h₃ = [-1.1790, 0.0788] ⊗ [-0.4885, -0.0470] = [[0.5759, 0.0554], [-0.0385, -0.0037]]

Q33. A scalar LSTM cell (input size 1, hidden size 1) has h₀ = 0, C₀ = 0, x₁ = 1.0, with weights (applied to z
= [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 1]): Wf = [0.5, 0.2], bf = 0; Wi = [0.3, −0.1], bi = 0.1; Wc = [0.6, 0.4], bc = 0; Wo = [0.2,
0.5], bo = 0.1. Compute f₁, i₁, c̃₁, C₁, o₁, h₁. [6 marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Forget gate: f₁ = σ(0.5×0 + 0.2×1 + 0) = σ(0.2) = 0.5498
Step 2 — Input gate: i₁ = σ(0.3×0 + (−0.1)×1 + 0.1) = σ(0.0) = 0.5
Step 3 — Candidate: c̃₁ = tanh(0.6×0 + 0.4×1 + 0) = tanh(0.4) = 0.3799
Step 4 — Cell state (C₀ = 0, so the forget term vanishes): C₁ = 0.5498×0 + 0.5×0.3799 = 0.19
Step 5 — Output gate: o₁ = σ(0.2×0 + 0.5×1 + 0.1) = σ(0.6) = 0.6457
Step 6 — Hidden state: h₁ = o₁ × tanh(C₁) = 0.6457 × tanh(0.19) = 0.1212


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                  Page 36 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                         Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Q34. Explain, using the forget-gate mechanism, why an LSTM can in principle remember information
for 100+ time steps, while a plain RNN struggles to. [3 marks]
Solution:
     •    If the forget gate learns a value close to 1 for a particular memory component, that component
          of the cell state is carried forward with almost no attenuation at every step: Ct = 1 × Ct−1 +
          (small/zero new term) ≈ Ct−1.
     •    Because this update is additive and element-wise (Section 3.5), the corresponding backward
          gradient ∂Ct/∂Ct−1 = ft ≈ 1 as well — so information (and its gradient) can survive many steps
          unchanged, in principle indefinitely.
     •    A plain RNN has no such mechanism: its hidden state is fully overwritten by tanh(…) at every step,
          and the corresponding gradient is repeatedly multiplied by Whhᵀ and a tanh-derivative < 1, which
          compounds toward zero (Section 2.7) — there is no learned way to “protect” a piece of
          information from this decay.

Q35. Compute the number of trainable parameters in an LSTM layer with input size d = 50 and hidden
size h = 32. [2 marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Recall the formula: Parameters = 4 × h(d + h + 1) (Section 6.2)
Step 2 — Substitute: = 4 × 32 × (50 + 32 + 1) = 4 × 32 × 83 = 10,624

Q36. Why does LSTM keep the output gate separate from the cell-state update, instead of always
outputting the full cell state as the hidden state? [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    Decoupling means the cell can continue to store information in Ct (for possible future use)
          without being forced to expose that information in ht right now.
     •    This is useful when a piece of context is relevant for a later prediction but irrelevant to the
          immediate output — e.g. remembering the subject of a sentence while the immediate output
          should focus on a verb; the output gate lets the network learn when to reveal vs. withhold each
          memory component (Section 3.2).

Q37. If a particular LSTM memory unit has a forget gate consistently equal to 0.99 and an input gate of
0 (no new writes) for 100 consecutive steps, what fraction of the original value in that memory unit
remains? [2 marks]
Solution:
With it = 0, the update reduces to Ct = ft × Ct−1 at every step, so after 100 steps: C₁₀₀ = (0.99)¹⁰⁰ × C₀ =
0.366 × C₀.
     •    About 36.6% of the original value survives — a forget gate very close to 1 is needed to preserve
          information over long spans; even f = 0.99 loses almost two-thirds of the signal over 100 steps,
          showing why training must push ft very close to 1 for genuinely long-range memories.

Q38. What would happen, structurally, if the forget gate were removed and ft were fixed at 1 for every
unit at every step? [2 marks]
Solution:




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                Page 37 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                            Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     •    The cell-state update would become Ct = Ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t — memory would only ever accumulate
          and could never be cleared or overwritten, since old content is never actively erased.
     •    This can cause the cell state to grow without bound over long sequences (in the worst case), and
          prevents the network from ever “resetting” its memory when the context genuinely changes (e.g.
          at a sentence boundary). This is essentially why the forget gate was added to the original LSTM
          design — without it, the earliest LSTM variant could exhibit unbounded cell-state growth on long
          sequences.

Q39. In one line each, state the role of the reset gate and the update gate in a GRU cell. [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    Reset gate rt: decides how much of the previous hidden state to use when computing the new
          candidate content h̃ t.
     •    Update gate zt: decides the blend ratio between keeping the old hidden state and adopting the
          new candidate, ht = (1−zt)⊙ht−1 + zt⊙h̃ t.

Q40. A scalar GRU cell (input size 1, hidden size 1) has h₀ = 0, x₁ = 1.0, with (applied to [h₀ ; x₁] = [0, 1]):
Wz = [0.4, 0.1], bz = 0; Wr = [0.2, 0.3], br = 0.1; Wh = [0.5, −0.2], bh = 0.05. Compute z₁, r₁, h̃ ₁, and h₁. [5
marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Update gate: z₁ = σ(0.4×0 + 0.1×1 + 0) = σ(0.1) = 0.525
Step 2 — Reset gate: r₁ = σ(0.2×0 + 0.3×1 + 0.1) = σ(0.4) = 0.5987
Step 3 — Apply reset gate to h₀ (which is already 0, so this has no numeric effect here): r₁ ⊙ h₀ = 0.5987
×0=0
Step 4 — Candidate hidden state: h̃ ₁ = tanh(0.5×0 + (−0.2)×1 + 0.05) = tanh(−0.15) = -0.1489
Step 5 — Final blend: h₁ = (1 − 0.525)×0 + 0.525×(-0.1489) = -0.0782

Q41. Why does GRU not maintain a separate cell state, and what is the practical trade-off of this design
choice? [2 marks]
Solution:
     •    GRU's designers merged the memory and the exposed hidden state into a single vector, relying
          on the update gate alone to control how much of that single vector changes at each step — there
          is no second, separately-protected “conveyor belt” as in LSTM (Section 4.1–4.2).
     •    Trade-off: fewer parameters and a simpler cell (faster to train, Section 6), at the cost of slightly
          less representational flexibility — GRU cannot store a value in “private” memory while showing
          something different at the output, the way LSTM's output gate allows.

Q42. Compute the number of trainable parameters in a GRU layer with input size d = 64 and hidden
size h = 48. [2 marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Recall the formula: Parameters = 3 × h(d + h + 1) (Section 6.2)
Step 2 — Substitute: = 3 × 48 × (64 + 48 + 1) = 3 × 48 × 113 = 16,272




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                   Page 38 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Q43. What does the GRU update reduce to when zt = 0 for all dimensions? What about when zt = 1? [2
marks]
Solution:
     •    zt = 0: ht = 1×ht−1 + 0×h̃ t = ht−1 — the hidden state is left completely unchanged; the new
          candidate is entirely ignored.
     •    zt = 1: ht = 0×ht−1 + 1×h̃ t = h̃ t — the old state is completely discarded and replaced by the new
          candidate.
     •    In practice zt learns intermediate values, blending the two continuously depending on the input.

Q44. Give an intuitive example of when a GRU's reset gate would be useful with a value close to 0. [2
marks]
Solution:
     •    Consider a document that is a list of unrelated short product reviews concatenated together. At
          the start of a new review, the content of the previous review is no longer relevant context for
          interpreting the new one.
     •    A reset gate close to 0 at that boundary lets the candidate h̃ t be computed almost entirely from
          the current input (ignoring the stale ht−1), effectively letting the network “start fresh” without
          needing to wait for the update gate to slowly overwrite the old state (Section 4.3).

Q45. Write the chain-rule factorisation of P(w₁, …, wᵀ) used by a language model, and explain in words
what each factor represents. [3 marks]
Solution:
                          P(w₁, …, wᵀ) = P(w₁) · P(w₂|w₁) · P(w₃|w₁,w₂) · ⋯ · P(wᵀ|w₁,…,wᵀ₋₁)

     •    This is simply the probability chain rule applied to a sequence: the joint probability of the whole
          sequence equals the product of each word's probability conditioned on every word before it.
     •    An RNN language model approximates every conditional factor P(wₜ | w₁,…,wₜ₋₁) with a single
          softmax output at step t, whose entire dependence on the (arbitrarily long) history w₁,…,wₜ₋₁ is
          compressed into the fixed-size hidden state hₜ₋₁ (Section 5.1–5.2).

Q46. A language model with vocabulary size 5 produces logits = [1.2000, 0.5000, -0.3000, 2.0000,
0.1000] at some time step. The true next word has index 3 (0-indexed). Compute the softmax
probabilities and the cross-entropy loss. [5 marks]
Solution:
Step 1 — Exponentiate each logit: exp([1.2000, 0.5000, -0.3000, 2.0000, 0.1000]) — compute e^1.2,
e^0.5, e^−0.3, e^2.0, e^0.1
Step 2 — Normalise (divide by the sum) to get softmax probabilities: P = [0.2337, 0.1161, 0.0522,
0.5202, 0.0778]
Step 3 — Cross-entropy loss uses only the probability assigned to the true index (3): L = − log P[3] = −
log(0.5202) = 0.6535
     •    Notice index 3 also has the largest logit (2.0) and correspondingly the largest probability (≈ 0.52)
          — since this is also the target, the loss is relatively small, reflecting a fairly confident, correct
          prediction.




Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                                     Page 39 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



Q47. A language model achieves an average cross-entropy loss of 2.3 nats per word on a test set.
Compute its perplexity. [2 marks]
Solution:
Perplexity = exp(average loss) = exp(2.3) = 9.9742
     •    A perplexity of ≈ 10 means the model's uncertainty at each step is comparable to choosing
          uniformly among about 10 equally likely words, regardless of how large the true vocabulary is.

Q48. Explain teacher forcing and describe one problem it can cause at inference (generation) time. [3
marks]
Solution:
     •    Teacher forcing: during training, the model is always fed the true previous word as input at each
          step, regardless of what the model itself would have predicted (Section 5.6).
     •    Problem — exposure bias: at generation time there is no ground truth to feed back in, so the
          model must feed in its own (possibly imperfect) previous prediction. Since the model never
          practised recovering from its own mistakes during training, small errors can compound as
          generation proceeds, leading to increasingly poor output quality — a mismatch between the
          training and inference conditions.

Q49. Give one application example each for plain RNN, LSTM, and GRU, and briefly justify each choice.
[3 marks]
Solution:
     •    Plain RNN: a short, fixed-pattern signal classifier (e.g. detecting a simple gesture from a few
          dozen accelerometer readings) — the sequences are short enough that vanishing gradients are
          not a serious concern, so the simplicity and speed of a plain RNN is an acceptable trade-off.
     •    LSTM: long-document sentiment analysis or long-range time-series forecasting (e.g. multi-week
          demand forecasting) — the long-range memory and fine-grained gating are worth the extra
          parameters when dependencies span long distances.
     •    GRU: on-device / mobile keyboard next-word prediction — a tight compute and memory budget
          favours GRU's roughly 25% parameter saving over LSTM, while still comfortably outperforming a
          plain RNN.

Q50. Summarise, in a short set of bullet points, the historical progression from RNN → LSTM → GRU →
Transformer, giving the main motivation behind each step. [4 marks]
Solution:
     •    RNN: introduced parameter sharing across time via a recurrent hidden state, solving the fixed-
          input-size and no-memory problems of feedforward networks (Section 1–2).
     •    → LSTM: added gated, additive memory (the cell state) specifically to fix the vanishing gradient
          problem that crippled plain RNNs on long sequences (Section 2.7 → Section 3).
     •    → GRU: simplified LSTM's gating (2 gates instead of 3, no separate cell state) to reduce
          parameters and training cost while keeping most of the long-range-memory benefit (Section 4).
     •    → Transformer (beyond this unit): replaced recurrence entirely with self-attention, allowing
          every position to directly attend to every other position. This removes the sequential step-by-
          step bottleneck (enabling full parallelisation across time during training) and provides a more
          direct path for gradients/information between distant positions than even LSTM/GRU can offer.


Dr. Manoj Kumar Sharma — Manipal University Jaipur                                               Page 40 of 41
CCE3144 – Deep Learning                                                        Unit: Recurrent Neural Networks



     •    Each step's motivation was the same underlying goal: let information from arbitrarily far back in
          a sequence influence the current prediction, as efficiently as possible.

1. Introduction to Deep Unsupervised Learning

1.1 What is Unsupervised Learning?
  ● Learning from data x that has no labels y — only the inputs are given, no “correct answer” is
    supplied.
  ● Goal: discover hidden structure, patterns, or the underlying probability distribution p(x) that
    generated the data.
  ● Classical examples: k-means clustering, PCA, hierarchical clustering — these use shallow, hand-
    designed feature spaces.
  ● Contrast with supervised learning: no loss like cross-entropy against a ground-truth label; the
    “supervision” instead comes from the data itself (e.g. reconstruct the input, distinguish real vs.
    fake, model the data density).

1.2 Why “Deep” Unsupervised Learning?
  ● Classical methods (PCA, k-means) can only capture linear / shallow structure.
  ● Real data (images, speech, text) lies on complex, non-linear low-dimensional manifolds inside a
    high-dimensional space.
  ● Deep neural networks, stacked in multiple layers, learn a hierarchy of features — simple patterns
    in early layers combine into abstract concepts in later layers — exactly what is needed to model
    such manifolds.
  ● This hierarchy is learned automatically from unlabelled data, which is abundant, instead of
    requiring expensive manual labelling.

1.3 Why do we care? (Applications)
  ● Representation / feature learning for downstream supervised tasks (pre-training).
  ● Data generation — synthesizing realistic images, audio, text (GANs, VAEs).
  ● Dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection (autoencoders).
  ● Density estimation — learning p(x) explicitly to compute likelihoods, detect outliers (RBM, DBN,
    DBM).
  ● Data compression and efficient coding (autoencoders, RBMs).

1.4 Roadmap: The Model Families in this Unit




                                     Page 3 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                   Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning




          Fig. 1.1 — The deep unsupervised learning models covered in this unit, grouped by how they learn p(x).


  Key idea that unifies this whole unit
     ● Every model in this unit answers the same question differently: “How do I learn a good model
       of p(x) using only unlabelled data?”
     ● Autoencoder / VAE: learn by compressing and reconstructing x through a bottleneck.
     ● GAN: learn by playing a two-player minimax game between a generator and a discriminator.
     ● Maximum Entropy: choose the least-biased distribution consistent with known constraints —
       the theoretical justification behind many of these models.
     ● RBM / DBN / DBM / ConvBM: define an energy function over (visible, hidden) units and learn
       its parameters so that observed data has low energy (high probability).

2. Autoencoders

2.1 Concept and Motivation
  ● An autoencoder is a neural network trained to copy its input to its output, through a narrow
    bottleneck.
  ● Because it is forced through a bottleneck, it cannot just memorise — it must learn a compressed,
    useful representation of the data.
  ● It is trained with no labels — the “label” for input x is x itself. This is called self-supervised learning.
  ● Two parts, trained jointly, end-to-end, by gradient descent:
        ◦ Encoder f: maps input x to a latent code z (compression)
        ◦ Decoder g: maps the code z back to a reconstruction x̂ (decompression)

2.2 Architecture




              Fig. 2.1 — Autoencoder: input is compressed to a low-dimensional code z, then reconstructed.


2.3 Mathematical Formulation
For input x ∈ ℝⁿ:

                                        Encoder:        z = f(x) = σ(Wx + b)

                                       Decoder:        x̂ = g(z) = σ(W′z + b′)

where σ is a non-linear activation (sigmoid / ReLU / tanh), and W, b, W′, b′ are learned weights and
biases.

Training minimises the reconstruction loss between x and x̂, most commonly Mean Squared Error:

                                          L(x, x̂) = (1) / (n) Σi=1n (xi − x̂i)2

                                          Page 5 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                  Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

  ● Significance: minimising this loss is exactly what forces the bottleneck to keep only the most
    important information needed to reconstruct x — unimportant/noisy variation is discarded.


✎ Worked Example 2.1 — Forward Pass Through a Small Autoencoder
Given input x = [0.8, 0.3] (n = 2), a 1-unit bottleneck, sigmoid activation, encoder weights W = [0.5, −0.3],
bias b = 0.1, decoder weights W′ = [0.6, 0.4]ᵀ, bias b′ = [0, 0]. Find the reconstruction and the loss.

  ● Step 1 — Encoder pre-activation (weighted sum of inputs). This is the encoder deciding how much
    each input contributes to the compressed code:

                        z_pre = (0.5)(0.8) + (−0.3)(0.3) + 0.1 = 0.40 − 0.09 + 0.10 = 0.41

  ● Step 2 — Apply activation. The sigmoid squashes the code into (0,1) and adds the non-linearity that
    lets the network represent more than a linear projection (unlike PCA):

                                       z = σ(0.41) = 1 / (1 + e−0.41) = 0.6011

  ● Step 3 — Decoder pre-activations. The single code value z is expanded back out to 2 numbers, one
    per output unit:

                        x̂1,pre = (0.6)(0.6011) = 0.3606,       x̂2,pre = (0.4)(0.6011) = 0.2404

  ● Step 4 — Apply activation to get the reconstruction:

                                 x̂ = [σ(0.3606), σ(0.2404)] = [0.5892, 0.5598]

  ● Step 5 — Reconstruction loss (MSE). This single number is the training signal — backpropagation
    adjusts W, b, W′, b′ to reduce it:

            L = (1) / (2)[(0.8 − 0.5892)2 + (0.3 − 0.5598)2] = (1) / (2)[0.0444 + 0.0675] = 0.0560



  ℹ Interpretation: the code z = 0.6011 is a single number that had to summarise both 0.8 and 0.3. The
  loss (0.056) tells us how much information was lost in that compression — with only 1 bottleneck
  unit for 2 inputs, some loss is expected.

Sparse Autoencoder — the sparsity penalty
Let ρ be the desired (small) target sparsity, e.g. 0.05, and ρ̂ⱼ the average activation of hidden unit j over
the training batch. The sparsity penalty for unit j is the KL-divergence between two Bernoulli
distributions:

                              KL(ρ ‖ ρ̂j) = ρ log((ρ) / (ρ̂j)) + (1−ρ) log((1−ρ) / (1−ρ̂j))


✎ Worked Example 2.2 — Sparsity Penalty Computation
Given target sparsity ρ = 0.05 and observed average activation ρ̂ = 0.20, find the KL penalty (natural log).

  ● Step 1 — First term (penalises unit being “on” too often relative to target):

                        0.05 × ln(0.05/0.20) = 0.05 × ln(0.25) = 0.05 × (−1.3863) = −0.0693

  ● Step 2 — Second term (penalises the “off” probability mismatch):

                        0.95 × ln(0.95/0.80) = 0.95 × ln(1.1875) = 0.95 × 0.1718 = 0.1632

  ● Step 3 — Sum:

                                KL(0.05 ‖ 0.20) = −0.0693 + 0.1632 = 0.0939 nats

ℹ Since ρ̂ (0.20) is far above the target ρ (0.05), the penalty is clearly positive; it would be exactly 0 if ρ̂ =
ρ, and gradient descent pushes ρ̂ back toward ρ, i.e. towards a sparser (mostly-off) hidden layer.



2.5 Applications
  ● Dimensionality reduction (a non-linear generalisation of PCA).
  ● Image denoising and inpainting.
  ● Anomaly / fraud detection (anomalies have high reconstruction error).
  ● Pre-training deep networks layer-by-layer before supervised fine-tuning.
  ● Learned code z used as a compact feature vector for retrieval, clustering, or as input to another
    model (e.g. the encoder of a VAE, Section 3).

3. Variational Autoencoders (VAE)

3.1 Motivation: Why Not Just Use a Plain Autoencoder?
  ● A plain autoencoder's latent space has no structure — codes for real inputs may be scattered in
    isolated clusters with large empty gaps between them.
  ● If we pick a random point z in that space and decode it, the result is usually garbage — so plain
    autoencoders are poor generative models.
  ● VAE fixes this by treating the code as random, not deterministic: it forces the distribution of z (for
    all the data) to look like a simple, known prior, typically N(0, I).
  ● Because the whole latent space is now “filled in” and shaped like a Gaussian, any z sampled from
    N(0, I) decodes into something realistic — VAE can generate new data.

3.2 Probabilistic Formulation
  ● Assume data is generated as: sample a latent z ∼ p(z) = N(0, I), then sample x ∼ pθ(x|z) (the
    decoder).
  ● We want the true posterior p(z|x), but it is intractable, so we approximate it with an encoder
    network qφ(z|x) — this is why the method is called “variational” (variational = approximate-
    inference).
  ● qφ(z|x) is chosen to be Gaussian: qφ(z|x) = N( μ(x), σ²(x) ), with μ(x) and σ(x) output by the encoder
    network.

3.3 Architecture




    Fig. 3.1 — VAE: encoder outputs a distribution (μ, σ), a sample z is drawn via the reparameterization trick, decoder
                                                       reconstructs x.


3.4 The Reparameterization Trick
  ● Problem: we need to backpropagate through the sampling step z ~ N(μ, σ²), but sampling is a
    random, non-differentiable operation.

                                           Page 8 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

  ● Trick: rewrite the random sample as a deterministic function of μ, σ and an independent noise
    source ε:

                                      z = μ + σ ⊙ ε,            ε ∼ N(0, I)

  ● Now the randomness (ε) is external to the network, and z is a differentiable function of μ and σ —
    gradients can flow from the reconstruction loss, through z, back into the encoder’s μ and σ outputs,
    and hence into all encoder weights.

3.5 Deriving the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)
We cannot maximise log p(x) directly (it needs the intractable integral over z), so we derive a tractable
lower bound on it, step by step:

Step 1 — Introduce the latent variable by marginalisation:

                                         log p(x) = log ∫ p(x, z) dz

Step 2 — Multiply and divide by qφ(z|x) (valid since qφ(z|x) > 0). This turns the integral into an
expectation under q:

                                   log p(x) = log Eq[ p(x,z) / qφ(z|x) ]

Step 3 — Apply Jensen's Inequality. Because log(·) is concave, log(E[X]) ≥ E[log(X)]:

                           log p(x) ≥ Eq[ log p(x,z) − log qφ(z|x) ] ≡ ELBO

  ● Significance: this step is what makes the objective tractable — we now have a lower bound we CAN
    compute and maximise, instead of the exact log p(x) which we cannot.
Step 4 — Factor p(x,z) = p(x|z)·p(z) and split the expectation into two interpretable terms:

                           ELBO = Eq[ log pθ(x|z) ]         −    KL( qφ(z|x) ‖ p(z) )

  ● Reconstruction term E[log pθ(x|z)]: how well the decoder reconstructs x from a sampled z — pulls
    z toward encoding useful information.
  ● Regularisation term KL(qφ(z|x)‖p(z)): keeps the encoder's distribution close to the prior N(0,I) —
    keeps the latent space smooth and generative.

  Final VAE training objective (minimised)
  Since we minimise a loss rather than maximise the ELBO, we flip the sign:

                              LVAE = − Eq[ log pθ(x|z) ] + KL( qφ(z|x) ‖ p(z) )

                              ≡ Reconstruction Loss + KL Divergence Loss

For a Gaussian encoder qφ(z|x)=N(μ,σ²) and prior N(0,1), the KL term has a convenient closed form (per
latent dimension):

                          KL( N(μ,σ²) ‖ N(0,1) ) = (1) / (2)( μ2 + σ2 − ln(σ2) − 1 )


✎ Worked Example 3.1 — Reparameterization and KL Divergence
The encoder, for a given x, outputs μ = 0.3, σ = 0.5. A noise sample ε = 1.0 is drawn from N(0,1). Find (a)
the sampled latent z, and (b) the KL-divergence loss term.

                                      Page 9 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                              Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

  ● Step 1 — Reparameterization trick (this IS the sampling step, made differentiable):

                                      z = μ + σ·ε = 0.3 + (0.5)(1.0) = 0.8

  ● Step 2 — Compute σ² and ln(σ²) needed for the KL formula:

                                       σ2 = 0.25,      ln(0.25) = −1.3863

  ● Step 3 — Substitute into the closed-form KL expression:

                    KL = (1) / (2)(0.09 + 0.25 − (−1.3863) − 1) = (1) / (2)(0.7263) = 0.3632



  ℹ Interpretation: z = 0.8 is the actual latent value passed to the decoder this iteration. KL = 0.363 nats
  is the “cost” charged for this encoder distribution N(0.3, 0.25) being different from the prior N(0,1)
  — training pushes μ toward 0 and σ toward 1 unless the reconstruction term needs otherwise.



3.6 Applications
  ● Generating new, realistic samples (faces, digits, molecules) by decoding z ~ N(0,I).
  ● Smooth latent-space interpolation between two data points.
  ● Semi-supervised learning and anomaly detection using the likelihood/ELBO as a score.
  ● Representation learning where a smooth, disentangled latent space matters (unlike plain AE).

4. Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN)

4.1 Concept: A Two-Player Game
  ● GAN trains two networks that compete against each other:
        ◦ Generator G: takes random noise z ~ p(z) and tries to produce fake samples G(z) that look real.
        ◦ Discriminator D: takes a sample (real or fake) and outputs the probability that it is real.
  ● G is trained to fool D; D is trained to catch G. Neither ever sees labelled data — the “supervision”
    comes entirely from this competition, so training is unsupervised at the data level.
  ● Unlike VAE, GAN has no explicit reconstruction loss and no explicit density p(x) — it learns to
    sample from p(x) implicitly.

4.2 Architecture




  Fig. 4.1 — GAN: Generator produces fakes from noise; Discriminator scores real vs. fake; gradients flow back to train
                                                        both.


4.3 The Minimax Objective
                        minG maxD V(D,G) = Ex~pdata[ log D(x) ] + Ez~pz[ log(1 − D(G(z))) ]

  ● D wants to maximise V: push D(x) → 1 for real x, and D(G(z)) → 0 for fakes.
  ● G wants to minimise V: push D(G(z)) → 1, i.e. make the discriminator think fakes are real.
  ● Training alternates: a few steps of gradient ascent on D (with G fixed), then a step of gradient
    descent on G (with D fixed).

Deriving the Optimal Discriminator D*(x)
For a fixed generator G (hence a fixed generator distribution pᵍ), find the D that maximises V:

Step 1 — Rewrite the second expectation as an integral over x using x = G(z):

                               V(D,G) = ∫x [ pdata(x) log D(x) + pg(x) log(1−D(x)) ] dx

                                          Page 11 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                             Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

Step 2 — For each fixed x this is a scalar function of y = D(x) alone: f(y) = a·log y + b·log(1−y), with a =
p_data(x), b = p_g(x). Maximise using df/dy = 0:

                          a/y − b/(1−y) = 0 ⇒ a(1−y) = by ⇒ y = a /(a+b)

Step 3 — Substitute back a, b:



                                    D*(x) = pdata(x) / ( pdata(x) + pg(x) )

  ● Significance: at the Nash equilibrium the generator matches the data exactly, pᵍ = p_data, so D*(x)
    = 1/2 everywhere — the best possible discriminator can do no better than a coin flip. This is the
    theoretical training target for a GAN.


✎ Worked Example 4.1 — Discriminator and Generator Loss
For one real sample, D(x) = 0.7; for one fake sample, D(G(z)) = 0.4. Compute the discriminator loss and
the (non-saturating) generator loss.

  ● Step 1 — Discriminator loss (negative of what D maximises — D wants this LOW):

                         LD = −[ log D(x) + log(1−D(G(z))) ] = −[ ln(0.7) + ln(0.6) ]

                                   = −[ (−0.3567) + (−0.5108) ] = 0.8675

  ● Step 2 — Generator loss, non-saturating form (used in practice — G wants this LOW):

                                   LG = − log D(G(z)) = − ln(0.4) = 0.9163



  ℹ Interpretation: D(G(z)) = 0.4 means D is already leaning toward “fake” but not fully certain — both
  losses are moderate, meaning both networks still have learning signal to improve.



4.4 Training Challenges

(a) Vanishing Gradients — Why the Non-Saturating Loss is Used
  ● Original minimax loss for G is log(1 − D(G(z))), minimised by G.
  ● Early in training, G is poor, so D confidently rejects fakes: D(G(z)) is small (say 0.2).
Compare the gradient magnitude of the two loss formulations with respect to s = D(G(z)) at s = 0.2:

                          Original: d/ds [log(1−s)] = −1/(1−s) = −1/0.8 = −1.25

                          Non-saturating: d/ds [−log s] = −1/s = −1/0.2 = −5.00

  ● The non-saturating gradient (5.00) is 4× larger in magnitude exactly when G is performing badly —
    it gives a much stronger learning signal precisely when G needs it most.
  ● This is why in practice G is trained to maximise log D(G(z)) (equivalently minimise −log D(G(z)))
    instead of minimising log(1−D(G(z))).


                                      Page 12 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

(b) Mode Collapse
  ● G discovers a few outputs that reliably fool D, and collapses to producing only those — losing the
    diversity of p_data.
  ● Symptom: generated samples look realistic individually but are highly repetitive.
  ● Remedies: mini-batch discrimination, unrolled GANs, Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) with gradient
    penalty, feature matching.

(c) Training Instability
  ● Because it is a minimax game (not a single loss being minimised), training can oscillate rather than
    converge.
  ● Remedies: careful learning-rate balance between G and D, spectral normalisation, WGAN loss (uses
    Wasserstein/Earth-Mover distance, which gives smoother gradients than the original JS-
    divergence-based loss).

4.5 Notable GAN Variants (brief overview)
  ● DCGAN: uses convolutional layers for stable image generation.
  ● Conditional GAN (cGAN): both G and D are additionally conditioned on a class label y.
  ● CycleGAN: unpaired image-to-image translation using a cycle-consistency loss.
  ● WGAN: replaces the JS-divergence objective with the Wasserstein distance for more stable
    gradients.

4.6 Applications
  ● Photorealistic image synthesis, super-resolution, image-to-image translation.
  ● Data augmentation for downstream supervised tasks.
  ● Deepfake / style-transfer / art-generation systems.

5. Maximum Entropy Distributions

5.1 Entropy — A Recap
  ● Entropy measures the uncertainty / unpredictability of a random variable X with distribution p.
  ● Discrete case:

                                          H(p) = −Σx p(x) log p(x)

  ● High entropy = very unpredictable (close to uniform); low entropy = predictable (probability mass
    concentrated on few outcomes).
  ● Base of the log sets the unit: base-2 → bits, base-e → nats.

5.2 The Maximum Entropy Principle
  ● Stated by E.T. Jaynes (1957): given only partial information about a distribution (some constraints,
    e.g. its mean), choose the distribution that has maximum entropy while satisfying those constraints.
  ● Why? The max-entropy distribution is the “most honest” / least biased choice — it assumes
    nothing beyond what is actually known. Any other distribution satisfying the same constraints
    implicitly encodes extra, unjustified assumptions.
  ● This turns distribution selection into a constrained optimisation problem, solved using Lagrange
    multipliers.

5.3 Derivation 1 — No Constraints ⇒ Uniform Distribution
For a discrete variable with n outcomes, maximise H(p) subject only to normalisation Σ pᵢ = 1.

Step 1 — Form the Lagrangian:

                                         ℒ = −Σi pi ln pi + λ(Σi pi − 1)

Step 2 — Differentiate w.r.t. each pᵢ and set to 0:

                              ∂ℒ/∂pi = −ln pi − 1 + λ = 0 ⇒ ln pi = λ − 1

Step 3 — Since the right side has no i in it, every pᵢ must be the SAME constant c:

                                         pi = eλ−1 = c (same for all i)

Step 4 — Apply normalisation to solve for c:



               n·c = 1 ⇒ c = 1/n     ⇒      pi = 1/n for every i (the UNIFORM distribution)

  ● Significance: with no information at all except that probabilities sum to 1, spreading probability
    equally is the least-biased choice — confirms intuition.

5.4 Derivation 2 — Mean & Variance Known ⇒ Gaussian Distribution



                                     Page 14 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                                Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

For a continuous variable, maximise H[p] = −∫ p(x) ln p(x) dx subject to three constraints: normalisation, a
fixed mean μ, and a fixed variance σ².

Step 1 — Lagrangian with one multiplier per constraint:

                        ℒ = −∫ p ln p dx + λ0(∫p dx−1) + λ1(∫xp dx−μ) + λ2(∫(x−μ)2p dx−σ2)

Step 2 — Take the functional derivative w.r.t. p(x) and set to 0:

                                       −ln p(x) − 1 + λ0 + λ1x + λ2(x−μ)2 = 0

Step 3 — Solve for p(x) — note this is already an exponential-family form:

                                        p(x) = exp( λ0−1 + λ1x + λ2(x−μ)2 )

Step 4 — Fixing λ₁ = 0 (required by the mean constraint being centred at μ) and identifying λ₂ =
−1/(2σ²) from the variance constraint, then fixing the remaining constant from normalisation, gives:



      p(x) = (1) / (√(2πσ2)) exp( −(x−μ)2 / 2σ2 )         —      the Normal / Gaussian distribution N(μ,σ²)

  ● Significance: this is exactly why the Gaussian appears everywhere — it is provably the least-
    assumption distribution whenever we only know (or only want to assume) the mean and variance
    of a variable. This is the formal justification behind e.g. using Gaussian priors/noise models
    throughout deep learning (including the VAE prior p(z)=N(0,I) in Section 3).


✎ Worked Example 5.1 — Entropy of a Discrete Distribution
Compare the entropy of p = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2] with the entropy of the uniform distribution over the same 3
outcomes (log base 2, i.e. bits).

  ● Step 1 — Compute each −pᵢ log₂ pᵢ term:

                −(0.5)log2(0.5) = 0.5000, −(0.3)log2(0.3) = 0.5211, −(0.2)log2(0.2) = 0.4644

  ● Step 2 — Sum for H(p):

                                H(p) = 0.5000 + 0.5211 + 0.4644 = 1.4855 bits

  ● Step 3 — Entropy of the uniform distribution over 3 outcomes, for comparison:

                                       H(uniform) = log2(3) = 1.5850 bits



  ℹ Interpretation: H(p) = 1.4855 < H(uniform) = 1.5850. This numerically confirms Derivation 1: among
  all distributions over 3 outcomes, the uniform distribution has the strictly highest entropy — any
  deviation from uniform (like favouring 0.5 for one outcome) reduces entropy.



5.5 Relevance to Deep Learning



                                         Page 15 of 47 | Manipal University Jaipur
CCE3144 Deep Learning                                                           Unit: Deep Unsupervised Learning

  ● Softmax: the softmax output of a classifier is precisely the maximum-entropy distribution over class
    labels, subject to matching the expected value of the network's logits — softmax is not an arbitrary
    choice, it is the least-biased one given those constraints.
  ● Boltzmann / Gibbs distribution: the form p(v,h) ∝ exp(−E(v,h)) used by every model in the rest of
    this unit (RBM, DBN, DBM, ConvBM) is exactly the maximum-entropy distribution subject to a
    constraint on the expected energy ⟨E⟩ — this is the theoretical bridge from this section into
    Sections 6–8.
  ● Regularisers such as entropy bonuses (e.g. in reinforcement learning policies) directly use H(p) to
    keep a learned distribution from collapsing prematurely.
